sources.title: Communicate with Mastery
sources.subtitle: Speak With Conviction and Write for Impact
sources.edition: 1st edition, January 2020 (hardcover; ebook editions also issued). Foreword by Joel Peterson. Title page reads 'How to Speak with Conviction and Write for Impact'; Wiley's product page omits 'How to'. Wiley lists 240 pages (front matter to p. xix, text and index to p. 211).
sources.author_credibility: JD Schramm (EdD) founded the Mastery in Communication Initiative at Stanford Graduate School of Business, where Wiley's author note says he served as lecturer in Organizational Behavior from 2007; he co-founded Stanford's LOWKeynotes talk program and has since taught at NYU Stern and USC Annenberg and coaches executives and speakers. Kara Levy (credited 'with Kara Levy') is an executive communication and leadership coach with a Columbia MFA in fiction who coached at Stanford GSB. Joel Peterson (Stanford GSB lecturer, former JetBlue chair) wrote the foreword and is not a co-author. The book is practitioner and teaching based: Schramm openly borrows several frameworks (AIM from Russell and Munter, the sparkline from Nancy Duarte, the pitch structure from Chris Lipp, Radical Candor from Kim Scott) and draws mostly on classroom and coaching cases rather than original research.
sources.evidence_base: Verified from the Wiley Chapter 1 excerpt, the Wiley table of contents and index PDFs, and the GBV scanned contents: the book rests on teaching and coaching anecdotes (named students, clients, Stanford colleagues) and on frameworks from practitioner books (Russell and Munter's Guide to Presentations, Duarte's Resonate and slide:ology, Osterwalder and Pigneur's Business Model Generation, Lipp's The Startup Pitch, Scott's Radical Candor, Heath and Heath's Made to Stick, Knaflic's Storytelling with Data, Abrahams's Speaking Up Without Freaking Out). The index shows it also mentions Amy Cuddy and Dana Carney on power poses (pp. 27-28) and Albert Mehrabian (pp. 29-30), both of which are contested or commonly misapplied findings; I could not read how the book frames them. It has a short bibliography (p. 187) and a recommended bookshelf (Appendix D). It does not present original empirical research.

sources.title: Connect
sources.subtitle: Building Exceptional Relationships with Family, Friends, and Colleagues
sources.publisher: Currency (Crown Currency, an imprint of Random House, Penguin Random House); UK edition Penguin Life
sources.edition: First edition, US hardcover, published February 9, 2021; 320 pages (publisher page). E-book ISBN 9780593237106; UK Penguin Life hardback ISBN 9780241406809 and trade paperback 9780241406816 (UK copyright page). Back matter includes Appendix A 'Vocabulary of Feelings', Appendix B 'Furthering Your Learning', Notes and Index.
sources.author_credibility: Bradford is Eugene O'Kelly II Senior Lecturer Emeritus in Leadership at Stanford GSB and Robin was the Dorothy J. King Lecturer in Leadership there; together they taught or ran the Interpersonal Dynamics ('Touchy Feely') elective for a combined roughly 75 years, a course Bradford developed over fifty years ago (he is called its 'father') and in which, per the book, over 85 percent of Stanford MBA students enroll; Robin joined about twenty years before publication and helped double the program. Both hold PhDs and Robin later co-founded the nonprofit Leaders in Tech. Their authority is primarily pedagogical and clinical (T-group facilitation), not experimental research; they have an obvious interest in promoting the course method and its descendant programs.
sources.evidence_base: The authors state the conceptual material is based on social science research, especially interpersonal psychology, plus their own experience. In practice the book relies mostly on decades of classroom and coaching observation, presented through composite stories of pairs of people (colleagues, partners, parents and adult children, friends) which the authors describe as amalgamations of real relationships they had or saw; five pair scenarios run through the book, plus end-of-chapter self-assessments and exercises. The methods descend from Kurt Lewin's T-group (laboratory training) tradition. Several ideas line up with independent research (self-disclosure and liking, the intimacy process model, correspondence bias, affect labeling, feedback-intervention research), but I could not verify which studies the book itself cites (the Notes section is only about four pages long, pages 289 to 292, suggesting few formal citations; I could not read it), so links to research below are my mapping unless stated otherwise. Structure (verified from the publisher extract's contents page): chapters 1 and 2 introduce the continuum; Part I 'Getting to the Meadow' (chapters 3 to 12) builds robust, functional relationships; Part II 'Tackling the Summit' (chapters 13 to 17) covers moving to exceptional; then an epilogue. The meadow and summit come from Bradford's mountain-climbing metaphor.

sources.title: How to Know a Person
sources.subtitle: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen
sources.edition: First edition, hardcover, Random House, October 24, 2023, 320 pages (publisher page). UK: Allen Lane 2023; Penguin Books paperback 2025, ISBN 9781802064308. Page references below follow the US hardcover pagination as given in a church discussion guide; the UK paperback contents page shows the same chapter start pages.
sources.author_credibility: David Brooks is a long-time New York Times opinion columnist (and, per his publisher, a writer for The Atlantic and regular PBS NewsHour commentator) and author of several books on character and social life (The Social Animal, The Road to Character, The Second Mountain). He is not a psychologist or researcher; the book is a synthesis of psychology, philosophy, literature and personal experience. He says he wrote it partly to fix his own reserved, emotionally distant habits, which makes it personal and motivational but also means some advice reflects his temperament and moral outlook more than tested method.
sources.evidence_base: Mixed. Some passages lean on peer-reviewed work: William Ickes on empathic accuracy and Nicholas Epley on the 'lesser minds' problem (both in the opening chapters, confirmed in the publisher sample), Dan McAdams's life-story interviews (Chapter 15), Big Five personality research and a 2022 review by Brent Roberts and Hee J. Yoon on personality change (Chapter 13), and developmental psychology for the life-tasks chapter (Erikson; summaries also name Robert Kegan). Much of the practical advice (Illuminators versus Diminishers, accompaniment, the Good Talks tips including looping and loud listening, the hard-conversations tools) comes from essays, philosophers such as Simone Weil and Iris Murdoch, practitioners, interviews and Brooks's own experience. The chapter on a friend in despair rests largely on one case, his friend Peter Marks, who died by suicide after years of depression. Reviewers find it engaging and practical but in places anecdotal.

sources.title: Humor, Seriously
sources.subtitle: Why Humor Is a Secret Weapon in Business and Life (and how anyone can harness it. Even you.)
sources.publisher: Currency, an imprint of Crown, Penguin Random House (listed by PRH as Crown Currency); UK edition titled Humour, Seriously (Penguin)
sources.edition: First edition, US hardcover, published February 2, 2021, 272 pages (per Penguin Random House product page; Open Library records 257 numbered pages)
sources.author_credibility: Jennifer Aaker is a behavioral scientist and professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business; Naomi Bagdonas is a Stanford GSB lecturer, executive coach, and former management consultant who trained in improv and sketch comedy at the Upright Citizens Brigade Theatre. The book grows out of their Stanford GSB course on humor in business. As teachers and promoters of a course, a TED talk and a speaking practice built on the premise that humor is underused at work, they have an incentive to emphasize benefits over limits.
sources.evidence_base: A mix of peer-reviewed behavioral science (Bitterly, Brooks and Schweitzer on humor and status; Gray, Parkinson and Dunbar on laughter and self-disclosure; Bazzini and colleagues on shared laughter in couples; Lehmann-Willenbrock and Allen on humor in team meetings; O'Quin and Aronoff on humor in a price negotiation), older or less transparent surveys (a Gallup global item on smiling or laughing, a 1987 survey of 290 workers on supervisor humor, a Hodge-Cronin survey of CEOs, the authors' own survey of roughly 700 people on why they avoid humor at work), interviews with comedians and executives, and many anecdotes. Several headline percentages (27 percent more motivating, 18 to 20 percent more paid with a joke, 30 percent more disclosure) are the authors' or press restatements of single older studies and cannot be checked against the abstracts, which do not report them in that form. Some brain-chemistry claims (dopamine, oxytocin, cortisol, endorphins) are stated more confidently than the underlying evidence supports. Comedy craft advice (truth and misdirection, rule of three, truth, pain and distance) rests on practitioner expertise from improv and The Second City rather than experiments.

sources.title: Improv Wisdom
sources.subtitle: Don't Prepare, Just Show Up
sources.publisher: Bell Tower, an imprint of Random House (title now listed under Harmony, Penguin Random House)
sources.edition: First edition, hardcover, published May 3, 2005, New York; 160 pages per Penguin Random House and Open Library (Publishers Weekly lists 159 pp). Ebook edition ISBN 9780307531841 (2010). ISBN 9781400081882 is the hardcover.
sources.author_credibility: Madson taught drama at Stanford from 1977 to 2005 after being denied tenure at an earlier post (Denison University), headed the undergraduate acting program, founded the Stanford Improvisors (1991), and received Stanford's Lloyd W. Dinkelspiel Award (1998). She studied with and brought Keith Johnstone to Stanford, and with her husband co-directs the California Center for Constructive Living, the practice David K. Reynolds built from Japanese Morita therapy and Naikan; both influences shape the book. She is an expert teacher and performer, not a researcher; the book is contemplative self-help that may overgeneralize stage rules to all of life. In one interview she cited an unnamed Stanford study claiming improv students had 40% higher self-esteem, which could not be traced.
sources.evidence_base: Practitioner wisdom: thirteen short maxim chapters (plus prologue, epilogue and resources) built from classroom experience, personal anecdotes, and more than 40 'Try this' exercises, with ideas and quotations from David K. Reynolds (Constructive Living), Keith Johnstone and Zen-flavored writers. No reliance on peer-reviewed studies was found in any source read. External research partly supports some ideas (improv exercises raising divergent thinking, uncertainty tolerance and positive affect; spotlight effect; high-quality listening; gratitude), but none of it tests the book's maxims directly.

sources.title: Made to Stick
sources.subtitle: Why Some Ideas Survive and Others Die
sources.edition: First edition, hardcover (US), Random House, published January 2, 2007, 336 pages per the publisher and Google Books listings (library catalogs record 291 numbered pages of main text); ISBN-10 1400064287. Trade paperback ISBN 9780812982008 (not separately verified on the publisher site).
sources.author_credibility: Chip Heath is a professor of organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business and has published peer-reviewed work on why ideas spread, including a study of urban legends (Heath, Bell and Sternberg, 2001, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Dan Heath is a senior fellow at Duke University's CASE center and a former course developer and educational publisher. The book blends Chip's academic research and teaching with practitioner case stories. As popular business authors with a commercial framework to sell (the SUCCESs checklist), they tend to choose vivid confirming cases and rarely discuss null or contrary findings.
sources.evidence_base: Mixed. Some principles rest on peer-reviewed psychology (the curse of knowledge in economics and cognitive psychology, concreteness effects on memory, Loewenstein's information gap theory of curiosity, the identifiable victim research of Small, Loewenstein and Slovic, mental simulation research by Pham and Taylor, and Chip Heath's own urban legend study). Much of the book is case evidence and anecdote (Southwest Airlines, the Army's Commander's Intent, Subway's Jared, the Don't Mess with Texas campaign, Nordstrom stories) plus classroom exercises from Chip Heath's Stanford course that are not peer-reviewed. Each principle chapter ends with a 'Clinic' applying it to a case. Some cited findings have since weakened under replication, notably the identifiable victim effect (a pre-registered replication found no effect) and a well-known adult curse of knowledge paradigm (Birch and Bloom, 2007), whose effect a large replication estimated at less than half the original size.

sources.title: Supercommunicators
sources.subtitle: How to Unlock the Secret Language of Connection
sources.edition: First edition, Random House hardcover, February 2024, 320 pages
sources.author_credibility: Duhigg is a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigative journalist (formerly The New York Times), a Harvard Business School MBA, and author of The Power of Habit and Smarter Faster Better. He is not a researcher: he synthesizes academic work (notably the Dartmouth group of Thalia Wheatley and Beau Sievers, Nicholas Epley at Chicago, Arthur and Elaine Aron, Salma Mousa) and interviews practitioners. His strength is accessible synthesis; the likely bias is narrative selection, where vivid success stories are chosen to illustrate a framework and the framework itself is his own construction rather than an empirically tested model. One reviewer (SSIR) notes he rarely examines cases where persuasive skill causes harm.
sources.evidence_base: A mix of peer-reviewed research (Sievers, Welker, Hasson, Kleinbaum and Wheatley on consensus-building conversation and neural alignment, Nature Communications 2024; Hasson's speaker-listener coupling work; the Arons' 1997 Fast Friends procedure; Epley's work on deep conversation; stereotype threat and identity research; Mousa's 2020 Science field experiment with Christian and Muslim soccer players in post-ISIS Iraq; the Harvard Study of Adult Development in the afterword) and long-form narrative case studies (FBI agent Felix Sigala in the prologue; CIA case officer Jim Lawler; the Leroy Reed jury and juror John Boly; surgeon Behfar Ehdaie with negotiation scholar Deepak Malhotra; Epley teaching hedge fund investors; NASA psychiatrist Terrance McGuire; The Big Bang Theory writers; the 2018 gun-rights and gun-control dialogue; pediatrician Jay Rosenbloom and physician Rima Chamie with vaccine-hesitant patients; Netflix's inclusion work under Verna Myers). The three-conversation typology, the matching principle and the four rules of a learning conversation are Duhigg's synthesis and have not themselves been tested as a package. The book's endnotes could not be read, so which specific papers he cites is only partly confirmed.

sources.title: Talk
sources.subtitle: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves
sources.edition: First US hardcover, Crown, January 21, 2025 (ISBN 9780593443491); ebook January 21, 2025 (ISBN 9780593443507); US paperback January 27, 2026 (ISBN 9780593443514); audiobook read by the author, 10 hours 1 minute (ISBN 9780593446096). 336 pages per the publisher and Google Books. UK edition published by Penguin.
sources.author_credibility: Alison Wood Brooks is the O'Brien Associate Professor of Business Administration and a Hellman Faculty Fellow at Harvard Business School, where she created and teaches an MBA course called TALK; she has published widely in top psychology and management journals on question-asking, humor, topic selection, apologies, and anxiety. The book draws heavily on her own lab's studies, so the author is promoting her own research program. Several of her papers were coauthored with Francesca Gino, whose work was found to contain data problems. The Many Co-Authors project lists the Gino-coauthored papers relevant here (Huang et al. 2017; Yeomans et al. 2020; Collins et al. 2022); in coauthor-submitted (unvetted) responses, none of their studies is attributed to Gino as data handler, and no misconduct finding against these papers or against Brooks was located. Readers may still weight Gino-coauthored findings cautiously.
sources.evidence_base: Mostly peer-reviewed experimental and field research (lab conversations, speed dates, sales calls, parole hearings, traffic stops, transcripts analyzed with natural language processing), from Brooks's lab and others (Epley, Mastroianni, Minson, Schweitzer, Aron). Supplemented by classroom exercises, observations, and anecdotes. Some topic-selection findings (topic preparation, topic prediction, topic switching) come from Brooks and Yeomans work for which no peer-reviewed article was located.

sources.title: Think Faster, Talk Smarter
sources.subtitle: How to Speak Successfully When You're Put on the Spot
sources.edition: First hardcover edition (US), Simon Element, published 2023-09-26. An updated edition adding an in-the-moment conflict chapter (Application 7) and AI-related content was announced by the author in October 2026; insight 16 comes from that edition.
sources.author_credibility: Matt Abrahams is a lecturer in organizational behavior at Stanford Graduate School of Business, where he teaches strategic communication, and hosts the Think Fast Talk Smart podcast. His methods come from long teaching and coaching practice, improv training (he credits Stanford drama professor Patricia Ryan Madson and her book Improv Wisdom), and selected psychology research. He is a practitioner and educator rather than a research scientist, and the book is partly a vehicle for his podcast, courses and coaching brand, so his frameworks are presented with more certainty than the evidence behind some of them warrants.
sources.evidence_base: A mix of selected peer-reviewed findings (for example Alison Wood Brooks's 2014 work on reappraising anxiety as excitement, research on breathing and anxiety, and survey data on fear of public speaking), insights from improv, guest experts from his podcast, and classroom and coaching experience. Most of the speaking structures (What/So What/Now What, Problem/Solution/Benefit, the four pitch sentence starters, ADD, 4 I's, AAA, WHAT, CLEAR) are practitioner heuristics that have not been tested as named frameworks in controlled studies, although they align with broader research on message organization, feedback and apologies. Sources the book names in the chapters seen include Alison Wood Brooks (anxiety reappraisal), Andrew Huberman (breathing), S. Christian Wheeler, the spotlight effect, Collins Dobbs, Julia Minson (conversational receptiveness), Joseph Grenny (Crucial Conversations), and many interviewees from his podcast.

sources.title: Pushing in the Dark: Causes and Consequences of Limited Self-Awareness for Interpersonal Assertiveness
sources.author_credibility: Ames is a Columbia Business School professor and a leading researcher on assertiveness and interpersonal perception; Wazlawek was a Columbia doctoral student. Published in a major peer-reviewed social psychology journal. Builds on Ames and Flynn (2007) in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
sources.evidence_base: Four studies. Three used MBA students in negotiation courses, rating their own and their counterpart's assertiveness after mock negotiations and predicting how the counterpart saw them; one was an online survey of about 500 US adults about real negotiations. Partner ratings, not only self-report. Companion paper Ames and Flynn (2007, JPSP 92(2), 307-324; three studies) found a curvilinear link between assertiveness and perceived leadership.

sources.title: SPIKES: A Six-Step Protocol for Delivering Bad News
sources.subtitle: Application to the Patient with Cancer
sources.publisher: The Oncologist 5(4), 302-311 (AlphaMed Press; now Oxford University Press)
sources.author_credibility: Baile (MD Anderson Cancer Center) and Buckman (University of Toronto and MD Anderson) are oncologists and long-time communication-skills educators. The paper is one of the most cited in medical communication and SPIKES is taught in medical and nursing curricula worldwide. The authors also run training based on the protocol, so they have an interest in its adoption.
sources.evidence_base: Expert consensus built on prior research about what patients want when receiving bad news; the authors state it meets published recommendations but was not derived wholly from empirical tests. At launch the only outcome data were trainee reports of increased confidence. A later systematic review and meta-analysis (Johnson and Panagioti, 2018, Academic Medicine, 17 studies) found that bad-news training raises observer-rated delivery skill (SMD 0.74) and clinician confidence (SMD 0.60), but only one study measured patient distress. Critiques (Dean and Willis, 2016) question rigid, single-meeting use.

sources.title: Nonverbal Overload: A Theoretical Argument for the Causes of Zoom Fatigue
sources.publisher: American Psychological Association (Technology, Mind, and Behavior 2(1))
sources.author_credibility: Bailenson is the founding director of Stanford's Virtual Human Interaction Lab and has published peer-reviewed work on mediated and virtual communication for over two decades, including his own studies of gaze and personal space with virtual faces. He states he has no conflicts of interest and that he uses Zoom himself; the article is framed as design critique, not an attack on the product.
sources.evidence_base: A theoretical argument, explicitly labeled by the author as arguments rather than findings. It builds on established research on gaze and interpersonal distance (Argyle and Dean 1965; Hall 1966), cognitive load on video versus audio (Hinds 1999), louder speech on video (Croes et al. 2019), mirror-induced self-evaluation (Duval and Wicklund 1972; Fejfar and Hoyle 2000 meta-analysis, small effect on negative affect; Ingram et al. 1988), and movement and cognition (Oppezzo and Schwartz 2014; Goldin-Meadow). Later survey work from the same lab (Fauville et al. 2023, Computers in Human Behavior Reports, convenience sample of 9,787) found that all four mechanisms were associated with self-reported fatigue and that women reported more of them; that is correlational and self-report.

sources.subtitle: How to Change Anyone's Mind
sources.author_credibility: Berger is a marketing professor at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, who publishes peer-reviewed research on word of mouth and social influence, and wrote Contagious and Invisible Influence. He also consults and speaks commercially on the ideas, which favors a confident, story-led presentation.
sources.evidence_base: Synthesis of established research (psychological reactance, endowment effect and status quo bias, latitude of acceptance from social judgment theory, trialability and risk in innovation adoption, social proof) illustrated with narrative cases (a hostage negotiator, a teen anti-smoking campaign, deep canvassing, free shipping, substance abuse counselors). The REDUCE framework as a package is untested, and some underlying findings, such as the size of the endowment effect, are debated.

sources.title: The Economic and Interpersonal Consequences of Deflecting Direct Questions
sources.publisher: American Psychological Association (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 118(5), 945-990)
sources.author_credibility: Schweitzer is a Wharton professor with a long research record on trust, deception and negotiation; Bitterly is a management researcher (now HKUST, previously Michigan) who also coauthored humor research. Published in a top social psychology journal. No obvious commercial conflict.
sources.evidence_base: Eight experiments, mostly online participants reading or reacting to scripted negotiation and interview exchanges (for example a buyer asked whether they own other pieces from an art collection). Responses compared: honest disclosure, declining to answer, lying, paltering, dodging, and deflection (answering a question with a question). Deflection caused less reputational harm than detected deception and less interpersonal harm than declining; in some cases it beat honest disclosure on both interpersonal and economic outcomes. Mechanism: observers infer a motive to seek information rather than hide it. Settings are scenarios, not live audience Q&A.

sources.title: A Racing Heart, Rattling Knees, and Ruminative Thoughts: Defining, Explaining, and Treating Public Speaking Anxiety
sources.author_credibility: Graham Bodie is a widely cited communication scholar (listening and communication apprehension research), writing in the National Communication Association's main instructional communication journal. The review is cited well over 150 times.
sources.evidence_base: Narrative review of the public speaking anxiety literature: defines the construct, develops a typology (trait and state forms, and its expression in physiology, thoughts and behavior), reviews causes, and reviews treatment techniques (systematic desensitization, cognitive modification, skills training, and combinations). Draws on decades of communication apprehension research, including Behnke and Sawyer's studies of how anxiety rises and falls across the speaking episode and Allen and colleagues' meta-analytic work on treatments. Much of the trait literature relies on self-report scales.

sources.title: Accuracy of Deception Judgments
sources.publisher: Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 214 to 234
sources.author_credibility: Bond (Texas Christian University) and DePaulo (University of Virginia, later UC Santa Barbara) are leading deception researchers; DePaulo also led the companion Cues to Deception meta-analysis (Psychological Bulletin, 2003). The paper is one of the most cited in the field and its central estimate has held up in later work.
sources.evidence_base: Meta-analysis of 206 documents and 24,483 judges in which people tried to tell lies from truths in real time without aids or training. Moderator analyses cover medium (video, audio, audiovisual, transcript), motivation, preparation, baseline exposure, interaction and judge expertise. Main limitation: most studies use low-stakes lab lies by strangers.

sources.title: The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?
sources.edition: Accepted manuscript read via University of Essex repository
sources.author_credibility: Peer-reviewed in Psychological Science. Clark (Yale) is a senior relationships researcher; Sandstrom leads research on talking to strangers; Boothby and Cooney study conversation. Data posted on the Open Science Framework. A different lab from the Epley group behind several existing miscalibration insights.
sources.evidence_base: Five studies: lab conversations between strangers (with video coded by outside observers), a study of the thoughts people had after talking, conversations of varying length up to 45 minutes, a personal development workshop with members of the public, and first-year college suitemates surveyed five times over an academic year. Effects concern perceptions; no intervention to close the gap was tested.

legal_access.note: Open-access accepted manuscript, read in full.

sources.title: Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors
sources.publisher: Taylor and Francis, Communication Monographs 83(4), 446 to 467
sources.author_credibility: Peer-reviewed in a flagship communication journal. Dillard (Penn State) is a leading persuasion and emotion scholar; Braddock (American University) researches narrative persuasion, including extremist recruitment. Independent of the Made to Stick authors.
sources.evidence_base: Meta-analysis of 74 studies, screened from about 6,400, that compared narrative messages with non-narrative controls. Effects are small: correlations of about .17 for beliefs, .19 for attitudes, .17 for intentions and about .23 for behaviors (behavior from only 5 studies, under 1,000 people). Medium and research design did not change effect size; fictionality results were mixed; outcomes were measured soon after exposure, so durability is unknown.

legal_access.note: The Decision Lab summary, read in full: sample, per-outcome effect sizes, fiction versus nonfiction results, limitations.

sources.title: Influence, New and Expanded
sources.subtitle: The Psychology of Persuasion
sources.edition: New and expanded edition, 2021 (adds a seventh principle, unity; earlier editions 1984 onward)
sources.author_credibility: Regents' Professor Emeritus of Psychology and Marketing at Arizona State University and one of the most cited researchers on compliance and social norms. He also runs a consulting and training firm (Influence at Work), which gives him a commercial incentive to present the principles favorably.
sources.evidence_base: Built on genuine peer-reviewed research, much of it by Cialdini and colleagues, but presented through vivid single studies and field anecdotes. Several flagship demonstrations show small, moderated or partly unreplicated effects: door-in-the-face moves words more than deeds (Feeley et al. 2012), foot-in-the-door is real but inconsistent (Burger 1999), the hotel towel advantage did not replicate in Germany (Bohner and Schlueter 2014), scarcity has a modest average effect with large heterogeneity (Lynn 1991). Principles are directionally sound; specific effect sizes should be treated cautiously.

sources.title: Influence Without Authority
sources.edition: Third edition, October 2017, 320 pages (first edition 1990, second 2005)
sources.author_credibility: Cohen is a management professor at Babson College (Distinguished Professor of Global Leadership) with a Harvard DBA; Bradford is Senior Lecturer on Organizational Behavior Emeritus at Stanford Graduate School of Business and coauthor of Connect, a core library book. Both are long-time consultants and executive educators, so the model is shaped by teaching and consulting cases rather than controlled tests.
sources.evidence_base: Practitioner framework built on decades of teaching and case experience, grounded in social exchange theory and the reciprocity norm. Extensive case examples; the exchange model as a package has not been experimentally tested.

sources.title: Psychological Interventions for the Fear of Public Speaking: A Meta-Analysis
sources.author_credibility: Clinical psychology researchers at the University of Bergen and Haukeland University Hospital, Norway, with a track record in internet-delivered treatment for anxiety. The review was preregistered on PROSPERO and restricted to randomized controlled trials. Some authors work on technology-delivered treatment, a possible interest in the finding that such delivery works as well as face to face.
sources.evidence_base: Meta-analysis of 30 randomized controlled trials (1,355 participants, 62 intervention arms) found through four databases. Most arms were cognitive or behavioral (desensitization, relaxation, cognitive behavioral therapy, exposure). Pooled post-treatment effect on fear of public speaking g = 0.74 with low to moderate heterogeneity, robust against both active and waitlist controls; follow-up effect g = 1.11; small further improvement after treatment ended (g = 0.20, adjusted for possible publication bias to 0.12). Self-report effects were larger than behavioral and physiological ones. Limitations noted by the authors: older trials with unclear risk of bias, mostly completers-only data, some signs of publication bias, only seven technology-delivered arms, and almost no adolescent samples.

sources.author_credibility: Feeley is a professor of communication at the University at Buffalo who studies persuasion and health communication; Aloe is a meta-analysis methodologist (University of Iowa). sources.evidence_base: Random-effects meta-analysis of door-in-the-face studies from roughly 1975 to 2010: 78 effect sizes for verbal compliance and 39 for behavioral compliance. Many primary studies are older, short, lab or campus requests, often prosocial (volunteering, donating), so transfer to workplace requests is an extrapolation.

sources.publisher: Social and Personality Psychology Compass (Wiley), 13(12), e12501
sources.author_credibility: Feinberg (Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto) and Willer (Stanford sociology, Polarization and Social Change Lab) ran many of the primary moral reframing experiments. As authors reviewing their own research program they have an interest in the effect, though the article openly discusses null and inconsistent findings.
sources.evidence_base: Narrative review of moral reframing experiments on environmental policy, military spending, immigration, same-sex marriage, candidates, vaccines and charity giving, plus one canvassing field experiment (Kalla, Levine and Broockman 2019). Rests on moral foundations theory, which has critics. Much of the base comes from the authors' labs; some studies found inconsistent effects.

sources.title: Getting to Yes
sources.subtitle: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
sources.edition: Third edition 2011 recommended; first edition 1981, second 1991 added Patton and 'Ten Questions People Ask'
sources.author_credibility: Developed at the Harvard Negotiation Project. Fisher was a Harvard Law professor and mediator; Ury and Patton are long-standing negotiation scholars and practitioners. The book has been a standard in law, business and diplomacy teaching for four decades.
sources.evidence_base: Argues from cases and the authors' practice rather than data. Early reviewers (White, 1984; McCarthy, 1985) criticized it for anecdote, for underplaying distributive bargaining and power struggles, and for overstating the case against positional bargaining, which Fisher partly conceded. Its core logic is consistent with later research such as the De Dreu, Weingart and Kwon (2000) meta-analysis of 28 studies, but the package as a whole has not been tested.

sources.subtitle: How the Science of Attachment Can Help You Make and Keep Friends
sources.author_credibility: Franco holds a PhD in counseling psychology from the University of Maryland, where she has taught as an assistant clinical professor; she writes for Psychology Today and the book was a New York Times bestseller. She is a practitioner-synthesizer rather than a primary friendship researcher.
sources.evidence_base: Practitioner synthesis citing friendship and social psychology research (for example the liking gap and Hall's time research) organized around attachment theory. The attachment framing is applied more confidently than friendship-specific evidence allows; individual claims should be traced to primary studies.

sources.title: What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 87(2), 228 to 245 (American Psychological Association)
sources.author_credibility: Gable (UC Santa Barbara) and Reis (University of Rochester) are leading close-relationships researchers; the paper appears in a top social psychology journal and launched a substantial line of capitalization research.
sources.evidence_base: Four studies using diaries and couples samples found that sharing positive events was linked to higher daily positive mood and life satisfaction beyond the event itself, and that perceiving a partner's response as active-constructive was linked to higher intimacy, satisfaction and trust. Follow-up work (Gable, Gonzaga and Strachman, 2006) used observed lab interactions and found responses to good news predicted relationship well-being and breakups two months later more strongly than responses to bad news. Peters, Reis and Gable (2018) review the later literature. Much of the data is self-report and correlational.

sources.edition: Journal article; accepted manuscript read via LSE Research Online

Published in a leading organizational behavior journal. Bohns's broader research program on perspective gaps could incline the team toward egocentrism explanations.
sources.evidence_base: Six main and two supplemental pre-registered experiments (N = 4,004). Study 1 used recall among public sector employees in Spain; the remaining main studies used US Prolific samples, with Studies 3 to 6 restricted to full-time employees, mostly reading hypothetical sender or receiver scenarios. Study 6 (854 US full-time employees) tested a one-line note from the sender.

sources.title: Saying No: The Negative Ramifications From Invitation Declines Are Less Severe Than We Think
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 126(6), 1103-1115 (American Psychological Association); online December 2023
sources.author_credibility: Givi (West Virginia University) and Kirk (New York Institute of Technology) are consumer and social psychologists who study gift giving and social decisions. Published in a top social psychology journal. Givi has said the study was prompted by his own reluctant wedding attendance.
sources.evidence_base: A pilot survey plus five experiments with more than 2,000 participants in total, mixing hypothetical scenarios (including an observer condition and a named real friend) with a study of real couples who wrote and declined invitations to each other. The decline reason was held constant (wanting to stay home and relax).

sources.title: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
sources.subtitle: A Practical Guide from the Country's Foremost Relationship Expert (revised edition)
sources.author_credibility: Gottman is professor emeritus of psychology at the University of Washington and ran long-running observational studies of couples (the 'Love Lab') with many peer-reviewed papers, including Gottman, Coan, Carrere and Swanson (1998) and Driver and Gottman (2004). Nan Silver is a science journalist. Gottman co-founded the commercial Gottman Institute, which sells workshops and therapist training based on these ideas, a conflict of interest worth noting.
sources.evidence_base: Translates decades of observational, physiological and longitudinal couples research into exercises. The basic associations (contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling predict worse outcomes; everyday positivity cushions conflict) are broadly consistent with other labs. The headline divorce-prediction accuracy figures were fit in-sample, and Heyman and Slep (2001) showed such accuracy drops sharply under cross-validation. The seven-principle program as a package has not been tested in independent randomized trials, and specific numbers (the 5 to 1 ratio, 69 percent perpetual problems, 86 versus 33 percent turning toward) come from Gottman's own samples.

sources.title: Speech Rate, Intonation, and Pitch: Investigating the Bias and Cue Effects of Vocal Confidence on Persuasion
sources.author_credibility: Fabrigar (Queen's University) is a leading attitudes and persuasion methodologist; Guyer has a program of research on paralinguistic cues and persuasion. The same group, with Petty and Brinol, published an open-access 2021 review in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior that situates this paper in the wider literature. No commercial conflicts declared.
sources.evidence_base: Three between-participants experiments (N = 394, 412, 397) using the elaboration likelihood framework. Experiment 1 manipulated speech rate (fast or slow) and end-of-sentence intonation (falling or rising); Experiments 2 and 3 manipulated pitch (raised or lowered). Each crossed vocal features with whether listeners were motivated to think carefully. Vocal features changed perceived speaker confidence. With high thinking, perceived confidence biased the favorability of listeners' thoughts, which shaped attitudes; with low thinking, it acted directly as a cue. Alternative explanations were tested and not supported. The 2021 review adds that falling intonation increased persuasion for strong arguments and decreased it for weak ones (Guyer et al. 2018), and that very fast speech can reduce processing and blunt the advantage of strong arguments (Moore et al. 1986). Samples were mostly students listening to audio recordings.

sources.publisher: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships 36(4), 1278 to 1296 (SAGE); online first March 2018
sources.author_credibility: Hall is a professor of communication studies at the University of Kansas who has published widely on friendship, everyday talk and well-being.
sources.evidence_base: Two studies: 355 US adults who had relocated in the previous six months estimated time spent with a new acquaintance (cross-sectional), and 112 first-year students reported hours with two new acquaintances three times over nine weeks. Hour thresholds are approximate estimates from self-reported time; a single paper, not yet a replicated body of work.

sources.title: Nonverbal Communication
sources.author_credibility: Judith Hall (Northeastern University) is among the most cited researchers on nonverbal behavior and interpersonal accuracy and coauthors the standard textbook in the field (Knapp, Hall and Horgan). Horgan (University of Michigan, Flint) and Murphy (Loyola Marymount) are established person-perception researchers. Annual Review of Psychology is an invited, highly selective review venue. As leaders of the interpersonal-accuracy research program they have an interest in the construct, but the review is descriptive rather than promotional.
sources.evidence_base: Narrative review of decades of research on the meaning of cues people send (encoding) and the accuracy of perceiving them (decoding), framed by the Brunswik lens model, with a section on measurement problems. Individual claims inherit the strength of the cited studies. Only the abstract, keywords and section headings were accessible here; the full text is paywalled.

sources.title: A Review and Meta-Analysis of Person-Centered Messages and Social Support Outcomes
sources.author_credibility: High and Dillard (Penn State) are established interpersonal communication researchers; the meta-analysis synthesizes the long-running person-centered comforting research program begun by Brant Burleson.
sources.evidence_base: Meta-analysis of 23 studies: a positive linear association between how person-centered a comforting message is and its actual effectiveness, and a stronger association with perceived effectiveness; effects weaker in designs using confederates. Many underlying studies rate written or hypothetical messages rather than live conversations, and the authors note the nine-level hierarchy needs sharper measurement.

sources.title: Optimizing stress responses with reappraisal and mindset interventions: an integrated model
sources.publisher: Taylor and Francis (Anxiety, Stress and Coping 31(3), 245-261)
sources.author_credibility: Jamieson (University of Rochester) leads arousal reappraisal research; Crum (Stanford) developed the stress mindset measure and interventions; Akinola (Columbia Business School) studies stress and performance at work. As originators of the interventions they review, they have an interest in favorable conclusions; Jamieson has separately cautioned that reappraisal is not a silver bullet.
sources.evidence_base: Integrative review proposing a combined model. Rests on randomized lab and classroom experiments: Jamieson, Nock and Mendes (2012), in which instructions to view stress arousal as functional produced more efficient cardiovascular responses and less attention to negative information than two control conditions; Crum, Salovey and Achor (2013), in which short videos shifted stress mindsets and an enhancing mindset was associated with moderate cortisol reactivity and more desire for feedback. Theory is the biopsychosocial model of challenge and threat. Later large-scale support came from Yeager and colleagues (2022, Nature): six double-blind randomized experiments with US students in which a roughly 30-minute online module combining growth and stress-can-be-enhancing mindsets improved stress appraisals, cardiovascular reactivity and anxiety symptoms, with benefits depending on addressing both mindsets.

sources.title: Speakers' overestimation of their effectiveness
sources.publisher: SAGE for the Association for Psychological Science (Psychological Science 13(3), 207-212)
sources.author_credibility: Boaz Keysar (University of Chicago) is a leading researcher on perspective taking and miscommunication in language use; his lab has extended this line for two decades. Published in a top general psychology journal.
sources.evidence_base: Lab experiment with 40 speaker-listener pairs of mostly undergraduate native English speakers, plus 37 overhearers. Speakers read 12 syntactically and 4 lexically ambiguous sentences aiming to convey a specified meaning, then estimated whether the listener understood. Per the University of Chicago student newspaper's report of the paper, speakers believed they were understood about 72 percent of the time, but in nearly half of those cases the listener had actually misunderstood; listeners' confidence was unrelated to their accuracy; informed overhearers estimated success at about 56 percent and did not systematically overestimate. Consistent with later work: Kruger, Epley and colleagues (2005) on email tone, and Lau, Geipel, Wu and Keysar (2022), who found speakers overestimated understanding even when listeners did not know the language.

sources.title: A Meta-analytic Systematic Review and Theory of the Effects of Perceived Listening on Work Outcomes
sources.publisher: Journal of Business and Psychology, 39, 295 to 344 (online 2023)
sources.author_credibility: Kluger (Hebrew University) coauthored the influential Kluger and DeNisi (1996) feedback-intervention meta-analysis; Itzchakov (University of Haifa) leads much of the experimental listening work; Aguinis (George Washington University) is a leading research methodologist. Kluger and Itzchakov are the main proponents of listening research, so this is not an independent check, but it pools studies from many independent labs and disciplines. The companion narrative review, Kluger and Itzchakov (2022), The Power of Listening at Work, Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior 9, was also read (author preprint).
sources.evidence_base: Registered systematic review with three-level meta-analyses: 664 effect sizes, about 400,000 observations. About 75 percent of the data are same-person self-reports, which inflates estimates; only about 30 effects come from experiments and only one study tested actual performance experimentally. The 2022 companion review summarizes experiments (mostly Israeli lab and field samples) on listening and speakers' attitudes, anxiety and psychological safety.

sources.title: The state of research on leader humor
sources.author_credibility: Peer-reviewed systematic review in Organizational Psychology Review. Cooper (University of Miami) is a leading leader-humor researcher; Sosik (Penn State) is an established leadership scholar; Kong publishes in top management journals. Independent of the Humor, Seriously authors, so it is a useful check on that book's claims.

The underlying studies are mostly cross-sectional field surveys, so links between leader humor and follower outcomes are associations, not demonstrated causes. sources.title: Dominance and Prestige: Meta-Analytic Review of Experimentally Induced Body Position Effects on Behavioral, Self-Report, and Physiological Dependent Variables
sources.author_credibility: Published in Psychological Bulletin, the leading review journal in psychology. Bushman is a highly cited social psychologist; Körner, Röseler and Schütz (Bamberg, Halle) research body posture and self-perception and have published critical commentary on earlier posture meta-analyses. Preregistered, with an open web app for updating results.
sources.evidence_base: Preregistered meta-analysis of 313 effects from 88 studies (9,779 participants), published and unpublished. Overall effect of body positions g = 0.35 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.42). Both expansive poses (dominance) and upright postures (prestige) affected self-report and behavioral measures but not physiological ones (for example testosterone and cortisol). Behavioral effects were sensitive to publication bias or outliers. Effects were noticeably larger in studies without cover stories and in within-subject designs, suggesting demand characteristics may partly explain them. Most studies lacked a neutral control condition, so it is unclear whether upright postures help or slumped ones hurt. Sex, student status and individualistic versus collectivistic culture did not moderate effects.

University of Halle press release via idw

sources.title: Self-talk as a regulatory mechanism: How you do it matters
sources.publisher: American Psychological Association (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 106(2), 304-324)
sources.author_credibility: Ethan Kross (University of Michigan) and Ozlem Ayduk (UC Berkeley) are leading researchers on self-distancing and emotion regulation; Jason Moser (Michigan State) studies anxiety neuroscience. Kross later popularized the work in the trade book Chatter (2021), a possible incentive to present it favorably.
sources.evidence_base: Seven studies (total N = 585). Two proof-of-principle studies showed that referring to yourself by name or as you during introspection increases self-distancing. In a first-impressions task and a public speaking task, the non-first-person group was rated as performing better by objective raters, reported less distress, and (in the speech study) ruminated less afterwards. Two further studies showed non-first-person self-talk led people to appraise upcoming stressors as more of a challenge and less of a threat. An internal meta-analysis found effects were not moderated by trait social anxiety. Mostly university student samples in the lab.

sources.title: Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?
sources.publisher: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 89(6), 925-936
sources.edition: Journal article; full text read via author-hosted PDF
sources.author_credibility: Kruger (then NYU Stern; co-author of the Dunning-Kruger paper) and Epley (University of Chicago Booth, a leading researcher on mind perception and egocentrism). Published in the flagship social psychology journal. Parker and Ng were at the University of Illinois.
sources.evidence_base: Five lab experiments plus a follow-up study, all with US university students (for example 12 Cornell students in Study 1, 54 and 58 Illinois students in Studies 4 and 5). Studies compared predicted and actual accuracy in conveying sarcasm, seriousness, emotions, and humor over email versus voice or face to face, and two studies manipulated the sender's own experience of the message to test the egocentrism mechanism.

sources.title: Dormant Ties: The Value of Reconnecting
sources.author_credibility: Levin (Rutgers), Walter (George Washington University) and Murnighan (Kellogg, Northwestern; died 2016) are established organizational researchers; Organization Science is a top management journal. Follow-up: Walter, Levin and Murnighan (2015), Reconnection Choices, Organization Science 26(5).
sources.evidence_base: 224 executives in four Executive MBA classes each reconnected with two people they had not contacted in at least three years (one formerly close, one formerly distant) and sought advice on a real, important work project, then rated the value against current ties. A second sample of 116 executives (95 completed) ranked their top 10 dormant contacts; a randomly chosen lower-ranked contact proved about as useful as the top choice. Outcomes are self-rated; reconnection was a course assignment.

sources.title: An Exploration of the Structure of Effective Apologies
sources.author_credibility: Lewicki (Ohio State, Fisher College of Business, emeritus) is a leading scholar of trust and negotiation; Lount (Ohio State) studies trust repair; Polin (Eastern Kentucky University) studies apologies and trust. Published in a peer-reviewed journal of the International Association for Conflict Management.
sources.evidence_base: Two experiments with 755 participants (333 online adults via MTurk; 422 undergraduates). Participants imagined being a hiring manager and rated a job candidate's apology for an earlier tax-filing error, framed as either a competence lapse or a deliberate integrity lapse. Apologies contained one, three, or all six components (described in Study 1, written out as statements in Study 2). Outcomes were ratings of effectiveness, credibility, and adequacy, not real forgiveness or behavior.

sources.author_credibility: Miller (Emeritus Distinguished Professor of Psychology and Psychiatry, University of New Mexico) introduced motivational interviewing (MI) in 1983; Rollnick (Cardiff University School of Medicine) cofounded it. MI has been tested in hundreds of randomized trials, many by independent groups. The founders also lead its training community, which gives them an interest in its spread.
sources.evidence_base: Strong trial base, read here through the companion meta-analysis Lundahl, Kunz, Brownell, Tollefson and Burke (2010, 119 studies): versus weak or no-treatment comparisons MI produced durable small effects (average g = 0.28); versus other specific treatments it was roughly equivalent (g = 0.09, not significant). Process research (Magill et al. 2018 meta-analysis) found that MI-consistent counselor behavior goes with a higher proportion of client change talk, and that client sustain talk predicts worse outcomes. Evidence is mostly from health, addiction and counseling settings; the 4th edition extends MI to management, coaching and education, where it is far less tested.

No experimental test of the method itself. Its authority is wide adoption in management consulting. Its core moves (conclusion first, explicit grouping, advance organizers) are consistent with reading research and with field experiments such as Rogers and Lasky-Fink's.

sources.publisher: Journal of Family Theory and Review 1(1), 20 to 37 (Wiley)

Supporting studies (Bolger, Zuckerman and Kessler, 2000; Gleason et al., 2008; Girme, Overall and Simpson, 2013) are diary and observational couples studies, often around specific stressors like exams.

sources.title: The Artful Dodger: Answering the Wrong Question the Right Way
sources.publisher: American Psychological Association (Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 17(2), 139-147)
sources.author_credibility: Rogers (Harvard Kennedy School) and Norton (Harvard Business School) are well-cited behavioral scientists; Rogers also coauthored Writing for Busy Readers. Rogers has said publicly he sees political dodging as a problem for democracy, which frames the paper's aims.
sources.evidence_base: Four experiments in which participants watched a recorded speaker answer a question. The same answer (about health care) was attached to a similar question (illegal drug use) or a clearly different one (the war on terror). Listeners largely failed to notice the similar-question dodge and did not rate the dodger worse; they noticed the clearly unrelated dodge. Detection rose when listeners were told to judge relevance or when the question stayed on screen during the answer. A fluent answer to a similar question was rated more positively than a disfluent answer to the actual question. Samples were online participants in a political debate setting.

sources.title: The illusion of transparency and the alleviation of speech anxiety
sources.author_credibility: Thomas Gilovich (Cornell) is a leading judgment and decision-making researcher who co-originated the spotlight effect and illusion of transparency research; Kenneth Savitsky (Williams College) co-authored that work.
sources.evidence_base: Two experiments with student speakers. Study 1: speakers giving impromptu speeches believed their nervousness was more visible than observers reported. Study 2: speakers were assigned to a control group, a reassured group (told anxiety is normal and not to worry), or an informed group (told about the illusion of transparency, that inner feelings are less visible to others than people think). The informed group rated their speeches more favorably and felt less nervous, and observers also rated their speeches as better. A later conceptual replication with live classroom audiences (MacInnis, Mackinnon and MacIntyre, 2010) confirmed speakers overestimate how anxious they appear, more so for people high in speaking anxiety.

sources.title: A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media
sources.author_credibility: Educational psychologists at TU Chemnitz in the multimedia learning and cognitive load tradition; Rey has published widely on instructional design principles. Published in a leading review journal in education.
sources.evidence_base: Meta-analysis of studies from 1970 to 2016 (103 studies, about 12,200 participants; 139 comparisons for retention and 70 for transfer) on signaling: cues such as highlighting, color, arrows, labels, headings and other emphasis that direct attention to key information or show its organization in learning materials. Per a Technical University of Munich clearinghouse summary: retention g = 0.53, transfer g = 0.33, lower cognitive load g = 0.25, small motivation gain g = 0.13, learners looked longer at signaled content. Signals in text were especially effective for retention; for pictures, color cues helped transfer while several other cue types did not, and blinking cues harmed transfer; no benefit in mathematics. Most studies were lab studies with university students; only a handful involved adults outside education.

insights.name: AIM: Audience, Intent, then Message
insights.takeaway: Before drafting, decide who your audience is and what you want them to do, then choose channel and structure.
insights.explanation: Before drafting anything, answer three questions in a fixed order. Audience: who exactly will receive this, what do they already know and care about, and who is the secondary audience (the people your listeners will pass it on to, or who might see it unintentionally). Intent: what you want them to think, say, or do as a result, framed from their side rather than yours ('I want to impress them' is about you). Message: only then choose the channel (from highly to minimally interactive, oral, written, or blended) and the structure. The ordering is the point: most people jump straight to the message. The book opens with AIM because Schramm uses it at the start of nearly every class and coaching session, and he credits the model to Lynn Russell and Mary Munter's Guide to Presentations rather than claiming it.
insights.when_to_use: At the start of any planned communication: a presentation, an email to a senior leader, a proposal, a hard conversation, or even a toast. Especially useful when you feel stuck on what to say, which usually means intent is unclear.
insights.worked_example: A product manager needs budget for a usability study. Her first draft email opens with three paragraphs on research methodology. Running AIM: the audience is a finance director who cares about cost avoidance and has five minutes; the intent is a yes on 18,000 dollars by Friday; so the message becomes a two-line ask up top, the cost of a failed launch last year as the reason, and the methodology moved to an attachment. At home the same week, she uses AIM before talking to her teenager about a curfew: the intent is agreement on a rule he will actually follow, not winning the argument, so she opens by asking what he thinks is fair.
common_mistakes: Defining intent as something about yourself ('impress them', 'inform them') instead of what the audience should think, say, or do
Ignoring the secondary audience, such as the senior partner who will actually decide, or the unintended reader of a forwarded email
Defaulting to a meeting or an email without considering the full range of channels
steps: Write one sentence describing the primary audience and one for the secondary audience: role, prior knowledge, what they care about, how much attention they will give
Research them: online sources, a contact who knows them, and ideally a small test audience
Write the intent as an observable action from the audience's side: 'After this, they will ...'
Choose the channel by asking how far the message must travel, how long it must last, how formal it is, and how interactive it needs to be
Draft the message structure, then check every section against audience and intent and cut what serves neither
situations: Planning a presentation to senior leadership
Writing an email that asks for a decision
Preparing a pitch to investors or a client
Raising a sensitive topic with a family member

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 1, Chapter 1 (Adopting a Communication Mindset), section 'Know Your AIM', pp. 3-14
source.underlying_research: The book credits the model to Lynn Russell and Mary Munter, Guide to Presentations (Figure 1.1 source line, p. 4). Audience analysis is long-standing consensus in rhetoric and business communication; the book cites no experimental study for it.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the Chapter 1 excerpt and highlighted by Matt Abrahams on Five Books. Strong practitioner and teaching consensus in business communication curricula, but not an empirically tested framework as such.

supporting_evidence.note: Applies audience-first analysis to the boss: understand their goals, pressures and how they prefer to receive information (reader or listener) before choosing message and format.

insights.name: ABC Writing: Active, Brief, Clear
insights.takeaway: After drafting, edit so the actor and real verb come first, filler is cut, and your point is easy to find.
insights.explanation: The book's core standard for written work is that it should be Active, Brief, and Clear. Active means the person or team doing the action appears first and the real verb is visible (for example 'we decided' rather than 'a decision was made', and 'decide' rather than 'make a determination'). Brief means editing hard: removing filler phrases, repetition, and padding until every sentence earns its place. Clear means the reader can find your main point and requested action quickly, without having to reconstruct your logic. The three checks are designed to be applied as an editing pass after the first draft, not while drafting.
insights.when_to_use: Every piece of writing someone else must act on: emails, status updates, memos, performance reviews, cover letters, even messages to a landlord or school.
insights.worked_example: An operations lead drafts: 'It has been determined that a review of the vendor onboarding process will be undertaken in Q3 due to the fact that there have been a number of delays.' ABC pass: 'We will review vendor onboarding in Q3 because three of the last five vendors started late.' Actor first, real verb, 37 words to 17, and a concrete reason. He later uses the same pass on an email to his child's school, turning a long apology-filled paragraph into a clear request for a meeting time.
common_mistakes: Using passive voice to avoid naming who is responsible, which reads as evasive
Cutting so much that context the reader needs disappears (brief is not the same as cryptic)
Hiding verbs inside nouns such as 'conduct an analysis of' instead of 'analyze'
steps: Draft freely without editing
Active pass: for each sentence, ask who is doing what, and put that actor and verb first; turn nominalizations back into verbs
Brief pass: delete filler ('due to the fact that', 'in order to', 'it should be noted'), duplicate points, and throat-clearing openings
Clear pass: confirm the main point and the requested action can be found in the first lines
Read it once as the recipient would, on a phone, and fix anything that slows you down
situations: Writing a project update email
Editing a report before sending it to leadership
Drafting a complaint or request to a service provider
Writing a self-review

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Part 1, Chapter 3 (Writing for Impact: Active, Brief, and Clear), sections Active (p. 46), Brief (p. 47), Clear (p. 48); also The Power of Editing, pp. 53-55, and Appendix A (Power Verbs)
source.underlying_research: The book draws on practitioner style sources (the index lists the SEC's Plain English Handbook, Nora Ephron, Anne Lamott, and Glenn Kramon of the New York Times, Appendix C). No experimental studies named. The advice aligns with plain-language research and with Joseph Williams' work on nominalizations in Style, which is my identification, not a book citation.

insights.confidence_rationale: The ABC structure is confirmed by the table of contents and the index (active voice pp. 46-47, eliminating weak verbs p. 48, reader attention span pp. 47-48). Well aligned with plain-language consensus. The specific editing passes in the steps are my operationalization.

supporting_evidence.note: Field evidence for Brief and Clear: a 49-word email beat a 127-word version (4.8 vs 2.7 percent response among 7,002 recipients), and truancy letters rewritten at a fifth-grade level were about 40 percent more effective at reducing absences than the standard 10th-grade letter.

insights.name: The Scan Test: Main Point on the Surface
insights.takeaway: Make sure a reader skimming only the subject line, headings, and first sentences still gets your point and request.
insights.explanation: A clear document is one whose argument and request survive a skim. If a busy reader looked only at the subject line, headings, and first sentences, they should still know what you are saying and what you need. The book's 'Clear' guidance includes writing informative headlines and headings, and reader notes report it suggests starting headlines with strong action verbs. 'Scan test' is this project's label for checking that, not the book's term.
insights.when_to_use: Longer emails, memos, proposals, and reports going to people with limited time, especially readers more senior than you or reading on mobile.
insights.worked_example: A nonprofit volunteer coordinator writes a two-page proposal to the board for a new weekend program. Her headings were 'Background', 'Details', 'Budget'. After applying the scan test, they become 'Weekend demand is up 40 percent', 'A pilot with 6 volunteers can cover it', 'We need 2,500 dollars and a vote on June 3'. A board member who reads only those lines knows the case and the ask. She uses the same idea for a family group chat about holiday plans: the first line states the proposed dates and asks for a yes or no by Sunday.
common_mistakes: Writing headings that label a section instead of stating its point
Putting the ask in the last paragraph, where skimmers never reach it
Assuming the reader will read every word because the topic matters to you
steps: Write your main point and your ask as two sentences before drafting
Put them in the subject line or opening lines
Turn each heading into a claim
Make each paragraph's first sentence its conclusion
Test: read only subject, headings, and first sentences; if the message is not clear, revise
situations: Sending a proposal to a busy executive
Writing a board or committee memo
Summarizing a long thread for someone who missed it

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 3, section Clear and headline writing (index: headlines/headings, pp. 48-51, 55, 80); Appendix A (Power Verbs)
source.underlying_research: None named in the book as far as I could verify. Related evidence (my identification): Nielsen Norman Group eye-tracking work on F-shaped scanning of web text, and the bottom line up front convention.

insights.confidence_rationale: Writing headings that carry the point is confirmed by the index and reader notes; the full skim test procedure and the 'scan test' name are not confirmed in the book text. Medium rating rests on strong practitioner consensus.

supporting_evidence.note: Minto's rule that headings and key-line points should be stated as ideas, not topic labels, is the structural basis for a document whose main point survives a skim.

Adds causal evidence for the scan test: in the authors' trial with 46,648 newsletter subscribers, adding headings doubled clicks on the lower part of the message without reducing engagement with the top. Rogers also endorses the military's bottom line up front rule.
Making the key points visible on the surface of a document is backed by signaling research showing better retention when important information and organization are explicitly cued.

insights.name: What, So What, Now What
insights.takeaway: Report the fact, explain why it matters to this audience, then state the action or decision it calls for.
insights.explanation: When you report information, synthesize rather than summarize. The book's 'Synthesis > Summary' section in the writing chapter presents 'What, so what, now what' as a way to deliver messages: the fact or development (what), why it matters to this audience (so what), and the action or decision it calls for (now what). A summary leaves the reader to do the thinking; a synthesis does it for them. Chapter 1 makes the same point when it urges students to synthesize case material into clear insights rather than restate it.
insights.when_to_use: Status updates, escalations, debriefs after meetings, reporting data or research results, and any time someone asks 'what's going on with X'.
insights.worked_example: An analyst is asked in a hallway how the customer survey went. Instead of reciting response rates, she says: 'Satisfaction dropped from 82 to 71 percent, almost all of it from onboarding complaints (what). That is the part of the journey we just changed, so it is probably our fault and fixable (so what). I would like to pull two people for a week to interview churned customers; can I get your OK (now what)?' At home, she uses the same shape when telling her partner the car inspection results: what failed, what it means for the budget, and the two options to decide between.
common_mistakes: Stopping at 'what' and calling it an update
Making the 'so what' about you instead of the listener's priorities
Leaving 'now what' vague, such as 'we should keep an eye on it'
steps: State the key fact or development in one sentence
Explain the implication for this specific listener
Name the action, decision, or next step and who owns it
If you need something, make the request explicit and time-bound
situations: Giving a weekly status update
Answering 'how did it go?' from a manager
Writing a post-meeting recap email
Explaining test results or news to a family member

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 3, section Synthesis > Summary, pp. 48-50 ('What, so what, now what' indexed at p. 49); see also Chapter 1, p. 23
source.underlying_research: The structure predates the book: it traces to Terry Borton's 1970 reflective model, later used by Rolfe, Freshwater and Jasper (2001), and Matt Abrahams teaches it for spontaneous speaking. The index lists Abrahams on p. 49, which suggests the book credits him there, but I could not read the page. No empirical test of it as a communication structure is known to me.

insights.confidence_rationale: Now confirmed in the book via the index and table of contents. A widely used structure in education and management practice, but not experimentally validated as a persuasion tool, so Medium.

supporting_evidence.note: Minto's vertical so-what test is the same move as synthesis over summary: each summary statement must state what the facts below it add up to.

insights.name: Parachute In: Skip the Preamble
insights.takeaway: Open at the most interesting moment, then add only the context needed; save names and logistics for later.
insights.explanation: Start at the most interesting or consequential moment instead of with introductions, agenda, or background. Schramm calls this parachuting in: drop the audience into the heart of the story, then supply only the context needed, leaving names and logistics for later or for whoever introduces you. He pairs it with a 'Goldilocks' rule for detail: too much loses the audience, too little leaves unintended questions. Reader notes on the speaking chapter add that he advises choosing your first and last words deliberately, since openings and closings shape what people remember.
insights.when_to_use: Openings of talks, pitches, stories, and emails; toasts and eulogies; introducing yourself in a networking or interview setting.
insights.worked_example: A hospital nurse speaking at a fundraising dinner had planned to start with her name, unit, and years of service. Instead she opens: 'At 3 a.m. last March, a seven-year-old asked me if she was going to die.' Her name and role follow in one sentence. She writes out and memorizes her last line so she does not trail off. Later that month she uses the same idea in a best-man speech, opening with the moment the couple met rather than thanking everyone first.
common_mistakes: Spending the first minute on logistics, thanks, and self-introduction when attention is highest
Parachuting in with drama that has nothing to do with the point
Leaving the ending to chance and closing with 'so, yeah, that's it' or 'any questions?'
steps: Identify the single most vivid or consequential moment in your material
Open there in one or two sentences
Add only the context the audience needs to follow
Script and rehearse your final sentence so it lands your intent
situations: Opening a keynote or team talk
Giving a wedding toast
Starting a pitch
Writing the first line of a cold email

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 4, section Storytelling, pp. 69-73 ('Parachute in' p. 70; 'Goldilocks theory' pp. 70-71); first and last words in Chapter 2, Verbal component (per reader notes); Schramm, 'How to Tell Your Story for Impact', Stanford GSB Insights (2011); '5 Steps to Sharper Stories', Communication Matters (Substack)
source.underlying_research: None named. Loosely consistent with serial-position (primacy and recency) effects in memory research (Murdock 1962; Ebbinghaus), although those findings come from word-list recall rather than speeches.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the index and in Schramm's own GSB workshop and newsletter. Expert consensus among speaking coaches; support from memory research is indirect (list-recall studies, not speeches).

supporting_evidence.note: Minto puts the answer immediately after a brief Situation-Complication-Question opening, a structured version of skipping the preamble.
Rogers highlights bottom line up front, noting it especially helps lower-status writers, who otherwise feel pressure to open with rapport-building preamble.

insights.name: One Thought, One Person
insights.takeaway: When presenting, deliver one complete thought while looking at one person, then move to someone else for the next.
insights.explanation: When speaking to a group, deliver one complete thought to one person while looking at them, then turn and deliver the next complete thought to someone else. This replaces scanning or staring at slides with a series of small conversations, which steadies your pace, reduces filler between thoughts, and makes each listener feel addressed. Reader notes report the book suggests holding eye contact for roughly four to five seconds, the length of a thought, and pairing it with a grounded stance and arms relaxed at your sides rather than tucked at the elbows. Schramm also encourages stepping toward the audience and using gestures rather than staying frozen in place.
insights.when_to_use: Presentations, meetings where you hold the floor, panel answers, and toasts. Adapts to video by treating the camera lens as the person.
insights.worked_example: A junior engineer presenting a design review tends to read from her slides and race. She practices finishing each sentence while looking at one colleague, pausing, then moving to another. Her pace slows naturally and her 'ums' drop because she breathes between thoughts. At a family reunion, she uses the same approach for a short tribute to her grandmother, landing each memory on a different relative.
common_mistakes: Darting eyes across the room mid-sentence (scanning) instead of finishing the thought
Fixating on one friendly face or only the most senior person
Treating the guidance as a rigid timer rather than one thought per person
steps: Break your content into short complete thoughts
Pick one listener and deliver a full thought to them
Pause briefly as you finish
Turn your body slightly and deliver the next thought to someone in a different part of the room
On video, deliver key thoughts to the camera lens
situations: Presenting to a room of colleagues
Answering a question on a panel
Giving a toast or eulogy
Speaking up in a large meeting

source.citation: Schramm with Levy, Communicate with Mastery, Chapter 2, Visual component (eye contact p. 37, gestures p. 38) and Chapter 4 storytelling ('one person with one thought', p. 71); Schramm, 'How to Tell Your Story for Impact', Stanford GSB Insights (2011)
source.underlying_research: None named in the book as far as I could verify. Eye contact research (for example, Kleinke 1986, Psychological Bulletin) links gaze to attention and perceived credibility, but I found no study supporting a precise duration such as four to five seconds.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the index and reader notes, and in Schramm's own workshop advice. The value of eye contact has research support; specific timings do not.

insights.name: Story Spine: Once Upon a Time to Until Now
insights.takeaway: Know your end point, then shape the anecdote as normal situation, disruption, consequences, and what has changed now.
insights.explanation: A simple sequence of prompts to turn an anecdote into a story with a point: once upon a time (the normal situation), then one day (the disruption), because of that (the consequences), until now (where things stand and what changed). Schramm stresses that the difference between talking and storytelling is intention: you must know the end point you want the audience to reach before you begin. For organizations, he argues stories should center on what changed for people rather than on how busy the organization has been.
insights.when_to_use: Pitches, fundraising, job interviews (behavioral questions), team kickoffs, explaining a change, and personal stories at gatherings.
insights.worked_example: A job candidate is asked about a time she handled a setback. Using the spine: our support team had a steady three-hour response time (once upon a time); then one day a product bug tripled ticket volume (then one day); because of that, I set up a triage rota and a public status page (because of that); until now, response time is under two hours even at peak, and the rota is standard practice (until now).
