Joking while delivering serious bad news, which can read as minimizing it
steps: Decide whether this message must be believed and acted on
If yes, state it plainly first; add a light line only after the point has landed, if at all
If it is a minor admission where you mainly want rapport, a light touch is fine
situations: Telling a manager you are overloaded
Flagging a project risk
Admitting a weakness in an interview
Raising a recurring issue with a partner

source.citation: Not found in Humor, Seriously in any source read; included as a boundary condition from the same research group the book draws on
source.underlying_research: Bitterly, T. B., and Schweitzer, M. E. (2019). The impression management benefits of humorous self-disclosures: How humor influences perceptions of veracity. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 151, 73-89. doi:10.1016/j.obhdp.2019.01.005. Five studies; disclosures paired with humor are judged less likely to be true, and humor can boost perceived warmth and competence; proposes the Speaker's Inferred Motive model.

insights.confidence_rationale: Abstract read and matches the explanation. Peer-reviewed, five studies, plausible mechanism, single research group, no independent replication found. Not confirmed in the book: none of the reviews, talks, or excerpts read mention it.

insights.name: Four Humor Styles: Stand-up, Sweetheart, Magnet, Sniper
insights.takeaway: Know your default humor style and your team's, so you can predict where your humor might misfire.
insights.explanation: The authors sort humor into four styles along two dimensions: content (from affiliative and uplifting to edgier and more aggressive) and delivery (from expressive and spontaneous to subtle and planned). The Stand-up is a bold, natural entertainer willing to ruffle feathers; the Sweetheart is earnest and understated and uses humor to lighten the mood; the Magnet is expressive, charismatic and happy to be silly; the Sniper is edgy, sarcastic and nuanced, a master of the unexpected dig. They say most people fall mainly into one or two styles and can flex depending on context. Knowing your default, and your team's, helps you predict where your humor might misfire.
insights.when_to_use: When joining a new team or culture; when your humor has landed badly and you want to understand why; when managing people whose humor differs from yours.
insights.worked_example: A sales manager with a Sniper style realizes his deadpan sarcasm reads as cutting on video calls with a new overseas team who do not know him. He shifts toward a warmer, more Sweetheart-like register with them (appreciative, specific callbacks to their wins) while keeping his dry humor for colleagues who know his intent. With friends who share his style, nothing changes.
common_mistakes: Treating the style as a fixed personality label
Using a Sniper or Stand-up style with people who lack the relationship to read your intent
Assuming your style is the universal standard for what is funny
steps: Place yourself on the two axes: is your humor more affiliative or edgy, more expressive or subtle?
Identify the blind spot of your style (for example Snipers can wound, Stand-ups can cross lines, Magnets can seem unserious, Sweethearts can go unnoticed)
Notice the dominant styles on your team or in your family
Flex toward warmer, more affiliative content with people who do not know you well
situations: Joining a new team
Working across cultures
Understanding why sarcasm hurt someone
Managing a team with mixed personalities

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, humor styles material with a Humor Styles Mini Quiz in the appendix; online quiz at humorseriously.com; Stanford GSB Class Takeaways video
source.underlying_research: Authors' own typology, described in the GSB video as coming from 'our research', with no published validation located. It resembles the two-dimension logic of the academic Humor Styles Questionnaire (Martin, Puhlik-Doris, Larsen, Gray and Weir, 2003, Journal of Research in Personality 37, 48-75), which distinguishes affiliative, self-enhancing, aggressive and self-defeating humor, but the book was not verified as deriving from or validating against it.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book and on the authors' site. No reliability or validity data for the four-style typology or its quiz were found in any source checked; it works like a personality-type quiz. The general point that affiliative humor is safer than aggressive humor has stronger support from HSQ research.

insights.name: Truth plus Misdirection
insights.takeaway: Build humor from a recognizable truth plus a surprise, putting the funny word last and being specific.
insights.explanation: The authors present humor as built from two parts: a truth the audience recognizes (an observation about shared experience) and a misdirection that sets up one expectation and then delivers a surprise. Practical devices include: listing things in threes where the third breaks the pattern, putting the funny word at the very end of the sentence, using contrast or exaggeration, being specific rather than generic, and calling back to something said earlier. The craft keeps humor grounded in what is real rather than in invented zingers.
insights.when_to_use: When preparing an opening for a talk or toast, writing a team announcement, or crafting a memorable line in a presentation.
insights.worked_example: Opening a quarterly review, an analyst says: 'This quarter we improved retention, cut costs, and discovered the office coffee machine has a descaling setting.' The first two items set a pattern; the third breaks it with a specific, true, shared detail. Later, when the coffee machine appears again in a slide on facilities spending, the callback gets a bigger laugh than the original. At a friend's birthday, she uses the same three-part structure in a short toast.
common_mistakes: Burying the punch word in the middle of the sentence
Being generic ('meetings are boring') instead of specific
Overusing a callback until it wears out
Reaching for invented or exaggerated stories that are not true and undermine trust
steps: Write down a few true, specific observations your audience shares
Pick one and set up an expectation (a list, a serious framing)
Deliver a twist at the end, ideally the final word
Keep it short and move on; look for a natural later moment to call back to it
situations: Opening a presentation
Giving a wedding or birthday toast
Writing a team newsletter
Closing a long workshop

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 3, The Anatomy of Funny (Principle 1, truth, p. 69; Principle 2, surprise and misdirection, p. 70); Stanford GSB review of the book on the rule of three
source.underlying_research: Comedy craft from improv and stand-up practitioners (The Second City's Anne Libera and Kelly Leonard among others); the book links misdirection to incongruity-resolution theory

insights.confidence_rationale: Truth and misdirection principles and the rule of three are confirmed in the book; specificity is confirmed in the authors' podcast. Strong practitioner consensus and incongruity accounts are widely accepted in humor research. Devices such as end placement and callbacks were not confirmed in sources read and remain craft knowledge rather than tested findings.

insights.name: Truth, Pain, Distance Check
insights.takeaway: Before a risky joke, check whether the bare statement is appropriate, how painful the subject is, and whether you have earned it.
insights.explanation: To judge whether a joke risks crossing a line, the authors adapt a framework from Anne Libera of The Second City. Truth: strip the humor away and ask whether the underlying statement is still appropriate for this audience and setting; if the bare claim would offend, the joke will too. Pain: how raw is the subject for the people present? Distance: has enough time passed, and are you close enough to the person or experience (or do you share it) to earn the right to joke? The more pain and the less distance, the higher the risk. They also stress reading the room: how will this make people feel, not just will it get a laugh.
insights.when_to_use: Before joking about anything sensitive: layoffs, illness, a recent failure, politics, identity, someone's personal situation; and when writing humor that may be forwarded to unknown readers.
insights.worked_example: A week after layoffs, a manager considers opening a meeting with a joke about 'surviving the Hunger Games.' He runs the check: the underlying truth (people lost jobs) is painful, the pain is fresh, and he was not among those affected. He drops it. Six months later, in a retrospective, a colleague who was nearly laid off herself makes a gentle joke about it, and it lands, because there is more distance and she has standing. Similarly, someone holds off on a joke about a friend's breakup until the friend jokes about it first.
common_mistakes: Assuming good intent makes a joke acceptable
Joking about a painful event too soon, or about pain that is not yours
Forgetting that written jokes travel to audiences you did not plan for
steps: Truth: remove the joke and say the underlying claim plainly; would it be fine in this room?
Pain: how much does the topic hurt the people present, or people who might hear about it?
Distance: is the event recent? Is it yours to joke about?
Audience: how will each person, not just the majority, feel?
If any answer is doubtful, choose a different target or skip the joke
situations: After layoffs or a reorg
When a colleague is grieving or ill
Posting in a company-wide chat channel
Comforting a friend after a breakup

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 7, Navigating the Gray Areas of Humor (pp. 181 to 186: truth, pain and distance; examine the truth, consider pain and distance, read the room); TED talk on checking your distance
source.underlying_research: Anne Libera (The Second City, Columbia College Chicago), truth, pain and distance framework from comedy practice; related to benign violation theory (McGraw and Warren, 2010), which the book was not verified as citing

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book with page references. Credible expert framework from a leading comedy institution, consistent with academic theories that humor needs a violation that also feels safe or distant. Not itself an empirically tested decision rule.

insights.name: Recovering After Crossing the Line
insights.takeaway: If a joke crosses a line, recognize it, understand why it hurt, and apologize directly without defending your intent.
insights.explanation: The authors distinguish between a joke that simply falls flat (usually harmless) and one that crosses a line, often without the teller noticing. The book offers a three-step recovery: recognize that a line was crossed, work out why it hurt so it does not recur, and correct it with an apology. In practice that means not defending your intent or suggesting the listener is too sensitive, and making the acknowledgment direct and specific.
insights.when_to_use: When a joke gets silence plus visible discomfort, when someone tells you afterward that a remark hurt, or when a written joke draws a negative reaction.
insights.worked_example: In a meeting, a team lead jokes that a colleague 'only speaks in acronyms like an engineer from the 90s.' Later the colleague, who is the oldest on the team, says it stung. Instead of saying 'it was just a joke,' the lead thanks him for telling her, says she can see it touched on his age, apologizes specifically, and, at the next meeting, avoids age-related humor entirely. With a sibling, the same approach works after a family dinner where a teasing comment about a job loss went too far.
common_mistakes: Responding with 'I was only joking' or 'you are too sensitive'
Over-apologizing for a joke that merely flopped, which draws more attention than the joke
Apologizing vaguely without naming what was hurtful
steps: Distinguish a flop (move on) from harm (address it)
Acknowledge: if harm, thank the person for telling you and accept that a line was crossed rather than defending intent
Diagnose: identify what made it hurtful (truth, pain, distance, status, audience)
Correct: apologize specifically and briefly, and change the behavior going forward
situations: A joke offended a colleague
A teasing comment hurt a family member
Your joke in a group chat drew a negative reaction

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 7, Navigating the Gray Areas of Humor (p. 181 notes the framework helps explain in retrospect why humor crossed a line); three-step recovery process described in Blaszczynski's review in Business Forum
source.underlying_research: Practitioner guidance; no specific study identified

insights.confidence_rationale: The three-step recovery (recognize, diagnose, apologize) is confirmed by an academic review of the book. Some detail in the steps (thanking the person, not defending intent) is my paraphrase of the spirit rather than confirmed wording. Consistent with research and consensus on effective apologies, but not itself tested.

insights.name: Shared Laughter Opens People Up
insights.takeaway: Share a laugh early in a relationship; it can make the conversation that follows more open and trusting.
insights.explanation: The authors argue that laughing together builds trust and connection quickly. They cite research in which strangers who watched a funny clip before a get-to-know-you exercise disclosed more intimate information than those who watched a neutral clip (the book and its promotion give the figure as about 30 percent more); in the paper the effect showed up in observers' ratings, not in participants' own. They also cite work finding that couples who recalled laughing together reported higher relationship satisfaction. Related research links social laughter to raised pain thresholds, read as a sign of endorphin release that may support bonding. The practical point: shared laughter early in a relationship can make the conversation that follows more open.
insights.when_to_use: At the start of a new working relationship, a kickoff, an offsite, a first date, or any meeting where you need candor.
insights.worked_example: Before a sensitive project retrospective, a facilitator opens with a quick exercise where each person shares the most ridiculous workaround they used during the project. The laughter that follows makes it easier for people to be honest about what actually went wrong. In personal life, a couple trying to reconnect plans an evening watching a comedy together before talking about something they have been avoiding.
common_mistakes: Treating laughter as a manipulation tactic to extract disclosure
Assuming shared laughter repairs a relationship where trust has been seriously broken
Using laughter at someone's expense, which bonds the group but not the target
situations: Project kickoff with a new team
Team offsite
First date
Opening a candid retrospective

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 2, This Is Your Brain on Humor (p. 44, humor builds bonds by quickening trust and self-disclosure); Chapter 8, A Secret Weapon in Life (p. 205); TED talk; Stanford GSB 2017 article
source.underlying_research: Gray, A. W., Parkinson, B., and Dunbar, R. I. M. (2015). Laughter's influence on the intimacy of self-disclosure. Human Nature, 26(1), 28-43 (cited by the authors). Bazzini, D. G., Stack, E. R., Martincin, P. D., and Davis, C. P. (2007). The effect of reminiscing about laughter on relationship satisfaction. Motivation and Emotion, 31(1), 25-34 (cited by the authors). Dunbar, R. I. M., et al. (2012). Social laughter is correlated with an elevated pain threshold. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 279(1731), 1161-1167 (related; not confirmed as cited, though the book claims laughter releases endorphins).

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book; Gray et al. and Bazzini et al. confirmed as cited. Peer-reviewed findings, and the broader idea that shared positive experiences build bonds is well supported. But the disclosure study is a modest student sample, the effect appeared only in observer ratings, the 30 percent figure is not in the abstract, and the hormone claims in the book (oxytocin, dopamine, cortisol) go beyond what these studies measured.

insights.name: A Light Opener Warms a Negotiation
insights.takeaway: Add a small, light line to a negotiation or sales offer; it can build trust and improve the outcome.
insights.explanation: The authors argue that a small dose of humor can make you more persuasive in a negotiation or sale. Their headline example is a 1981 experiment in which participants haggled over the price of a piece of art: when the seller's final offer ended with a throwaway line about including a pet frog, buyers made larger concessions (the authors report about 18 percent more, rounded to nearly 20 percent in their TED talk). Separate research on email negotiations found that pairs where one side opened with a humorous message reported more trust and satisfaction and reached better joint outcomes, with the person who used humor also doing better individually.
insights.when_to_use: Opening an email negotiation with a vendor or client, salary discussions where tension is rising, or any back-and-forth where the other side may see you as an adversary.
insights.worked_example: Before a contract renewal with a supplier, a procurement lead opens her email with a short, friendly line about how both companies' legal teams must be competing for a record in comment bubbles, then states her position clearly. The reply comes back warmer, and the counterpart is more forthcoming about what flexibility they have. She keeps the humor to one line and does not joke about the price itself.
common_mistakes: Joking about the substance (price, terms) so your position seems less serious
Using sarcasm in writing, which can read as hostility without tone of voice
Overdoing it so you seem unprepared
steps: Open with one brief, warm, non-sarcastic line about a shared experience
State your actual position plainly and seriously
If tension rises later, a light, self-directed comment can reset the tone
situations: Negotiating a vendor contract by email
Salary negotiation
Resolving a billing dispute with a client
Splitting household chores with a partner or roommate

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 2, This Is Your Brain on Humor (humor and power, p. 44); TED talk (pet frog line); Stanford GSB 2017 and 2021 articles
source.underlying_research: O'Quin, K., and Aronoff, J. (1981). Humor as a technique of social influence. Social Psychology Quarterly, 44(4), 349-357, doi:10.2307/3033903 (the book's frog study; the 18 percent figure comes from the authors' summaries, not checked against the paper). Kurtzberg, T. R., Naquin, C. E., and Belkin, L. Y. (2009). Humor as a relationship-building tool in online negotiations. International Journal of Conflict Management, 20(4), 377-397 (two experiments, 122 executive MBA and 216 MBA students; abstract read; not confirmed as cited in the book).

insights.confidence_rationale: The book's negotiation study is now identified (O'Quin and Aronoff, 1981). It is a single, old lab study whose effect size is known here only from the authors' summaries. Kurtzberg et al. add peer-reviewed experimental support with student samples in simulated negotiations. No large replication found, so Medium rather than High.

supporting_evidence.note: Brief personal conversation before an email negotiation improved economic and social outcomes (Morris et al. 2002), consistent with warming up a negotiation before business.

insights.name: Small Levity in Everyday Writing
insights.takeaway: Replace autopilot formality in routine messages with small warm touches, choosing clear lightness over sarcasm.
insights.explanation: The authors encourage replacing autopilot formality with small, human touches in routine communication, such as a more personal email sign-off, a specific observation in a status note, or a playful subject line, rather than trying to be funny in big ways. The bar is low: the aim is a moment of warmth and recognition, not laughter. In writing, choose warm, clear lightness over sarcasm, since tone is easily misread without voice and faces.
insights.when_to_use: Routine emails, team chat, status updates, calendar invites, out-of-office messages, thank-you notes.
insights.worked_example: Instead of signing every email 'Best regards,' an operations analyst ends a Friday report with 'Wishing you a weekend with zero spreadsheet errors.' Her out-of-office reply says she is offline hiking and will return with fewer emails and more blisters. Colleagues mention that her messages are the ones they actually read. She keeps the sarcastic jokes out of channels where new or senior people may misread them.
common_mistakes: Using sarcasm or irony in text with people who do not know you well
Adding levity to messages delivering bad news or formal decisions
Making every message cute so the content gets lost
steps: Identify one routine message you send often (sign-off, out-of-office, weekly update)
Swap the default phrasing for something specific, warm, and true
Keep the substance first and clear
Check for tone misreading: would a stranger or a senior leader read it as intended?
situations: Writing a weekly status email
Setting an out-of-office message
Posting in team chat
Sending a thank-you note

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 4, Putting Your Funny to Work (communicating with levity: email sign-offs, out-of-office messages, Deloitte's Bullfighter tool for jargon); TED talk; Stanford GSB Class Takeaways video
source.underlying_research: Practitioner advice and case stories; the book's argument that language shapes behavior is framed loosely. Tone-misreading risk in text is consistent with research on email egocentrism (Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng, 2005), not verified as cited in the book.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book's Chapter 4. Plausible, low-risk advice, but no direct evidence that small levity in routine messages improves outcomes. The caution about sarcasm in text rests on separate, stronger research.

supporting_evidence.note: Supports choosing warm lightness over sarcasm in writing: in Study 5, senders who had seen jokes performed expected email recipients to find them funnier, although recipients' ratings were no different.

insights.name: Leaders Set the Levity Culture
insights.takeaway: As a leader, make room for humor by laughing at others' jokes, accepting gentle teasing, and building light rituals.
insights.explanation: The authors argue that the most powerful way a leader shapes a culture of humor is not by being the funniest person but by making room for others: laughing at others' jokes, being willing to be the target of gentle teasing, celebrating small absurdities, and building light rituals into team life. Gravity and levity can coexist: you can take the work seriously without taking yourself too seriously. They cite a field study of 54 team meetings in which back-and-forth humor patterns (a joke, then laughter, then another joke) went with better team performance immediately and two years later, though not in teams with high job insecurity. They also report that employees who see their boss as having any sense of humor rate that boss 27 percent more motivating and admired and are 15 percent more satisfied; treat those percentages loosely.
insights.when_to_use: When you lead a team, run a recurring meeting, plan an offsite, or notice that people are guarded and quiet.
insights.worked_example: A new engineering manager notices her team rarely jokes in her presence. She starts by being an appreciative audience (genuinely laughing at a teammate's dry comment in standup), shares a small mistake of her own lightly, and introduces a monthly 'best bug of the month' award with a silly trophy. Over a few months, people start teasing her gently about her many sticky notes, which she takes as a sign of trust. A parent can do the same at the dinner table by laughing at kids' jokes rather than always being the one making them.
common_mistakes: Mandating fun or forcing participation in humor activities (the book quotes Ed Catmull: fun is not top-down)
Being the only one allowed to joke
Using humor to dodge accountability during serious moments
Pushing levity while people fear for their jobs, when the research shows its benefit fades
steps: Be a generous audience: laugh at and build on others' humor
Model low-stakes self-directed humor and accept gentle teasing
Create a small, optional ritual that celebrates absurd or human moments
Keep serious moments serious; levity complements rather than replaces gravity
situations: Becoming a new manager
Running a weekly standup
Planning a team offsite
Family dinners

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 5, Leading with Humor (pp. 134 to 147) and Chapter 6, Creating a Culture of Levity (pp. 155 to 161); TED talk; Stanford GSB podcast (being generous with laughter)
source.underlying_research: Lehmann-Willenbrock, N., and Allen, J. A. (2014). How fun are your meetings? Investigating the relationship between humor patterns in team interactions and team performance. Journal of Applied Psychology, 99(6), 1278-1287 (54 videotaped team meetings; humor patterns, not humor alone, predicted performance; boundary condition of job insecurity). The 27 percent figure: CNBC reports the authors cite a study in Social Behavior and Personality; the matching paper appears to be Decker, W. H. (1987), Managerial humor and subordinate satisfaction, Social Behavior and Personality 15(2), 225-232 (survey of 290 workers; those rating supervisors high in humor reported higher job satisfaction and rated supervisors higher on other qualities). The abstract does not report 27 or 15 percent, so the mapping is inferred. The book also cites a 2018 Gallup engagement report on approachable managers.

insights.confidence_rationale: Raised from Low to Medium: verification found a peer-reviewed field study the book cites (Lehmann-Willenbrock and Allen, 2014) with real teams and a two-year follow-up, plus a likely source for the leader statistic. Still not High: the field study is correlational with an important boundary condition, the 1987 survey is cross-sectional same-source self-report from which the exact percentages cannot be checked, and much of the chapter rests on executive anecdotes.

supporting_evidence.note: An independent systematic review confirms leader humor is positively associated with follower outcomes, but the evidence is mostly correlational survey data with unresolved measurement problems. Treat confident percentage claims about leader humor (such as 27 percent more motivating) as illustrative, not established effects.

The meta-analysis links supervisor positive humor with subordinate satisfaction, workgroup cohesion and perceived supervisor performance, which supports the direction of the book's claim; but the associations are correlational and modest, so they do not show that a leader adding humor will produce those results.

The review summarizes Lehmann-Willenbrock and Allen (2014), where humor and laughter patterns in recorded team meetings triggered constructive behaviors such as proposing solutions and predicted team performance, including two years later.

insights.name: The Bad Idea Brainstorm
insights.takeaway: Ask your group for the worst, silliest ideas possible to lower the stakes and surface unusual options worth building on.
insights.explanation: Asking a group for good ideas makes people censor anything that sounds silly, and that filter also removes many unusual ideas worth having. The authors describe a leader who instead asks for the silliest, worst ideas possible. The request lowers the stakes, makes the session playful, and gives people permission to say odd things, some of which turn out to be useful once the group starts building on them. The book also argues that starting a work session with levity helps people break out of habitual thinking.
insights.when_to_use: When a brainstorm keeps producing safe, predictable ideas; when a team is anxious about looking foolish; when kicking off a creative session.
insights.worked_example: A product team stuck on how to reduce customer churn spends ten minutes generating the worst possible retention ideas: hide the cancel button inside a riddle, send a sad violin video to anyone who leaves, call each customer's mother. After the laughter, the facilitator asks what is underneath each bad idea. The 'call their mother' idea leads to a real one: a personal call from a support rep in the first month, aimed at customers who have not set up the product. At home, a family planning a cheap holiday does the same, and 'camp in the backyard' turns into a weekend at a nearby campsite.
common_mistakes: Mocking the bad ideas or the people who offer them, which shuts the exercise down
Stopping at the laughter without flipping the bad ideas into usable ones
Announcing it as a fun team-building exercise in a way that feels forced
steps: Frame the ask explicitly: we want the worst, silliest ideas we can come up with
Set a short time box and capture everything without judgment
For each bad idea, ask what makes it bad and what the opposite or underlying need is
Pick the most promising flipped ideas and develop them in a normal round
situations: Running a stuck brainstorm
Kicking off a creative workshop
Planning something with family or friends
Helping a nervous team speak up

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 4 material on shifting mindsets and unlocking creativity on teams (pp. 119 to 124), quoting Teller, the head of Alphabet's X lab (Astro Teller)
source.underlying_research: Leader anecdote; the book also cites a general claim that humor reveals new connections and creates psychological safety. No study testing the bad-idea format specifically was identified in sources read.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via a review's quotations, but it rests on one leader's practice. It is plausible and low-risk and fits wider brainstorming practice (reverse brainstorming), yet thinly supported as a tested technique.

supporting_evidence.note: Both tackle self-censorship in group ideation; Rogelberg's silent brainstorming rests on the well-replicated production-blocking literature, which gives a stronger evidence base for the same goal of getting unfiltered ideas.

insights.name: A Light Line Makes the Point Stick
insights.takeaway: Attach a light moment to the point you most want remembered, not to a side detail.
insights.explanation: The authors argue that humor makes ideas more memorable, so a small, well-placed light moment can become the thing an audience remembers. Their example is a long State of the Union address in which a brief, mild joke about overlapping regulation of salmon became the word listeners most often recalled the next day. Lab research supports the general effect: humorous sentences are recalled better than plain versions of the same content, apparently because they draw more attention and rehearsal. The practical lesson is to attach the light moment to the point you most want remembered, not to a side detail.
insights.when_to_use: When a long presentation, training or update has one point that must stick; when writing an all-hands message or a pitch.
insights.worked_example: A safety manager giving a 40-minute quarterly briefing has one critical message: badge in at the loading dock every time. Instead of a joke in the opener, she places a short, true line right on that point: the loading dock door has now been propped open by more people than attended last year's holiday party. Weeks later, people repeat the line, and with it the rule. A parent uses the same idea, putting the silly rhyme on the one house rule that matters.
common_mistakes: Putting the memorable joke on a tangent, so people remember the joke and not the point
Using so much humor that nothing stands out
Assuming a remembered joke means the message was persuasive
situations: Delivering a long training or briefing
Writing an all-hands announcement
Pitching an idea to executives
Teaching a child a house rule

source.citation: Aaker and Bagdonas, Humor, Seriously, Chapter 2, This Is Your Brain on Humor (p. 44, humor makes our ideas more memorable); Stanford GSB Think Fast, Talk Smart podcast (State of the Union salmon example and NPR listener survey); Stanford GSB 2017 article
source.underlying_research: Schmidt, S. R. (1994). Effects of humor on sentence memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 20(4), 953-967 (humorous sentences better recalled; effect strongest when humorous and plain items are mixed). Not confirmed as cited in the book. The salmon example is an informal NPR listener poll, and the authors' dopamine explanation is not tested in these sources.

insights.confidence_rationale: The claim is confirmed in the authors' material and the memory advantage for humorous material is supported by peer-reviewed lab work. But the lab effect is largely limited to mixed lists, the book's example is anecdotal, and memorability does not equal persuasion.

insights.name: Say Yes to the Offer
insights.takeaway: Treat what others bring you as material to accept and build on, without becoming someone who agrees to everything.
insights.explanation: In improv, anything a partner says or does is an offer, and the scene only moves when you accept it and build on it. Madson applies this to daily life: treat what other people bring you (an idea, a request, a complaint, a joke) as material to work with rather than something to block, correct, or explain away. Saying yes here means accepting the reality of what was offered and adding to it, not becoming a pushover who agrees to everything; she explicitly separates it from being a yes-man.
insights.when_to_use: Brainstorms, early-stage discussions of a colleague's idea, playful or emotional bids from a partner or child, and any conversation where your reflex is to say 'yes, but' before you have understood what was offered.
insights.worked_example: In a planning meeting, a junior analyst suggests running the customer survey by text message. Your instinct is to say the response rates will be terrible. Instead you say: 'Yes, and if we try it with one segment first, we would know within a week whether it beats email.' The idea gets tested, the analyst keeps contributing, and you still raised the risk, just as a next step rather than a veto. At home, your partner says 'let's skip cooking and have breakfast for dinner'; you add 'and eat it on the balcony' instead of listing what is in the fridge.
common_mistakes: Treating 'yes, and' as agreeing to commitments you cannot keep or decisions that are actually wrong
Saying the words 'yes, and' while the content still blocks or replaces the other person's idea
Using it to avoid raising real risks, which erodes trust later
steps: Notice the offer: name to yourself what the other person actually proposed or expressed
Accept the core of it out loud (acknowledge it as real and worth considering)
Add one concrete build: a next step, a variation, or a question that extends it
Raise concerns as additions ('and to make that work we would need...') rather than vetoes
Reserve an honest no for commitments and decisions, not for ideas in exploration
situations: Brainstorming with a team
Responding to a colleague's half-formed idea
Responding to a partner's spontaneous suggestion
Playing with children

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 1 'Say Yes' (about pp. 27-32 per the Admired Leadership summary; blocking defined around p. 29, yes-and around p. 30)
source.underlying_research: None cited in the book. Related but indirect: Felsman, Gunawardena & Seifert (2020, Thinking Skills and Creativity 35) found that 20 minutes of improv exercises, versus a matched social-interaction control, raised divergent thinking, positive affect and uncertainty tolerance; Lewis & Lovatt (2013, Thinking Skills and Creativity 9) linked improvisation to higher divergent thinking. No controlled study isolates 'yes, and' versus 'yes, but' on workplace outcomes.

insights.confidence_rationale: Strong practitioner consensus across the improv and applied-improv field, and lab studies show improv exercises (which embed accepting offers) aid divergent thinking and uncertainty tolerance. But the specific 'yes, and' rule has not been isolated experimentally, and business evidence is mostly workshop self-report.

supporting_evidence.note: Ury's accommodate trap marks the limit of saying yes to every offer: accepting a request you should refuse harms both your interests and, through later resentment, the relationship. Accept the reality of the request, then answer it with a Positive No when needed.

insights.name: Drop the Script (Don't Over-Prepare)
insights.takeaway: Prepare your purpose and material, then set the script aside and respond to what is actually happening.
insights.explanation: Madson argues that rehearsing exactly what you will say pulls your attention into your head and the future, so you miss what is actually happening and sound canned; in the chapter she frames 'don't prepare' as letting go of ego involvement and redirecting energy to the present. In interviews she says she is not against preparation: prepare as much as you like, then set it aside and show up, since your whole life is your preparation. The useful distinction for communicators is between preparing your purpose and material (good) and scripting lines and anticipating every reply (often counterproductive in live interaction).
insights.when_to_use: Networking, Q and A sessions, job interviews, difficult personal conversations, and social situations where you notice yourself rehearsing your next line instead of listening.
insights.worked_example: Before a one-on-one with a new skip-level manager, you were going to rehearse a three-minute speech about your accomplishments. Instead you prepare two facts you want her to know and one question you genuinely want answered, then walk in and respond to what she raises. When she opens by asking about a customer escalation you had not planned for, you can engage with it because you are not waiting to deliver a script.
common_mistakes: Reading 'don't prepare' literally and skipping research for high-stakes presentations or negotiations
Memorizing word-for-word, then freezing when the order breaks
Planning your reply while the other person is still talking
steps: Prepare the substance: your goal and two or three key points or facts
Skip scripting exact sentences or imagined dialogues; if you need notes, write questions to yourself rather than sentences
Before you go in, set the preparation aside
In the conversation, put attention on the other person and what they just said
Let your points surface when they connect to what is happening
situations: Answering unexpected questions in a meeting
Job interview follow-up questions
Meeting a senior leader one-on-one
Making small talk at an event

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 2 'Don't Prepare' (about pp. 35-44); Madson on Stanford GSB Think Fast Talk Smart episode 100 (2023) and in the Humor That Works interview
source.underlying_research: Not research-based in the book. Felsman, Gunawardena & Seifert (2020, Thinking Skills and Creativity) found brief improv exercises, versus a matched social-interaction control, raised tolerance of uncertainty. Counterpoint: mainstream public-speaking instruction holds that preparation and practice help performance and reduce anxiety (general consensus, no specific study checked here), so the literal slogan is contestable; Madson herself disclaims it.

insights.confidence_rationale: The narrower claim (scripting conversation reduces responsiveness; improvising builds comfort with uncertainty) has credible expert support and some lab evidence. The broad slogan is contested by evidence that preparation helps; use the narrow version.

insights.name: Show Up and Act Now (Action Before Readiness)
insights.takeaway: Do not wait to feel ready; show up and take the next concrete step while still nervous.
insights.explanation: Just Show Up (chapter 3) and Act Now (chapter 11) are separate chapters in the book, but they share one idea drawn from David K. Reynolds's Constructive Living: you do not need to feel confident, motivated, or ready before acting. Just Show Up is about getting your body to where things happen, since motivation and good feelings are not prerequisites; Act Now recasts the order as ready, fire, aim, with action itself supplying the information about what to do next. Feelings are not controllable on demand, but behavior is, so you take the next concrete step while the nervousness is still there; on the Stanford podcast she put it as step first, then see where you are.
insights.when_to_use: When you are avoiding a networking event, delaying a hard call, waiting to 'feel ready' to speak up in meetings, or putting off reaching out to an estranged friend.
insights.worked_example: You have been putting off calling a client about a missed deadline because you dread the reaction. Instead of waiting until you feel calm, you accept the knot in your stomach, dial within the next ten minutes, and open with the facts and your recovery plan. Personally, you have wanted to reconnect with an old friend for months; rather than composing the perfect message, you send 'Thought of you today, coffee soon?' and let the conversation take shape from there.
common_mistakes: Waiting for anxiety to disappear before acting
Treating action-first as license to skip thinking about consequences in high-stakes situations
Showing up physically but staying mentally elsewhere (phone, rehearsing)
steps: Name the feeling (nervous, reluctant) without trying to argue it away
Identify the smallest concrete next action (send the invite, raise your hand, dial)
Do it now, with the feeling present
Once in motion, look at what is in front of you and take the next step
situations: Going to a networking event alone
Making a dreaded phone call
Speaking up for the first time in a meeting
Reaching out to a friend you have drifted from

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 3 'Just Show Up' (about pp. 45-52) and chapter 11 'Act Now' (about p. 122); Stanford GSB Think Fast Talk Smart episode 100 (2023)
source.underlying_research: The book quotes David K. Reynolds (Constructive Living, itself based on Morita therapy and Naikan) rather than research. Related external evidence: behavioral activation and exposure-based treatments (well-established literatures, cited here as general context, not a specific study) support acting despite feelings. Brooks (2014, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 143) found that reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement improved singing, public speaking and math performance; this is related (working with anxiety rather than waiting for calm) but tests reappraisal, not action-first. Morita therapy has limited Western trial evidence.

insights.confidence_rationale: The principle that action can precede and reduce anxiety aligns with well-established exposure and behavioral activation research, but the book presents it as philosophy, and its Morita source has thin controlled evidence.

supporting_evidence.note: Randomized-trial evidence that repeatedly doing the feared speaking task, as part of a structured program, reduces fear of public speaking substantially (pooled g = 0.74), giving an evidence base to acting before you feel ready.

insights.name: Start Anywhere, Start With the Obvious
insights.takeaway: When stuck, start with the most obvious thing in front of you and adjust as you go.
insights.explanation: Paralysis often comes from searching for the perfect beginning or the clever idea. Madson advises that with a big task or confusing problem you begin with the most obvious thing, whatever is in front of you, then sculpt and redirect as you go. In interviews she ties this to her 'Be Average' maxim: great improvisers are not afraid to say the most ordinary thing, and the obvious choice often reads as original because it is genuinely yours. For speaking, the chapter suggests replacing a written script with questions to yourself, which you answer in natural speech. For communicators this means opening with the plain, natural thing rather than straining for wit.
insights.when_to_use: Blank-page writing, impromptu remarks, toasts, starting small talk, or any time you feel stuck hunting for a brilliant opening.
insights.worked_example: You must write a project kickoff email and have rewritten the first line five times. You start with the obvious: 'We are starting the billing migration on Monday; here is what changes for your team.' The rest follows. At a party, instead of searching for a clever opener, you comment on the obvious shared thing: 'This guacamole is disappearing fast, have you tried it?'
common_mistakes: Assuming the obvious is boring and discarding it
Starting with lengthy context or apologies instead of the obvious point
Waiting to start until the whole structure is clear
steps: Notice what is directly in front of you (the setting, the last thing said, the plain fact)
Say or write the most obvious first sentence
For a talk, write questions to yourself instead of a script and answer them aloud
Build from there and refine as you go, editing later if writing
situations: Starting a hard email
Giving an impromptu toast
Opening small talk with a stranger
Being asked to say a few words with no notice

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 4 'Start Anywhere' (about pp. 53-58); the obvious-response idea also discussed under chapter 5 'Be Average' in the Humor That Works interview
source.underlying_research: None identified. Keith Johnstone's improv teaching (Impro, 1979), a confirmed influence on Madson, is the likely lineage of 'be obvious'. Lewis & Lovatt (2013) on improvisation and divergent thinking is only indirectly relevant.

insights.confidence_rationale: Widely taught in improv and writing practice and plausible, but rests on practitioner experience rather than tested evidence.

insights.name: Be Average (Permission for an Ordinary First Try)
insights.takeaway: Aim for an ordinary, adequate contribution rather than brilliance, so you actually contribute and focus on others.
insights.explanation: Trying to be impressive makes people self-conscious, slow, and stiff. Madson's counsel is to aim for an ordinary, adequate contribution, because waiting for brilliance means you rarely contribute at all, and average first attempts are how skill grows. She acknowledges her Stanford students found it sounded like bad advice; her point is that striving to be witty takes you out of ordinary human relating, while your plain response is often a revelation to others. Lowering the bar reduces the self-monitoring that blocks spontaneity and frees attention for the other person.
insights.when_to_use: When perfectionism makes you stay silent in meetings, over-edit messages for hours, avoid volunteering to present, or hesitate to share ideas.
insights.worked_example: In a weekly leadership meeting you usually stay quiet because you want your comment to be insightful. You set a rule: contribute one ordinary but useful observation each meeting, such as 'The support team mentioned the same complaint three times this week.' Your visibility rises, and occasionally the plain observation turns out to be the most useful thing said.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'be average' with low effort on work that needs high quality
Over-polishing low-stakes messages
Comparing your first attempts with others' polished results
situations: Speaking up in meetings when you feel junior
Sending a quick reply instead of a polished essay
Trying a new skill like presenting
Sharing an unfinished idea

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 5 'Be Average'; Humor That Works interview
source.underlying_research: None cited. External: Sirois, Molnar & Hirsch (2017, European Journal of Personality 31) meta-analysis found perfectionistic concerns modestly associated with more procrastination (perfectionistic strivings slightly with less); Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 78) showed people overestimate how much others notice their actions and appearance (the spotlight effect).

insights.confidence_rationale: Consistent with solid research on perfectionism and the spotlight effect, though the book itself offers only experience and the prescription has not been tested directly. Distinct from the 'shoot for average, fail cheerfully' line on the GSB podcast, which was voiced by Dan Klein, not Madson.

insights.name: Pay Attention: Notice What Is Actually There
insights.takeaway: Put your attention on the other person and surroundings, listening as if you had to repeat it in detail.
insights.explanation: Madson treats attention as the improviser's core skill: what we attend to largely shapes how we experience the world, and when your focus is on your partner and surroundings, responses come naturally; when it is on yourself, you get stuck. Her exercises include taking a familiar route and noticing something new, and once a day listening to someone with full attention, as if you had to repeat it in detail, gently setting aside drifting thoughts. On small talk she advises noticing something about the other person instead of trying to sound interesting. Stanford's Oral Communication Program also credits her with attention games such as Sound Ball. Applied to communication, this is listening to take in what someone means, not to reload.
insights.when_to_use: Listening to a frustrated colleague or partner, client discovery calls, meetings where you tend to plan your reply, and any time you feel self-conscious in conversation.
insights.worked_example: A direct report is describing why the release slipped. You catch yourself composing your answer, so you shift attention to her words and tone, and notice she mentioned the QA handoff twice with a flat voice. You ask, 'It sounds like the QA handoff is the sore point, what happened there?' and the real issue surfaces. At dinner, you put your phone away and notice your teenager is unusually quiet, which opens a conversation you would have missed.
common_mistakes: Planning your reply while the other person talks
Mistaking silence for listening while mentally elsewhere
Self-monitoring (how am I coming across?) instead of other-focus
steps: When you notice self-focus, move attention outward to the person's words, tone, and body
Notice one specific detail you would usually miss
Reflect it back or ask about it before adding your own content
Practice daily by noticing something new in a familiar setting
situations: One-on-one with a struggling team member
Client discovery call
Conversation with a quiet teenager
Feeling self-conscious at a social event

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 6 'Pay Attention' (about pp. 67-74; listen-completely exercise around p. 74); Stanford GSB Think Fast Talk Smart episode 100 (small-talk tip); Stanford Oral Communication Program improv games crediting Madson
source.underlying_research: None cited in the book. External: Itzchakov, Kluger & Castro (2017, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 43) found across four experiments that high-quality listening reduced speakers' social anxiety and defensiveness; Castro, Kluger & Itzchakov (2016, European Journal of Social Psychology) found listening increased speakers' psychological safety on average. Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113) found asking more questions, especially follow-ups, increases liking (integrity note: Francesca Gino is a coauthor; this paper has not been retracted, but treat Gino-coauthored work with caution). Self-focused attention is a maintaining factor in the Clark & Wells (1995) cognitive model of social phobia.

insights.confidence_rationale: The underlying claim (outward attention and genuine listening improve interactions, self-focus fuels social anxiety) is supported by multiple independent experimental lines and a widely tested clinical model, though the book's specific exercises are untested.

supporting_evidence.note: Explains why turning attention outward helps: self-monitoring for visible anxiety rests on an overestimate of how transparent you are and feeds a loop of more anxiety.

insights.name: Face the Facts: Work With What You Are Given
insights.takeaway: Accept the situation and people as they are, and respond to the conversation you are actually in.
insights.explanation: Rather than fighting reality or wishing people were different, Madson advises accepting the situation and the people as they are and building with what you have. Where saying yes is accepting the bite of an offered apple, facing the facts is chewing it and letting it nourish you: letting the offer shape your next move. She adds that working skillfully and kindly with people you find difficult is the real mark of an improviser, and that life is about balancing rather than being balanced. In communication this means responding to the conversation you are actually in, not the one you wanted.
insights.when_to_use: When a meeting goes off-agenda, a stakeholder rejects your plan, a family member reacts in a way you dislike, or plans fall apart at the last minute.
insights.worked_example: Your executive sponsor cuts your presentation from twenty minutes to five as you walk in. Instead of complaining or rushing all twenty slides, you accept it and say: 'Given five minutes, here is the one decision I need from you and why.' With your in-laws, rather than hoping a relative stops bringing up politics, you accept that they will and plan a warm redirect.
common_mistakes: Confusing acceptance with approval or giving up on change
Spending energy complaining about constraints in the moment
Expecting people to change their style before you engage
situations: Presentation time cut at the last minute
Plan rejected by a stakeholder
Dealing with a difficult relative
Meeting derailed from the agenda

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 7 'Face the Facts' (about pp. 77-82)
source.underlying_research: None cited. Conceptually related to acceptance-based approaches (Morita therapy via Constructive Living; Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which has a substantial trial literature), though the book does not cite them as evidence.

insights.confidence_rationale: Plausible and consistent with acceptance-based psychology, but the book's version is philosophical and untested in communication settings.

insights.name: Stay on Course: Keep the Purpose in View
insights.takeaway: Ask what your purpose is now, not what you feel like doing, and stay flexible about how to reach it.
insights.explanation: Spontaneity does not mean aimlessness. Madson says improv always has a point, and suggests replacing 'what do I feel like doing?' with 'what is my purpose now?', since feelings are fleeting and a poor guide for action. For conversations, this is holding a clear purpose (what should be different after this exchange?) while staying flexible about how you get there.
insights.when_to_use: Meetings that drift, conflict conversations that spiral into old grievances, sales or negotiation calls, and long email threads that lose focus.
insights.worked_example: A budget review meeting drifts into debating the office move. You say: 'Good topic for another time; to get our purpose done, we need to agree on Q3 headcount before we leave.' In an argument with your partner about chores that slides into past hurts, you return to the purpose: 'I want us to agree on who handles dinners this week.'
common_mistakes: Going into a conversation without a clear purpose
Treating flexibility as permission to drift
Steering so rigidly that you ignore important new information
steps: Before the conversation, state the purpose in one sentence
When the exchange drifts, acknowledge the tangent briefly
Redirect to the purpose explicitly
If the purpose itself was wrong, change it openly rather than drifting
situations: Running a meeting that keeps drifting
Arguments with a partner that spiral
Negotiation call
Long email thread losing focus

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 8 'Stay on Course' (about p. 84)
source.underlying_research: None cited; the purpose-over-feelings framing echoes David K. Reynolds's Constructive Living. Goal clarity's benefit for performance is well established in goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham, 2002, American Psychologist 57), but not tested for this conversational use.

insights.confidence_rationale: Consistent with broad goal-setting research and expert consensus on communication, but the book offers it as practical advice without evidence.

insights.name: Wake Up to the Gifts (Naikan-Style Reflection)
insights.takeaway: Regularly notice what others have given you, and thank people specifically, including those doing thankless jobs.
insights.explanation: Madson encourages noticing everything you receive from others and from the world, much of which goes unseen (her example is the many unknown people behind the chair you are sitting on). It is the longest chapter, and in it she describes a week of intensive Naikan practice in Japan. Naikan reflection asks three questions about a person: what have I received from them, what have I given them, and what trouble have I caused them. She also suggests practical habits such as thanking people for thankless jobs and finding varied ways to say thank you each day. Seeing gifts more clearly shifts attention from grievances to appreciation and tends to make your thanks specific and sincere.
insights.when_to_use: Before a hard conversation with someone you resent, at the end of a project to acknowledge contributors, when a relationship feels one-sided, or as a regular reflection habit.
insights.worked_example: You feel irritated by a peer who 'never helps'. Before your one-on-one, you list what you received from her this month: she covered a client call, shared a template, flagged a bug. You open with specific thanks for the template, and the conversation about workload is noticeably calmer. At home, a weekly Naikan reflection about your spouse surfaces dozens of small things they did that you had not acknowledged.
common_mistakes: Generic thanks ('thanks for everything') that does not show you noticed
Using gratitude to bypass a real problem that needs addressing
Making the third question a self-punishment exercise rather than honest reflection
steps: Pick one person and a time period
List concretely what you received from them
List what you gave them
List troubles or inconveniences you caused them
Express one specific thank-you based on what you noticed
situations: Thanking a team at the end of a project
Preparing for a conversation with a colleague you resent
Feeling taken for granted by a partner
Reconnecting with a parent

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 9 'Wake Up to the Gifts'; she calls it 'notice the gifts' in the Humor That Works interview
source.underlying_research: Naikan (developed by Yoshimoto Ishin) via David K. Reynolds's Constructive Living; Naikan has little rigorous Western trial evidence. External: Algoe (2012, Social and Personality Psychology Compass) find-remind-bind theory and related studies show expressed gratitude strengthens relationships; Emmons & McCullough (2003, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 84) found gratitude journaling improved well-being; Dickens (2017, Basic and Applied Social Psychology) meta-analyses found gratitude interventions have small to moderate positive effects.

insights.confidence_rationale: Expressed, specific gratitude has credible relational research behind it, though effect sizes are modest and the Naikan method itself is thinly studied.

insights.name: Make Mistakes, Please (Mistakes as Offers)
insights.takeaway: Take risks, and when you slip, acknowledge it lightly, use it if you can, and keep going.
insights.explanation: Madson's classroom message is that if you are not making mistakes, you are not really improvising. She invites people to take risks and keep going boldly, and to respond to a mistake by noticing it, acknowledging it, and using it if possible, asking what comes next rather than how it happened; she is clear this is about resilience, not sloppiness. She suggests a 'circus bow' to celebrate a flub, and on the Stanford podcast told of starting a ceremonial reading too early, sitting back down, and getting a warm laugh when she restarted. In communication, recovering gracefully (acknowledge lightly, continue) matters more than never stumbling.
insights.when_to_use: When fear of saying the wrong thing keeps you quiet, after a verbal slip in a presentation, when learning a new language or skill, or when leading a team where people hide errors.
insights.worked_example: Halfway through a client demo you click the wrong tab and show an internal dashboard. Rather than apologizing at length, you smile, say 'Wrong door, but since we are here, this is the view our support team uses to catch your issues early,' and move on. As a manager, you share one of your own recent errors in team meetings so others feel safe surfacing theirs.
common_mistakes: Over-apologizing, which draws more attention to the error than the error itself
Using 'mistakes are fine' to excuse repeated carelessness on high-stakes work
Hiding errors rather than surfacing them early
steps: Expect errors in any live interaction
When one happens, notice it and acknowledge it briefly and without drama (Madson's 'circus bow': arms up, 'ta-da')
Look for a way to use it (a joke, a bridge, a learning point)
Keep going
Afterward, ask what comes next and what to adjust, not who to blame
situations: Recovering from a slip in a presentation
Speaking a second language at work
Admitting an error to your team
Trying something new socially

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 10 'Make Mistakes, Please' (about pp. 104-113); Humor That Works interview (circus bow); Stanford GSB Think Fast Talk Smart episode 100 (graduation reading story)
source.underlying_research: None cited. External: Felsman, Seifert & Himle (2019, The Arts in Psychotherapy 63) studied 268 students in a ten-week school improv program (single-group pre/post, no control); reduced social anxiety among those who screened positive predicted gains including willingness to make mistakes. Savitsky & Gilovich (2003, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology) found that informing speakers about the illusion of transparency reduced their anxiety and improved rated speech quality; Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000) on the spotlight effect. Edmondson (1999, Administrative Science Quarterly) linked team psychological safety to learning behavior. The pratfall effect (Aronson, Willerman & Floyd, 1966, Psychonomic Science) is often cited but replicates inconsistently.

insights.confidence_rationale: Graceful recovery and error-tolerance are supported by spotlight-effect and psychological-safety research and by correlational improv studies, but the improv-anxiety findings lack control groups and the pratfall claim is contested.

supporting_evidence.note: Post-speech rumination is identified in the research as part of the anxiety problem, which supports treating mistakes lightly and moving on rather than replaying them.

insights.name: Make Your Partner Look Good
insights.takeaway: Focus on making your partners succeed: avoid undermining them, cooperate, and do whatever the moment needs.
insights.explanation: Under Take Care of Each Other, Madson describes the improviser's ethic of shared control: there are no fixed leaders, you do what needs to be done, you make your partner look good, and you notice mistakes and refocus on what is needed. In interviews she adds that improvisers avoid undermining or contradicting partners and choose cooperation over competition. When everyone focuses on making others succeed, the group performs better and each person feels safer. This applies directly to co-presenting, meetings, and family life.
insights.when_to_use: Co-presenting, panel discussions, meetings where a colleague is floundering, introducing people, and supporting a partner in social settings.
insights.worked_example: During a joint presentation to leadership, your colleague blanks on a revenue figure. Instead of jumping in to correct him, you say, 'Mark, this connects to the chart you built, I can pull it up while you walk them through the trend,' giving him a lifeline. At a dinner party, when your partner's story falls flat, you add a detail that sets up the punchline instead of letting the moment die.
common_mistakes: Correcting a partner publicly when a quiet assist would do
Taking over the floor when rescuing
Supporting only people you like or who outrank you
steps: Before shared events, agree on roles and how to signal for help
During the interaction, watch your partner for signs of struggle
Offer a bridge or prompt that hands the spotlight back to them
Credit others' contributions explicitly
Save disagreements for private
situations: Co-presenting with a colleague
A teammate struggling in front of leadership
Introducing two contacts
Supporting a partner at a social event

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 12 'Take Care of Each Other' (about pp. 126-135; shared-control tips including 'make your partner look good' around p. 129); Brent Sverdloff interview with Madson (2015)
source.underlying_research: None cited. External: Edmondson (1999, Administrative Science Quarterly) found team psychological safety predicts learning behavior; Google's Project Aristotle (internal people-analytics project, published on re:Work, not peer reviewed) reported psychological safety as the top factor in team effectiveness. Sawyer's Group Genius (2007) on collaborative improvisation is practitioner-scholar support.

insights.confidence_rationale: Strong practitioner consensus plus indirect support from psychological safety research; specific tactics are untested.

insights.name: Enjoy the Ride (Play Loosens the Mind)
insights.takeaway: Treat conversations and presentations partly as play, not a test, so you stay flexible and responsive.
insights.explanation: Madson closes with the idea that having fun loosens the mind, making people more flexible and generous; she urges finding play and wonder in daily life and borrows Rick Steves's line about being fanatically positive. Treating a conversation or presentation partly as play, rather than a test, lowers threat and lets humor and responsiveness emerge.
insights.when_to_use: Before presentations or interviews when you feel tense, in team rituals, in long-term relationships that have become routine, and when helping others relax.
insights.worked_example: Before a quarterly review, your team usually braces for a grilling. You open with a two-minute 'one surprising thing I learned this quarter' round. People laugh, the tone relaxes, and the hard questions later get franker answers. With your partner, you turn a dreaded weekend errand run into a game of finding the oddest item in each store.
common_mistakes: Forcing levity in serious or grieving moments
Using humor to deflect from real problems
Mistaking enjoyment for not caring about outcomes
situations: Opening a tense team review
Calming nerves before an interview
Refreshing a routine relationship
Hosting a social gathering

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 13 'Enjoy the Ride' (about pp. 137-140)
source.underlying_research: None cited. External: Isen, Daubman & Nowicki (1987, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 52) found induced mild positive affect improved creative problem solving; Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory (2001, American Psychologist) proposes positive emotions broaden thinking (well cited, some specific findings contested). Felsman, Gunawardena & Seifert (2020) found improv exercises raised positive affect versus a control.

insights.confidence_rationale: Positive affect aiding flexible thinking has experimental support, but the book's application is general advice and some broaden-and-build claims are contested.

insights.name: Questions, Not a Script (Speak From Prompts)
insights.takeaway: Replace a word-for-word script with a list of questions to yourself, and answer them naturally when speaking.
insights.explanation: For talks and prepared remarks, Madson recommends replacing a word-for-word text with a list of questions to yourself, then answering them in your natural voice. Reading a script focuses you on reading well and makes it hard to add anything, while answering a question forces your mind to organize information live, which sounds more natural, attentive and persuasive. She argues that real, improvised speech is more engaging than its scripted sibling.
insights.when_to_use: Short talks, toasts, team updates, interview answers you have anticipated, and any time you are tempted to memorize or read a text.
insights.worked_example: You have a five-minute update at an all-hands meeting. Instead of writing paragraphs, your card says: 'What did we ship?', 'What surprised us?', 'What do we need from other teams?' You rehearse by answering each question aloud in different words each time. On the day, a question from the floor fits naturally because you are not tied to a text.
common_mistakes: Writing questions so vague they do not prompt any content
Secretly memorizing answers word for word, which recreates the script
Skipping rehearsal entirely and confusing this with no preparation
steps: List the three to five things the audience needs to know
Turn each into a question to yourself
Rehearse by answering aloud, varying the wording each time
Bring only the questions on your notes
Deliver by answering each question to the audience as if asked
situations: Giving a short team update
Delivering a toast
Preparing for anticipated interview questions
Presenting without reading slides

source.citation: Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, chapter 4 'Start Anywhere' (about pp. 56-58 per the Admired Leadership summary); Humor That Works interview
source.underlying_research: None cited. Related only indirectly: Madson's Stanford colleagues on the GSB podcast make the same point that recited answers sound less human. No study found directly comparing question prompts with full scripts.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book and the author's interview, and consistent with widespread expert speaking advice against reading scripts, but supported by practitioner experience rather than tested evidence.

insights.name: Windshield Wipers for Attention
insights.takeaway: When distracting thoughts arise while listening, gently set them aside without self-criticism and return to the person.
insights.explanation: When distracting thoughts (what will I say next, how am I doing) cloud your listening, you neither fight them nor scold yourself. You mentally thank your brain for the thought and gently sweep it aside, like a windshield wiper, then return your attention to the person in front of you, as often as needed. The idea treats distraction as normal and makes refocusing quick and kind rather than self-critical.
insights.when_to_use: Listening in meetings or interviews when you catch yourself rehearsing, conversations where you feel self-conscious, and Q and A sessions.
insights.worked_example: In a client call you notice you are drafting your rebuttal while the client is still explaining. You silently think 'thanks, brain', let the draft go, and look back at the client's face and words. A minute later it happens again, and you repeat the sweep without frustration. You end up catching a budget concern you would otherwise have missed.
common_mistakes: Criticizing yourself for drifting, which adds another distraction
Trying to suppress thoughts forcefully
Treating one refocus as enough rather than a repeated practice
steps: Notice that your attention has moved into your own head
Acknowledge the thought kindly ('thank you, brain')
Sweep it aside
Return full attention to the speaker's words, tone and body
Repeat whenever it happens
situations: Catching yourself rehearsing during a meeting
Listening to a client's concerns
Feeling self-conscious at a networking event

source.citation: Attributed to Madson by Adam Tobin on Stanford GSB Think Fast Talk Smart episode 100 (2023); not located in the book
source.underlying_research: None cited. Conceptually similar to attention-refocusing in mindfulness practice; the listening research under improv-wisdom-06 (Itzchakov, Kluger & Castro, 2017) supports the value of attentive listening but did not test this technique.

insights.confidence_rationale: A secondhand attribution from a colleague on a podcast; not confirmed in the book and not directly tested.

insights.name: The Curse of Knowledge
insights.takeaway: Assume your audience lacks your context, and use concrete examples, stories, and outsider tests to check your message.
insights.explanation: Once you know something, it becomes very hard to imagine not knowing it. Experts, managers and anyone close to a project unconsciously assume their audience shares their background, vocabulary and context, so they speak in abstractions that feel full of meaning to them but land as empty to listeners. The Heaths treat this as the main villain of clear communication: the problem is rarely a lack of information but an inability to see your message from the outside. The fix is not simply trying harder to empathize but using deliberate tools (concrete examples, stories, analogies, testing the message on an outsider) that work even when your own sense of clarity is unreliable.
insights.when_to_use: Any time you are explaining something you know well to someone who does not: briefing a new team member, writing a status update for executives, explaining a technical decision to a non-technical partner, or giving instructions to family members.
insights.worked_example: A data engineer tells her director that the pipeline migration is 'blocked on schema drift in the upstream CDC feed.' The director nods and leaves confused. Recognizing the curse, she rewrites it: 'The sales system changed the format of its customer records without telling us, so our nightly import breaks. We need the sales team to agree to warn us before changes. Until then, reports may be a day late.' At home the same week, she catches herself telling her father to 'just clear the cache' and instead walks him through what to tap, one screen at a time.
common_mistakes: Assuming that because a message feels obvious to you, it is clear to others
Trying to fix it by adding more detail and jargon rather than examples
Testing the message only on colleagues who share your knowledge
Mistaking polite nodding for understanding
situations: Explaining a technical issue to a non-technical manager
Onboarding a new team member
Writing a project update for senior leaders
Helping a parent use new technology
Teaching a skill you have done for years

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Introduction: What Sticks? (tappers and listeners; the Curse of Knowledge as the villain of the book)
source.underlying_research: Elizabeth Newton's 1990 Stanford psychology dissertation ('tappers and listeners'), as reported in the book: tappers predicted listeners would name about half of the tapped songs; listeners named 3 of 120 (2.5 percent). The term comes from Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber (1989), 'The curse of knowledge in economic settings: An experimental analysis', Journal of Political Economy 97(5), 1232-1254. Related work: Birch and Bloom (2007), 'The curse of knowledge in reasoning about false beliefs', Psychological Science 18(5), 382-386; a seven-experiment high-powered replication (Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt, 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3), e92406) found an effect in the same direction but less than half the original size.

insights.confidence_rationale: The broad phenomenon (difficulty ignoring privileged knowledge, closely related to hindsight bias and egocentric projection) is well supported across economics and psychology, and the authors also published it as an HBR article. However, the tapping study the book leans on is an unpublished dissertation not replicated as a standalone experiment, and a high-powered replication of a prominent adult curse of knowledge paradigm (Birch and Bloom, 2007) found the effect to be real but less than half as large. Rated Medium rather than High for these reasons; the practical advice to test messages on outsiders is low-risk.

supporting_evidence.note: Direct experimental evidence for the curse of knowledge in speech: speakers overestimated how often they were understood, while informed overhearers did not, which points to the speaker's own privileged knowledge of their intent.

Extends the curse of knowledge to tone: the paper frames email overconfidence as the same egocentrism seen in Newton's tapping study, and shows that the richer the sender's own experience of a message, the larger the gap.

insights.name: The SUCCESs Checklist
insights.takeaway: Diagnose a weak message against simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and story, then strengthen the one or two weakest traits.
insights.explanation: The Heaths argue that ideas that stick (urban legends, proverbs, great campaigns) share six traits, captured in the mnemonic SUCCESs: Simple (a stripped-down core), Unexpected (breaks a pattern to grab attention), Concrete (sensory, specific), Credible (believable on its own terms), Emotional (makes people care), and Stories (gets people to act on it). It is a checklist, not a formula: you do not need all six, and the value is in using it to diagnose a weak message and pick the one or two traits that would strengthen it most. The authors also note that the hard work happens after you have found your answer, in the separate stage of telling it to others.
insights.when_to_use: When preparing any message that needs to be remembered or acted on later: a pitch, a change announcement, a presentation, a safety rule, a fundraising appeal, or a family rule you want kids to remember.
insights.worked_example: A team lead drafts an all-hands slide: 'Q3 priority: improve customer-centricity across touchpoints.' Running the checklist, she sees it is not simple (no single priority), not concrete, and has no story. She revises to: 'This quarter, every customer email gets a human reply within one business day.' She adds a short story of a customer who cancelled after waiting six days, and a surprising fact: their fastest competitor answers in two hours. In a personal setting, a parent uses the same check on 'be responsible with money' and turns it into a concrete rule with a story from their own first credit card.
common_mistakes: Trying to force all six traits into every message
Treating the checklist as decoration added after the content is fixed, rather than as a diagnostic
Using surprise or emotion as gimmicks disconnected from the core point
Confusing 'simple' with 'dumbed down'
steps: Write your message in one or two sentences as you would naturally say it
