Ask of it: Is it Simple? Unexpected? Concrete? Credible? Emotional? Is there a Story?
Mark the weakest one or two traits that matter most for this audience
Rework the message to strengthen those traits (see the other insights from this book for tools)
Test it: tell it to someone outside the topic, wait a while, and ask what they remember
situations: Preparing a pitch or proposal
Announcing an organizational change
Designing a training session
Writing a fundraising or volunteer appeal
Setting a household rule children will remember

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Introduction: What Sticks? (the six principles); Chapters 1 to 6 (Simple, Unexpected, Concrete, Credible, Emotional, Stories, one per principle, each ending in a 'Clinic'); Epilogue: What Sticks
source.underlying_research: Authors' synthesis of case studies, urban legend analysis (Heath, Bell and Sternberg, 2001), and classroom exercises. The framework itself has not been tested as a whole in controlled studies.

insights.confidence_rationale: Several individual components have research support (concreteness, curiosity, emotional content in spread), but the six-part framework is the authors' synthesis, supported mainly by selected cases. It is a useful diagnostic, not a validated model.

insights.name: Find the Core (Commander's Intent)
insights.takeaway: Find the single most important point, state it plainly as the goal, and cut everything else, even good points.
insights.explanation: Simple, in the Heaths' sense, means finding the single most important thing and ruthlessly cutting everything else, even good points. They borrow the military idea of Commander's Intent: a short plain statement of what success looks like, so people can still act sensibly when the detailed plan falls apart. A well-found core works as a decision filter. Their example is Southwest Airlines framing itself as THE low-fare airline: former CEO Herb Kelleher illustrated it with a hypothetical marketing proposal to serve a chicken Caesar salad on the Houston to Las Vegas route, which fails the test because it does not make Southwest the low-fare carrier on that route. The discipline is forced prioritization: if you say three things, you say nothing.
insights.when_to_use: When delegating, kicking off a project, writing a long email or report, setting team priorities, or when people keep making decisions that drift from what you wanted.
insights.worked_example: A manager going on two weeks' leave writes a five-page handover. Instead she adds one line at the top: 'If you only remember one thing: the client launch on the 14th must not slip; everything else can wait.' Her deputy later faces a choice between fixing an internal dashboard and testing the client release, and the one line settles it. At home, a couple planning a renovation agrees on a core ('the kitchen must work for cooking together') and uses it to say no to an expensive island that blocks the walkway.
common_mistakes: Listing several priorities and calling them all the core
Writing a core so abstract ('excellence', 'customer focus') that it cannot guide a real decision
Cutting the core to a slogan that loses the actual meaning
Assuming people will infer the priority from a long, detailed plan
steps: Ask: if the audience remembers only one thing, what must it be?
Write it in one sentence of plain language
Test it against a realistic tradeoff: would this sentence tell someone what to do?
Cut or move supporting points that compete with it
Lead with the core in speech and writing, then add detail beneath it
situations: Delegating a task before going on leave
Kicking off a project
Writing the first line of a long email
Setting priorities for a team
Agreeing on goals for a family decision

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 1: Simple
source.underlying_research: US Army doctrine on Commander's Intent; Southwest Airlines case: Kelleher's chicken Caesar salad illustration, which the Heaths take from James Carville and Paul Begala's book Buck Up, Suck Up... and Come Back When You Foul Up (2002), as noted by readers' summaries. The chapter's discussion of decision paralysis relates to Tversky and Shafir (1992), 'Choice under conflict: The dynamics of deferred decision', Psychological Science 3(6), 358-361; that the book cites this specific paper was not confirmed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Commander's Intent is established military practice and leading with the main point is a strong consensus in professional writing guidance. Evidence in the book is case-based rather than experimental. The Southwest salad story is a single anecdote, framed by Kelleher as a hypothetical illustration and reaching the book secondhand through Carville and Begala.

supporting_evidence.note: The single governing thought at the top of the pyramid enforces the same discipline as finding the core: one main point that everything else serves.
Supports finding the core with experimental data: each additional idea or request in a practical message reduces the chance the main one is read and acted on.

insights.name: Borrow a Schema (Analogies That Do the Work)
insights.takeaway: Explain a new idea by linking it to something your audience already understands, choosing analogies that guide decisions.
insights.explanation: One way to make a complex idea simple without losing substance is to attach it to something the audience already understands. The Heaths' example: explaining an unfamiliar fruit (a pomelo) as 'like a supersized grapefruit with a thick soft rind' instantly loads a whole picture. Good analogies are compact and also generative: they help people make new decisions. The book cites Disney calling employees 'cast members', which tells staff how to behave in countless situations no rulebook covers. Weak analogies are merely decorative; strong ones carry the logic of the idea.
insights.when_to_use: When explaining a new concept, product, or role to people without background; when you need people to apply an idea to situations you cannot anticipate.
insights.worked_example: A security lead tries to explain zero-trust networking to the leadership team and loses them. She switches to: 'Today our network is like an office with a guarded front door, but once inside you can walk into any room. We are moving to a hotel model, where your key card opens only your own room.' Executives immediately start asking useful questions about which 'rooms' matter. In a personal setting, someone explains a friend's chronic fatigue to family using the 'spoon theory' (a fixed number of spoons of energy per day), which helps relatives stop taking cancelled plans personally.
common_mistakes: Choosing an analogy that is vivid but misleading on the key point
Using an analogy the audience does not actually know (sports or cultural references they do not share)
Stretching one analogy to cover details it does not fit
Stacking several analogies so none sticks
steps: Identify the core feature of the idea people must grasp
List things the audience already knows that share that feature
Pick one whose implications point people toward the right behavior
State the analogy, then name where it breaks down if that matters
Check: can listeners use it to answer a new question correctly?
situations: Explaining a technical concept to executives
Pitching a new product category
Describing a health condition to family
Explaining a role or culture to new hires

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 1: Simple (schemas, generative analogies)
source.underlying_research: General cognitive psychology of schemas and analogical reasoning; the book's support is mainly illustrative examples (pomelo, Disney cast members, Hollywood high-concept pitches).

insights.confidence_rationale: That prior knowledge (schemas) aids comprehension and that analogies support learning has broad support in education research, but the book itself relies on examples rather than citing specific studies; specific claims about 'generative' analogies are expert judgment.

insights.name: Break the Guessing Machine
insights.takeaway: Identify what your audience expects, then break that expectation in a way that makes sense and reinforces your core point.
insights.explanation: People stop paying attention to what they can predict. To capture attention, the Heaths advise identifying what your audience expects about your topic and then deliberately violating that expectation, in a way that is tied to your core message rather than a random gimmick. A surprise must be 'post-dictable': once explained, it makes sense and deepens the point. Their journalism-class example: students write a lead about a list of speakers at a school meeting, then learn the real news is that there will be no school next Thursday, which reframes what a lead is for. Common sense is the enemy of memorable messages, so find the part of your idea that is counter-intuitive.
insights.when_to_use: Opening a presentation or meeting, starting a written proposal, introducing a change people think they already understand, or getting a distracted audience to re-engage.
insights.worked_example: A safety manager knows staff tune out the annual training. He opens with: 'Most injuries in our warehouse last year did not involve forklifts or heavy loads. They happened walking to the break room.' Staff look up, and he connects it to his core point about wet floors and phone use. A parent uses the same move at dinner: instead of a lecture about screen time, she says 'I read that the average teenager checks their phone more often than they blink in a minute' (after checking it is true), opening a real conversation.
common_mistakes: Using shock or a joke unrelated to the core point, which wins attention but hijacks memory
Inventing or exaggerating a surprising statistic
Surprising people repeatedly until it feels manipulative
Assuming your counter-intuitive point is counter-intuitive to the audience without checking what they expect
steps: Write down your core message
List what the audience currently assumes about the topic
Find the part of your message that contradicts one of those assumptions
Open with that contradiction
Explain it so the surprise makes sense and points back to the core
situations: Opening a presentation
Starting a mandatory training session
Writing the first line of a proposal
Getting teenagers to listen to a safety message

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 2: Unexpected
source.underlying_research: General attention and schema-violation research on surprise; book support is largely anecdote and examples (Nordstrom stories, a journalism teacher's lesson on leads, airline safety announcements).

insights.confidence_rationale: That novelty and expectation violation capture attention is well established in psychology, but the specific practice advice is supported by illustrative cases rather than controlled comparisons of message openings.

insights.name: Open a Curiosity Gap
insights.takeaway: Before giving facts, raise a question or mystery your audience cares about, show what they do not know, then answer it.
insights.explanation: Surprise grabs attention; curiosity holds it. Drawing on George Loewenstein's information gap theory, the Heaths explain that curiosity arises when people notice a gap between what they know and what they want to know, and they feel an itch to close it. So instead of leading with facts, first highlight a question or mystery the audience cares about, show them what they do not know, and then fill the gap. Mystery-style framing works well for presentations and teaching. Note the theory's own boundary: people need some knowledge to feel a gap, so total novices or total experts are less curious.
insights.when_to_use: Presentations, teaching, long reports or emails where you need sustained attention, and pitching ideas that require people to stay with a line of reasoning.
insights.worked_example: A finance analyst presenting quarterly results starts with: 'Our revenue went up 12 percent, yet our cash on hand went down. By the end of this ten-minute update you will know why, and it is not what most people guess.' The room stays engaged until she reveals delayed customer payments. At home, someone trying to interest their partner in a budget review asks first: 'Want to guess which of our subscriptions we used least this year?'
common_mistakes: Opening a gap and never closing it, which frustrates people
Creating clickbait-style gaps that oversell a dull answer
Assuming curiosity exists when the audience lacks the background to care
Revealing the answer in the first sentence out of habit
steps: Identify the most interesting question your content answers
Check the audience knows enough to care about the question
Pose the question or puzzle before giving facts
Release information in a sequence that progressively narrows the gap
Close the gap clearly and link the answer to your core point
situations: Presenting quarterly results
Teaching a workshop
Opening a long written report
Getting a partner interested in a household budget

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 2: Unexpected (gap theory of curiosity)
source.underlying_research: George Loewenstein (1994), 'The psychology of curiosity: A review and reinterpretation', Psychological Bulletin 116(1), 75-98 (the book names Loewenstein and his gap theory). Tested by Kang, Hsu, Krajbich, Loewenstein and colleagues (2009), 'The wick in the candle of learning', Psychological Science 20(8), 963-973, which found an inverted-U relation between confidence and curiosity consistent with the theory.

insights.confidence_rationale: Loewenstein's theory is influential and has supporting experiments (for example Kang et al., 2009), but it is a theoretical framework with competing accounts (novelty-based curiosity) and no direct replication program of applied communication effects. Practical use is low-risk.

insights.name: Make It Concrete (Velcro Memory)
insights.takeaway: Replace abstract words with concrete details people can see or picture, so your idea is understood, remembered, and shared consistently.
insights.explanation: Abstract language (strategy, value, synergy, quality) is hard to understand and easy to forget. Concrete language describes things people can see, hear, touch or picture, and it helps both understanding and memory. The Heaths describe memory as Velcro: the more hooks (sensory details, emotions, associations) an idea has, the more ways it can stick. Concreteness also coordinates teams, because a concrete goal ('a man on the moon by the end of the decade') means the same thing to everyone, whereas an abstract goal invites each person to imagine something different.
insights.when_to_use: Setting goals, writing job descriptions or feedback, explaining abstract strategy, describing a problem you want fixed, or giving instructions anyone will follow later.
insights.worked_example: Instead of telling a direct report 'you need to be more proactive with clients', a manager says: 'Last week the Acme client emailed twice asking for the timeline before we replied. I'd like clients to hear from you before they have to ask, for example a Friday note with what happened and what's next.' At home, rather than 'help out more around the house', one partner says 'can you own taking out the bins on Tuesday nights and emptying the dishwasher each morning?'
common_mistakes: Believing abstraction sounds more professional or strategic
Giving one concrete example and then retreating to abstraction
Being concrete about trivial details while the main goal stays vague
Using vivid detail that is inaccurate
steps: Circle the abstract words in your draft (improve, quality, support, engage)
For each, ask: what would this look like if I filmed it?
Replace with a specific example, number, name, place or observable behavior
Where possible, show the thing (a prototype, a real email, a sample) rather than describe it
Check that two different people would picture the same thing
situations: Giving feedback to a direct report
Setting team goals
Writing a job description
Asking a partner for help at home
Explaining a company strategy

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 3: Concrete
source.underlying_research: Concreteness effect in memory and comprehension: Allan Paivio's dual coding theory (concrete material is encoded both verbally and as imagery); Sadoski, Goetz and Fritz (1993), 'Impact of concreteness on comprehensibility, interest, and memory for text', Journal of Educational Psychology 85(2), 291-304 (concrete text rated more comprehensible and interesting and better recalled). Caveat from Marschark and colleagues that the imagery explanation is debated. The 'Velcro Theory of Memory' is the authors' own term (named in the publisher description).

insights.confidence_rationale: The concreteness advantage in recall and comprehension is one of the more robust findings in memory research, replicated from single words to longer text. The mechanism (dual coding) is debated, but the practical effect is well supported. The Velcro metaphor is the authors' framing, not a technical model.

supporting_evidence.note: An imaginable plot, one listeners can picture, was among the strongest storyteller drivers of transportation (about .29), backing the case for concrete, sensory detail.

insights.name: Let the Audience Test It (Internal Credibility)
insights.takeaway: Build credibility inside your message with vivid details, human-scale statistics, one strong proof case, and claims people can test.
insights.explanation: When you lack authority or your audience is skeptical, the Heaths suggest building credibility from inside the message rather than from credentials. Tools include: vivid, accurate details that signal you know the subject; statistics translated to human scale so people can feel what they mean; the 'Sinatra test' (one example so strong it proves the general case, like 'if you can make it there, you can make it anywhere'); and 'testable credentials', inviting the audience to check the claim for themselves ('try it this week and see'). They also note that anti-authorities, people with lived experience, can be more credible than experts.
insights.when_to_use: Proposing an idea when you are junior or new, persuading a skeptical stakeholder, presenting data, making a case to family or friends who doubt you, or pitching a vendor without a track record.
insights.worked_example: A junior analyst wants approval for a new reporting tool. Rather than citing vendor marketing, he says: 'Give me one week with it on last month's sales data; if I can't produce the board report in half the time, we drop it.' He also notes they already use the tool's parent product in finance (a Sinatra-style example). With a skeptical parent who thinks a used electric car is a bad idea, he translates the fuel savings into human scale: 'it covers your monthly phone bill and then some.'
common_mistakes: Burying people in statistics instead of translating one into human terms
Using vivid details that turn out to be wrong, which destroys credibility
Leaning on borrowed authority the audience does not respect
Offering a test you are not confident will succeed
steps: Identify why the audience might doubt you
Pick the strongest single example that would convince a skeptic (Sinatra test)
Translate key numbers into a comparison from everyday life
Add one or two specific, verifiable details
Where possible, invite the listener to verify the claim themselves
situations: Proposing an idea as a junior employee
Presenting data to a skeptical audience
Pitching a new vendor or tool
Persuading a doubtful family member

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 4: Credible
source.underlying_research: Mostly case examples (for example the 'Where's the beef?' advertising campaign as a testable credential, and a smoking-harm spokesperson as an anti-authority). No controlled studies verified in this session for the Sinatra test or testable credentials specifically.

insights.confidence_rationale: Ideas such as human-scale numbers and verifiable evidence fit broader persuasion and numeracy research, and the advice is credible practitioner guidance. However, the specific tools are named and supported by cases rather than tested experimentally; some vivid-detail claims rest on single studies the book summarizes briefly.

supporting_evidence.note: Letting people test a claim for themselves is echoed in Berger's uncertainty barrier: trials, samples and reversible pilots lower the risk of trying and let experience persuade.

insights.name: One Person, Not a Million (Identifiable Victim)
insights.takeaway: To make people care, show one specific person or case before, or instead of, large statistics.
insights.explanation: The Heaths argue that people care more about one specific individual than about large statistics (the publisher calls it the Mother Teresa Effect, after a remark attributed to her that she would act for the one, not the mass). They cite a study in which people given five dollars donated, on average, more than twice as much after reading about Rokia, a seven-year-old girl in Mali, as after reading statistics about millions facing hunger, and gave less when the statistics were added to her story, suggesting that putting people into analytic mode dampens feeling. The communication lesson: when you want people to care, show a specific person or case before (or instead of) aggregate numbers. Important caveat: the underlying research has replicated poorly, so treat the size of this effect with caution.
insights.when_to_use: Fundraising or volunteer appeals, making the case for a customer-facing fix, explaining why a policy matters to real people, or persuading friends and family to care about a cause.
insights.worked_example: A product manager asking for engineering time to fix accessibility bugs starts with Maria, a long-time customer who uses a screen reader and was locked out of paying her invoice for a week, and only then shows that 4 percent of users rely on assistive technology. For a neighborhood food bank drive, a volunteer writes about one family's week rather than leading with county hunger statistics.
common_mistakes: Using a sad story that is not representative, misleading the audience
Exploiting someone's story without consent
Dropping the data entirely when decision-makers need it
Assuming the effect is large and reliable in every setting
situations: Writing a fundraising appeal
Arguing for a bug fix that affects customers
Explaining why a policy change matters
Asking friends to support a cause

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 5: Emotional
source.underlying_research: Small, Loewenstein and Slovic (2007), 'Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims', Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 102(2), 143-153. Study 3 (159 participants, each given five one-dollar bills): mean donations were $2.38 for the Rokia letter, $1.14 for the statistics letter and $1.43 for Rokia plus statistics; the book reports the $2.38 versus $1.14 comparison. Replication: Maier, Wong and Feldman (2024), 'Revisiting and rethinking the identifiable victim effect: Replication and extension of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007)', Collabra: Psychology 9(1), 90203, a pre-registered far replication of Studies 1 and 3 using hypothetical (not real) donations, found no support for the effect; the same paper's robust Bayesian reanalysis of Lee and Feeley's (2016) meta-analysis (Social Influence 11(3), 199-215, which reported a significant but modest r = .05 across 41 studies) indicated publication bias.

insights.confidence_rationale: The original study was influential, but a pre-registered replication of Small et al. (2007) found no identifiable victim effect, and a bias-corrected reanalysis of the meta-analytic evidence suggests the average effect may be near zero. The replication used hypothetical rather than real donations, so the question is not fully settled. The general advice to pair data with a concrete human example is still reasonable on concreteness grounds, but the specific claim that statistics reduce giving should be treated as contested.

supporting_evidence.note: Identifiable characters were one of three storyteller factors that reliably increased transportation (corrected correlation about .20), consistent with the advice to tell about one person rather than a crowd.

insights.name: Answer 'What's in It for Them', Vividly
insights.takeaway: Help people vividly imagine themselves enjoying the benefit, and remember they care about growth and meaning, not just money.
insights.explanation: To make people care, the Heaths say appeal to self-interest, and do it concretely: help people imagine themselves enjoying the benefit rather than listing features. They describe a study where homeowners who were asked to imagine how cable TV would improve their lives subscribed at much higher rates than those simply told its benefits. They also caution against assuming people only care about basic needs (money, security): communicators often underestimate how much others care about learning, growth, meaning and recognition, the higher levels of Maslow's hierarchy, which the authors call the mistake of living in 'Maslow's basement'.
insights.when_to_use: Pitching a change to a team, selling an idea to a client, recruiting, persuading someone to adopt a habit, or asking a partner or friend to try something new.
insights.worked_example: A team lead introducing a new ticketing system skips the feature list and says: 'Picture Friday afternoon with no one pinging you on chat to ask about status, because they can see it themselves.' She also notes the system's reporting will give each person a visible record of the hard problems they solved, appealing to recognition, not just convenience. Persuading a friend to join a running club, someone describes the Saturday coffee afterwards, not the training plan.
common_mistakes: Listing features instead of helping people picture the benefit
Assuming money is the only motivator
Making benefits so generic that no one can imagine them
Overpromising benefits that will not materialize
steps: List what the audience gets, from their point of view
Include higher-level benefits (growth, recognition, meaning) not just material ones
Turn the top benefit into a short scene they can imagine themselves in
Use 'you' language and ask them to picture it
Keep claims realistic so the picture survives contact with reality
situations: Rolling out a new tool to a team
Pitching to a client
Recruiting a candidate
Encouraging a friend to try a new habit

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 5: Emotional (self-interest and Maslow's hierarchy)
source.underlying_research: Gregory, Cialdini and Carpenter (1982), 'Self-relevant scenarios as mediators of likelihood estimates and compliance: Does imagining make it so?', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 43(1), 89-99 (cable TV door-to-door study in Tempe, Arizona; the book's contents list a section on cable television in Tempe). Maslow's hierarchy of needs as a framing device ('Avoiding Maslow's basement' is a section of the chapter). The extrinsic incentives point matches Chip Heath (1999), 'On the social psychology of agency relationships: Lay theories of motivation overemphasize extrinsic incentives', Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 78(1), 25-62; that the book cites this paper by name was not confirmed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Focusing on audience benefits is strong consensus in persuasion practice, and the imagery study is a published peer-reviewed experiment; however, it is a single 1980s study and later research has found that imagery appeals can backfire when the scenario is hard to imagine. Maslow's hierarchy as a strict hierarchy has weak empirical support, so it is used here only as a reminder that people value non-material benefits.

supporting_evidence.note: Answering what is in it for them is generalized into a diagnostic of the other person's pressures, metrics and five kinds of currency (practitioner framework, not tested).

Gives experimental backing to framing for the listener's concerns: arguments framed around the audience's own moral values persuaded political opponents more than arguments framed around the speaker's values (review of moral reframing studies).

Rogers reports a subject-line test in which emphasizing the volunteer's benefit (free concert entry) rather than the organization's need reportedly improved response about fourfold, consistent with appealing to what the audience values.

insights.name: Appeal to Identity
insights.takeaway: Connect your request to who your audience believes they are, framing it as what someone like them would do.
insights.explanation: People often decide not by calculating costs and benefits but by asking 'what would someone like me do here?' The Heaths list appealing to identity as one of their three ways of making people care (alongside associations and self-interest), and use the Don't Mess with Texas anti-litter campaign as the example: rather than appealing to civic duty or fines, it framed littering as something real Texans do not do, aimed at the young men who littered most and using figures they admired. The identity-based model of decision-making associated with James March fits this idea. The lesson is to connect your request to who your audience believes they are (a professional, a good parent, a team player, a proud member of a community).
insights.when_to_use: Behavior change requests, culture-setting messages, persuading groups with a strong shared identity, and personal requests where values matter more than incentives.
insights.worked_example: An engineering manager wants more thorough code reviews. Instead of announcing a new policy with penalties, she says: 'We're the team other teams copy. The way we review code is part of what people mean when they say our work is solid.' In a family, a parent encourages a teenager to call an elderly grandparent by saying 'you're the one in this family who always notices when someone is lonely', which lands better than a reminder about obligations.
common_mistakes: Appealing to an identity the audience does not hold or resents
Using identity as a guilt trip ('a real team player would...')
Implying the listener's identity is in question, which provokes defensiveness
Picking messengers who do not represent the identity
steps: Identify which identity is most relevant to the decision (profession, role, community, values)
Ask what a person with that identity would naturally do in this situation
Frame your request as consistent with that identity
Use messengers or examples the audience sees as their own
Avoid implying they are failing at the identity
situations: Changing team habits without new rules
Running a community or volunteer campaign
Encouraging a teenager's behavior
Setting cultural norms for a new team

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 5: Emotional (appealing to identity)
source.underlying_research: Don't Mess with Texas campaign (created in 1985 by Tim McClure and Mike Blair of the agency GSD&M for the Texas Department of Transportation) as a case study. James G. March's identity-based (logic of appropriateness) model of decision-making; the Heaths explicitly use March's identity model in their later book Switch (2010), but whether Made to Stick names March was not confirmed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Identity-based motivation and social identity effects are well studied in social psychology, and March's framework is a respected theory, but the book's support is a case study (a single, famous campaign) rather than experiments directly testing identity framing. Appealing to identity is confirmed as a book theme; the March attribution within this book is not confirmed.

supporting_evidence.note: Cialdini's seventh principle, unity, holds that people say yes more to those they see as part of a shared we (family, place, group); it overlaps with identity appeals but has little independent testing as a compliance tactic.

Identity appeals help only when the link is genuine and the messenger is not distrusted; a reframed appeal from a reviled outgroup source is likely to be rejected, and some reframing studies found inconsistent effects.

insights.name: Stories as Simulation and Inspiration
insights.takeaway: Collect real stories from daily work and use them to show people how to act and to inspire them.
insights.explanation: The Heaths argue stories do two jobs: they act as mental flight simulators (showing people how to handle situations so they can act well later) and as inspiration (motivating action). They point to research showing that mentally rehearsing the process of reaching a goal improves performance more than imagining the outcome. They also say you do not need to invent stories: spot them in daily work and file them. Three plot types are especially useful for inspiration: the Challenge plot (overcoming odds), the Connection plot (people bridging a gap), and the Creativity plot (a breakthrough or new way of solving a problem). A related classroom observation: students in Chip Heath's Stanford class remembered stories from short speeches far better than statistics.
insights.when_to_use: Training and onboarding, motivating a team, presenting a case for change, teaching children lessons, or making a personal point to a friend without lecturing.
insights.worked_example: Instead of a slide on 'escalation best practices', a support manager tells the story of a night when a junior agent noticed an unusual pattern in three tickets, escalated it despite feeling unsure, and caught an outage early. New hires now know what to do and that it is welcome (simulation plus a Challenge plot). At a family dinner, a grandmother tells how she and an estranged sister reconnected (Connection plot), which says more to two quarrelling siblings than advice would.
common_mistakes: Telling a story with no clear connection to the point
Making stories too long or full of irrelevant detail
Using only polished success stories that feel unrealistic
Forgetting to collect real stories, so you fall back on generic ones
Over-trusting a single story as evidence for a general claim
steps: Decide whether you need the story to teach (simulate) or to motivate (inspire)
Keep a running file of real stories from work and life
Pick a story whose turning point illustrates your core message
Match it to a plot (Challenge, Connection, Creativity) when you want inspiration
Tell it with concrete detail, and state the lesson briefly if it is not obvious
situations: Onboarding or training new staff
Motivating a team after a setback
Making a case for change
Giving advice to family without lecturing
Opening a keynote or toast

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 6: Stories (flight simulator, Jared, the three plots); the Stanford crime-speech exercise is described in the Epilogue
source.underlying_research: Pham and Taylor (1999), 'From thought to action: Effects of process- versus outcome-based mental simulations on performance', Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 25(2), 250-260 (students who simulated the study process studied more and earned better grades than those imagining the outcome). The stories-versus-statistics result comes from Chip Heath's classroom exercise, not a peer-reviewed study: in one-minute speeches about nonviolent crime, the typical student used about 2.5 statistics and only one in ten told a story, yet on recall about ten minutes later 63 percent of listeners remembered the stories and 5 percent remembered any individual statistic.

insights.confidence_rationale: Process simulation is supported by a published experiment and related mental-simulation research, and narrative advantages in engagement are broadly accepted. The memorable classroom figures are informal and frequently misquoted (and inflated claims such as 'stories are 22 times more memorable' have no verifiable source). The three plot types are the authors' taxonomy rather than an empirical finding.

supporting_evidence.note: Narratives do shift beliefs, attitudes, intentions and behavior, but the meta-analytic effects are small (r about .17 to .23), so the classroom figure of 63 percent recalling stories versus 5 percent recalling statistics should not be read as the general size of the story advantage in persuasion.

The meta-analysis gives a measured mechanism for the book's simulation idea: absorbed listeners empathize with characters and imagine the plot, and transportation goes with story-consistent attitudes and intentions.

insights.name: Spread by Emotion, Not Just Truth
insights.takeaway: Give accurate messages emotional and concrete hooks, and be wary of ideas that spread because they grip rather than inform.
insights.explanation: Ideas compete for attention and retelling, and the ones that win are not necessarily the truest. Chip Heath's own research on urban legends found that stories evoking stronger shared emotions (in that case disgust) were more widely passed on. For communicators this cuts two ways: accurate messages need emotional and concrete hooks to compete with sticky falsehoods, and you should be wary of ideas (rumors, office gossip, viral claims) that spread because they are emotionally gripping rather than accurate.
insights.when_to_use: Correcting misinformation or a workplace rumor, designing a message that must be retold by others, and evaluating claims that spread quickly in your team, family chat or social feeds.
insights.worked_example: A rumor spreads that the company will close the regional office. The site manager realizes a dry 'no changes are planned at this time' email cannot compete with an anxious story. She holds a short meeting, names the rumor, gives concrete facts (the new five-year lease signed last month, the hiring plan for two roles), and invites questions. In a family group chat, a sibling pauses before forwarding an alarming health claim, noticing it spreads because it is scary, and checks it first.
common_mistakes: Assuming the truth will spread on its own merits
Repeating the false claim prominently when correcting it
Fighting emotional rumors with abstract reassurance
Forwarding emotionally gripping claims without checking them
situations: Correcting an office rumor
Responding to misinformation in a family group chat
Writing a message employees must retell to customers
Announcing uncertain news before details are final

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Introduction: What Sticks? (urban legends such as the Kidney Heist) and Chapter 5: Emotional; the urban legend research is Chip Heath's own
source.underlying_research: Heath, Bell and Sternberg (2001), 'Emotional selection in memes: The case of urban legends', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 81(6), 1028-1041 (people were more willing to pass on versions that evoked stronger disgust, and legends with more disgust motifs were more widely distributed on urban legend websites). That the book cites this paper by name was not confirmed; its use of urban legends and emotional selection is.

insights.confidence_rationale: Supported by a peer-reviewed study by one of the authors, consistent with later research showing emotional and novel content spreads further online. The study focused on disgust and urban legends, so generalizing to all emotions and workplace communication is an extrapolation; note the author has an interest in the finding.

insights.name: Translate Numbers to Human Scale
insights.takeaway: Translate big numbers into a familiar comparison people can picture, so they feel the size and act on it.
insights.explanation: Large or technical numbers rarely land on their own. The Heaths' human scale principle says to re-express a statistic in terms of something people already know and can picture, because what you want them to remember is usually the relationship, not the figure. Their examples include an activist who conveyed the size of the world's nuclear arsenal by dropping BBs into a metal bucket, one BB per Hiroshima bomb, and a comparison of how rarely sharks kill people with how often deer do. The aim is not to drop the number but to give it a familiar comparison so the audience can feel its size and act on it. The Heaths later devoted a whole book (Making Numbers Count, 2022) to this idea.
insights.when_to_use: Presenting budgets, risks, performance data or survey results to people who are not specialists; writing reports, pitches or donation appeals that rely on a key figure; explaining a bill, loan or medical risk to family.
insights.worked_example: An IT manager wants funding to fix slow laptops. Instead of '11,000 hours lost per year', she says: 'Our staff lose about the same time each year as six full-time employees sitting idle, just waiting for laptops to start.' At home, someone weighing a car loan reframes '$4,800 in interest' as 'about four months of our grocery budget', which makes the cost easy to compare with the alternatives.
common_mistakes: Choosing a comparison the audience does not actually know well
Using a vivid comparison that distorts the real size of the number
Translating every number, so the key one gets lost
Dropping the original figure entirely when decision-makers need it
steps: Pick the one number that matters most for the decision
Decide what you want people to grasp about it (size, rate, comparison)
Find a familiar unit or everyday comparison the audience uses (time, people, money, a known object)
State the comparison first, then give the precise figure
Check with someone outside the topic that the comparison leaves the right impression
situations: Presenting a budget request
Explaining a risk or metric to leadership
Writing a fundraising appeal with statistics
Comparing loan or purchase costs with a partner

source.citation: Chip Heath and Dan Heath, Made to Stick (2007), Chapter 4: Credible (statistics and the human scale principle; the BBs in a bucket and deer versus shark examples)
source.underlying_research: Barrio, Goldstein and Hofman (2016), 'Improving comprehension of numbers in the news', Proceedings of CHI 2016, 2729-2739: across three randomized online experiments with over 3,200 participants, short 'perspective' sentences that re-expressed numbers improved recall, estimation and error detection. Not cited in the book (it postdates it); supports the principle independently. Book examples (Ainscow's BBs in a bucket; deer versus shark) are confirmed through quoted passages in reader notes.

insights.confidence_rationale: The principle is named in the publisher's description and in reader summaries of the Credible chapter, and randomized experiments (Barrio et al., 2016, and follow-up work by the same group) support re-expressing numbers to improve comprehension and recall. Rated Medium because that evidence comes mainly from one research group and online samples, and the book itself supports the principle with cases.

insights.name: Three Kinds of Conversations
insights.takeaway: Notice whether a conversation is about solving a problem, feelings, or identity, and respond in the same layer.
insights.explanation: Duhigg sorts what is happening in any exchange into three overlapping layers. A practical conversation is about solving or deciding something (What's this really about?). An emotional conversation is about how people feel and whether those feelings are recognized (How do we feel?). A social conversation is about identity, belonging and how people see themselves and each other (Who are we?). Most real conversations shift among these layers, and many misfires happen because one person is in one layer while the other is in another, for example offering solutions to someone who wants to be understood.
insights.when_to_use: Whenever a conversation feels stuck, tense, or oddly unsatisfying despite everyone being reasonable; before important one-on-ones, feedback talks and family discussions.
insights.worked_example: A project lead tells her manager the launch date is impossible. The manager responds with a revised Gantt chart (practical). She grows quieter. He pauses and asks how she is doing with the workload; she admits she feels her team is being seen as the bottleneck again (emotional and social: how her team is perceived). Once that is named, they return to the schedule and agree on a realistic date in ten minutes.
common_mistakes: Treating every conversation as practical problem solving because that feels productive.
Labelling a conversation once and not noticing when it shifts layers midway.
Assuming identity topics only mean politics or demographics, rather than also roles, professions and self-image.
steps: Early on, ask yourself which question is driving this: what are we deciding, how do we feel, or who are we to each other?
Listen for clues: requests and plans (practical), stories, sighs or emotion words (emotional), references to groups, roles, status or what 'people like us' do (social).
If unsure, ask directly what the other person most wants from the conversation (Duhigg relays a teacher's version: do you want to be helped, hugged, or heard?).
Respond in the same layer first before moving to another.
situations: Partner vents about their day and you start fixing
Team member pushes back on a deadline
Family disagreement that keeps repeating
One-on-one that feels off for no obvious reason

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Prologue and Part I (The Three Kinds of Conversations), Chapter 1 (The Matching Principle). Part II covers What's This Really About? (Chapter 2), Part III How Do We Feel? (Chapters 3 to 5), Part IV Who Are We? (Chapters 6 and 7).
source.underlying_research: Duhigg's own synthesis; no single study validates this three-part typology. The SSIR review notes he links the three types to distinct brain systems, a neuroscience framing that is looser than the research itself. Partially echoes the 'three conversations' of Stone, Patton and Heen (Difficult Conversations: what happened, feelings, identity); Sheila Heen appears in the book's Chapter 5, but a direct citation of that framework was not confirmed.

insights.confidence_rationale: A useful and intuitively valid diagnostic that overlaps with established practitioner frameworks (Harvard Negotiation Project), but the specific three-part typology is a journalistic synthesis, not an empirically tested taxonomy.

insights.name: The Matching Principle
insights.takeaway: Notice which kind of conversation and mood the other person brings, meet them there, and only later invite a shift.
insights.explanation: Connection happens when people are having the same kind of conversation at the same time. Duhigg's core claim is that skilled communicators first notice which kind of conversation the other person wants (practical, emotional, or social) and the energy and mood they bring, then meet them there, and only later invite a shift. Matching is not mimicry; it is aligning on the type of conversation and its emotional register so the other person feels understood and is willing to match you in return.
insights.when_to_use: At the start of any important conversation and whenever you sense the other person is not hearing you.
insights.worked_example: A friend texts that her mother's diagnosis came back worse than expected. Instead of sending links to treatment options, you reply that you are so sorry and ask how she is holding up. Two days later she asks which specialists you would recommend, and only then do you switch to practical help.
common_mistakes: Copying body language or phrases mechanically, which reads as manipulative.
Matching negative escalation (raising your voice because they did) rather than matching the type of conversation.
Never moving on: matching is the entry point, not the whole conversation.
steps: Notice the type of conversation the other person is in and their energy (pace, volume, seriousness).
Respond in kind: a practical answer to a practical question, acknowledgment to feelings, recognition to identity concerns.
Signal your own intent so they can match you back.
Once aligned, propose a shift if needed (for example, 'Would it help to talk through options now?').
situations: Supporting a friend after bad news
Recruiting or onboarding someone who is hesitant
Talking with an upset client
Reconnecting with a teenager

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part I, Chapter 1 (The Matching Principle), illustrated with CIA case officer Jim Lawler.
source.underlying_research: Sievers, Welker, Hasson, Kleinbaum and Wheatley (2024), Consensus-building conversation leads to neural alignment, Nature Communications 15, 3936 (preprint 2020, cited in the book excerpt); Uri Hasson's speaker-listener neural coupling work, which Duhigg quotes (Stephens, Silbert and Hasson, 2010, PNAS, is the canonical paper; the exact paper he cites is not confirmed). The Lawler story is a single narrative case.

insights.confidence_rationale: Neural and behavioral synchrony during good conversation is a real, replicated correlational finding, but the step from synchrony to 'match the conversation type and you will connect' is an inference. The illustrating cases (Lawler) are single anecdotes. The advice is consistent with mainstream empathy and counselling practice.

supporting_evidence.note: Person-centered comforting is a concrete form of matching an emotional conversation rather than shifting to a practical one.

insights.name: The Learning Conversation (Four Rules)
insights.takeaway: Notice the conversation type, share goals and ask theirs, exchange feelings, and check whether identities matter to the discussion.
insights.explanation: Duhigg's practical summary of the book is the learning conversation: an exchange where both sides try to understand how the other sees the world and help the other understand them, rather than simply win. He says effective communicators (happy couples, good negotiators, influential leaders) tend to have them. The author's own companion gives the four rules as: pay attention to what kind of conversation is occurring; share your goals and ask what others are looking for; ask about others' feelings and share your own; and explore whether identities are important to the discussion. Each later part of the book elaborates one rule.
insights.when_to_use: Planned important conversations: performance reviews, negotiations with colleagues, family decisions, mending a strained friendship.
insights.worked_example: Two co-founders disagree about hiring a senior sales lead. One opens by saying, 'My goal is to stop being the bottleneck on deals; what is yours?' The other says her goal is to protect the culture. They each say how the debate is making them feel (anxious, sidelined), then notice that one sees herself as 'the builder' and the other as 'the closer'. The decision becomes a shared design problem instead of a contest.
common_mistakes: Running the rules as a checklist without genuine curiosity.
Sharing goals but not asking for theirs, which turns it into a pitch.
Skipping the feelings and identity rules because they feel awkward at work.
steps: Pay attention to which kind of conversation is occurring (practical, emotional, social).
Share your goals and ask what others are looking for from the conversation.
Ask about others' feelings and share your own.
Explore whether identities (roles, groups, values) are important to this discussion, and name shared ones.
situations: Resolving a disagreement with a co-founder or peer
Planning a major family decision
Performance review that may be tense
Cross-functional prioritization debate

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part I' (rules introduced); rule 2 in the Part II guide, rule 3 in the Part III guide, rule 4 in the Part IV guide.
source.underlying_research: Synthesis of the book's cases and research. Wording of all four rules confirmed against the author's book club companion. The Part I guide also relays a study in which employees who wrote down their goals before meetings had far fewer verbal arguments (nearly 80 percent fewer); the study itself was not identified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Each rule aligns with established practitioner guidance (interest-based negotiation, emotional disclosure, identity in conflict), but the four-rule package is the author's synthesis rather than a tested protocol. Wording now verified against the author's own companion guide.

insights.name: Every Conversation Is a Quiet Negotiation
insights.takeaway: Ask open questions about what others want, state your goals, add options, and match practical or emotional logic to the conversation.
insights.explanation: Duhigg argues that every meaningful conversation contains a quiet negotiation over what will be discussed and how decisions will be made, and that the prize is learning what everyone wants rather than winning. Supercommunicators surface this by asking open-ended questions about values and experiences, watching for cues of interest or disengagement (leaning in, eye contact, distraction), stating their own goals, and adding new options to the table so a win-win becomes possible. He also distinguishes two kinds of persuasive logic: costs and benefits for practical discussions, and similarities (stories, empathy) for emotional ones, and advises matching the logic to the conversation.
insights.when_to_use: Group decisions, meetings with mixed agendas, negotiations, and any conversation where people seem to be talking past each other.
insights.worked_example: In a budget meeting, a quiet engineer mentions 'last time this broke in production'. Rather than moving on, the chair says, 'That sounds like it matters; is reliability the main thing you want us to weigh?' He nods, and the group adds a reliability criterion that unlocks agreement.
common_mistakes: Ignoring small asides that are actually bids to raise a concern.
Assuming everyone shares your goal for the meeting.
Stating your goals in a way that sounds like a demand rather than an opening.
steps: Before an important conversation, take a moment to jot down a few topics or goals.
Open with open-ended questions about what people want and what the issue means to them.
Watch for cues: leaning in and smiling, or going quiet and distracted.
State what you hope to get from the conversation and ask what others hope to get.
If stuck, add new options or questions to the table to find a win-win.
Notice whether the group is reasoning by costs and benefits or by similarity and stories, and argue in that mode.
situations: Budget or prioritization meeting
Jury-like group decision with a split room
Salary or contract negotiation
Dinner-table discussion that keeps veering off

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part II, Chapter 2 (Every Conversation Is a Negotiation): the Leroy Reed jury and juror John Boly; surgeon Behfar Ehdaie and Deepak Malhotra with prostate cancer patients; 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part II'.
source.underlying_research: Narrative cases (a jury deliberation and a surgeon's patient conversations) plus negotiation research on integrative (win-win) bargaining. The Part II guide relays Harvard research that people are poor at detecting when partners want to change topic or end a conversation, and a study that briefly preparing topics beforehand reduces anxiety and awkward pauses; neither study was identified from the endnotes. Gottman's work on 'bids' is consistent but not confirmed as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: The chapter rests on two narrative cases, but the underlying advice (surface interests, ask open questions, look for integrative options) has solid support in negotiation practice and research.

supporting_evidence.note: Getting to Yes provides the operational method behind the idea that the prize in a negotiation is learning what everyone wants: separate interests from positions, invent options, and use criteria.

insights.name: Deep Questions
insights.takeaway: Ask about someone's values, beliefs, or experiences rather than facts, like whether they love their job, not where they work.
insights.explanation: A deep question invites someone to talk about their values, beliefs, or experiences rather than facts. Duhigg's own example: on meeting a lawyer, ask whether they always wanted to practice law or whether they love the job, rather than which firm they work for. Such questions are easy to ask, do not feel intrusive, and the answer also reveals what kind of conversation the other person wants. He draws on the Fast Friends procedure (escalating mutual disclosure builds closeness between strangers, but only when partners alternate asking and answering) and on Nicholas Epley's finding that people expect deep conversations with strangers to be more awkward than they turn out to be.
insights.when_to_use: Networking, first meetings with new colleagues or clients, dates, reconnecting with old friends, team offsites.
insights.worked_example: At a conference dinner you learn the person next to you is a hospital pharmacist. Instead of asking about the hospital's size, you ask what drew her to pharmacy. She tells you about a grandparent's medication error, and the conversation becomes the one you both remember from the event.
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to very personal questions without context, which feels invasive.
Asking a deep question and then not reciprocating with something about yourself.
Treating a list of 'deep questions' as a script instead of following the actual answer.
steps: Start with a normal factual question.
Follow with a question about values, choices, feelings or meaning (why, what do you love, what was hard).
Listen fully, then share something comparable about yourself.
Escalate gradually if the other person reciprocates.
situations: Networking event conversation
First coffee with a new teammate
Date or new friendship
Reconnecting with an estranged relative

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, Chapter 3 (The Listening Cure): Fast Friends procedure and Nicholas Epley's session with hedge fund investors; Duhigg's Next Big Idea Club summary (idea 2, Ask deep questions).
source.underlying_research: Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone and Bator (1997), The experimental generation of interpersonal closeness: A procedure and some preliminary findings, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 23(4), 363-377 (the 36 questions; confirmed as discussed in the book). Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2022), Overly shallow?: Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 122(3), 367-398. The book presents Epley's research on this point, but citation of the specific 2022 paper is not confirmed from the endnotes.

insights.confidence_rationale: The Fast Friends procedure has been used and replicated widely in lab settings, and the underestimation of deep conversation has been shown across multiple experiments. Effects are measured mostly with strangers in labs, so transfer to workplaces is reasonable but less tested.

insights.name: Ask More, Especially Follow-Ups
insights.takeaway: Talk less and ask more questions, especially follow-ups; admitting confusion and encouraging others builds shared understanding and liking.
insights.explanation: In a Dartmouth study Duhigg describes (Beau Sievers, Thalia Wheatley and colleagues), small groups had to agree on interpretations of confusing silent film clips. Groups run by a dominant, talkative leader showed the least neural alignment. The groups that aligned best had one or two 'high centrality' participants, people with large real-world social networks, who spoke less, asked many more questions (Duhigg says ten to twenty times as many), encouraged others, admitted confusion and laughed at others' jokes. Separately, research finds that asking questions, especially follow-ups, increases how much people like the asker.
insights.when_to_use: Meetings, interviews, group discussions, any time you are tempted to fill silence with your own view.
insights.worked_example: A new manager runs her first retro. Instead of presenting her diagnosis, she asks each person what surprised them, then asks a follow-up on each answer ('What made that harder than expected?'). The team later describes her as easy to talk to, and the retro surfaces a process problem she had missed.
common_mistakes: Rapid-fire questions that feel like an interrogation.
Switching topics with each question instead of following up.
Using questions as disguised statements ('Don't you think we should...?').
steps: Before speaking, ask yourself whether a question would serve better than a statement.
Make most questions follow-ups that build on the last answer.
Draw in people who have not spoken.
Resist dominating; let the group reach its own conclusions.
situations: Running a team retrospective
Job interview as interviewer or candidate
Leading a brainstorming session
Meeting a partner's friends for the first time

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part I, Chapter 1 (The Matching Principle); excerpt adapted in Behavioral Scientist; Duhigg's Next Big Idea Club summary (idea 2).
source.underlying_research: Sievers, Welker, Hasson, Kleinbaum and Wheatley (2024), Consensus-building conversation leads to neural alignment, Nature Communications 15, 3936 (cited in the excerpt as the 2020 PsyArXiv preprint). The abstract supports the core claim: high-status participants who spoke more and had unequal turn-taking produced lower alignment, while socially central participants encouraged others to speak and raised alignment. The ten to twenty times figure appears in Duhigg's text but not in the abstract. Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson and Gino (2017), It doesn't hurt to ask: Question-asking increases liking, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113(3), 430-452; not confirmed as cited by Duhigg. Integrity note: Francesca Gino is a coauthor; she has been the subject of data-fabrication findings on other papers, and this paper has not been implicated; a follow-up (Yeomans et al., 2019) defended its speed-dating analysis.

insights.confidence_rationale: The question-asking and liking effect is supported across several studies, and the Sievers paper is peer reviewed. The specific claim that supercommunicators ask 10 to 20 times as many questions comes from one lab's study as relayed by Duhigg and is not in the published abstract; treat the number as illustrative.

supporting_evidence.note: The review's checklist tells leaders to actively encourage everyone to participate and to intervene when communication patterns become dysfunctional, consistent with the finding that dominant talkers reduce group alignment.

Rogelberg's meeting research and his advice to hand agenda items to others and use silent idea generation converge with the finding that groups led by a dominant talker align least; he adds the data point that leaders systematically overrate their own meetings.

insights.name: Looping for Understanding
insights.takeaway: Ask a question, restate the answer in your own words, and check if you got it right until they confirm.
insights.explanation: Looping is a way to prove you are listening, not just to listen. You ask a question, restate what you heard in your own words (not parroting), and then ask whether you got it right. If not, you repeat until the other person confirms. The goal is that the other person feels understood, which lowers defensiveness and makes them more willing to hear you, even if neither of you changes your position.
insights.when_to_use: Conflict, emotionally charged feedback, customer complaints, partner arguments, and any time the stakes of misunderstanding are high.
insights.worked_example: A client says the report 'missed the point'. Rather than defending it, the consultant says, 'So it sounds like you needed a recommendation you could take to your board, and what we gave you was mostly analysis. Is that right?' The client says, 'Partly, and also I needed the cost numbers up front.' The consultant loops again, and the revision brief is clear in five minutes.
common_mistakes: Repeating their words verbatim, which sounds robotic or mocking.
Sneaking your rebuttal into the summary.
Skipping the 'did I get that right?' check, which is what makes it a loop.
Using it in fast, purely practical exchanges where it feels patronizing.
steps: Ask a question to understand their view.
Summarize what you heard in your own words, including the feeling or concern beneath it.
Ask whether you got it right.
If they correct you, incorporate the correction and loop again until they confirm.
Only then share your own perspective.
situations: Client says your work missed the mark
Argument with a partner about chores
Political disagreement with a relative
Receiving critical feedback from a manager

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, Chapter 5 (Connecting Amid Conflict) and 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part III'; Duhigg's Next Big Idea Club summary (idea 4).
source.underlying_research: Practice-based: taught to gun-control and gun-rights advocates at a 2018 dialogue organized with Advance Local and Essential Partners (Reflective Structured Dialogue), with Harvard's Sheila Heen involved; Duhigg says on NPR it is taught at Stanford and Harvard. The method closely matches the 'loop of understanding' of mediators Gary Friedman and Jack Himmelstein (Challenging Conflict, 2008); whether Duhigg credits them could not be verified. Related research on paraphrasing and high-quality listening (e.g., Itzchakov and Kluger) is generally supportive, though Weger and colleagues (2014) found paraphrasing added little over simple acknowledgment in some conditions.

insights.confidence_rationale: Widely used in mediation and supported by listening research in general, but evidence for looping specifically is mostly practitioner experience. Duhigg's own case (the guns dialogue) produced modest results: people felt heard but rarely changed views, and the conversation deteriorated when moved online.

supporting_evidence.note: The book's communication advice (listen actively, acknowledge, and restate the other side's view) applies looping to adversarial negotiation, where showing understanding is separated from agreeing.
Looping is the listener-side check; this study shows why the speaker-side equivalent matters too, since speakers systematically overrate their clarity.

Listening to make people feel understood is supported at scale, but the authors report trainees resist mechanical paraphrasing and note that no single overt behavior is necessary or sufficient to signal good listening.
Independent clinical evidence that reflecting and summarizing what someone said, rather than arguing, is part of a method with replicated effects on behavior change.

Explicit verbal evidence of understanding (validation, follow-ups) linked to stronger connection and faster, smoother turn-taking, consistent with proving you are listening rather than just listening.

insights.name: Vulnerability Invites Trust
insights.takeaway: Share how you felt about something first; when the other person reciprocates, trust grows, so do not wait to feel safe.
insights.explanation: Many people wait to feel safe before opening up. Duhigg argues the sequence often runs the other way: when someone shares how they feel and the other person reciprocates, trust grows. He calls this emotional reciprocity and links it to emotional contagion, the tendency to catch the feelings of those around us. Emotional sharing need not be dark or dramatic; any mention of how you reacted to something counts. He also notes the reverse failure: after his father died, few people asked him about it, though he wanted to talk.
insights.when_to_use: Building trust on a new team, repairing a strained relationship, difficult conversations where both sides are guarded.
insights.worked_example: A director meeting a skeptical new team says, 'Honestly, I am nervous about stepping into a group that already works well; I don't want to break what you have built.' Two people respond by sharing their own worries about the reorganization, and the meeting turns into a real discussion.
common_mistakes: Oversharing or trauma-dumping, which burdens the listener.
Performative vulnerability used as a tactic, which people detect.
Disclosing without leaving space for the other person to reciprocate.
Ignoring power differences: a junior person bears more risk when disclosing.
steps: Share a modest, honest feeling relevant to the situation.
Pause and ask how the other person sees it.
Acknowledge what they share without judging or fixing.
Escalate disclosure gradually as trust grows.
situations: New leader meeting a skeptical team
Making friends as an adult
Repairing trust after a falling out
Opening up to a partner about stress

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, Chapter 3 (The Listening Cure) and 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part III'.
source.underlying_research: Aron et al. (1997) Fast Friends (confirmed as discussed, including the requirement that partners alternate); emotional contagion (Hatfield, Cacioppo and Rapson, 1993/1994; the concept is named in the book, the specific citation not confirmed); self-disclosure and liking meta-analysis (Collins and Miller, 1994, Psychological Bulletin; not confirmed as cited); Nicholas Epley's research on emotional conversation.

insights.confidence_rationale: Reciprocal self-disclosure building closeness is well established, and emotional contagion is a robust phenomenon. The broader framing that vulnerability reliably precedes trust is an extrapolation, and workplace power dynamics limit it.

insights.name: Read and Match Emotional Signals (Including Laughter)
insights.takeaway: Read whether someone's mood is positive or negative and their energy high or low, then match both to connect.
insights.explanation: Much of what people feel shows up in tone, posture, pace and laughter rather than words. Duhigg suggests you do not need to identify the exact emotion: reading two dimensions, mood (positive or negative) and energy (high or low), is enough to respond well, and matching that mood and energy shows you want to connect. His illustration is NASA psychiatrist Terrance McGuire, who, when screening astronauts for long missions, reportedly spilled papers, laughed loudly, and watched whether candidates matched his laugh. Duhigg also says most laughter (about 80 percent) is not a response to anything funny but a signal of wanting to connect. The Big Bang Theory writers used matched and mismatched emotions to make awkward characters readable.
insights.when_to_use: Interviews, client meetings, video calls, family visits, any setting where people may not state their feelings directly.
insights.worked_example: On a video call, a colleague says 'Sure, that works' in a flat voice and looks away. Instead of moving to the next agenda item, you say, 'You sound less sure than the words suggest; what's the hesitation?' He admits the timeline overlaps with his parental leave.
common_mistakes: Forcing laughter or mirroring to seem attuned.
Reading too much into one cue; look for clusters.
Matching anger or panic rather than acknowledging it calmly.
steps: Notice the other person's mood (positive or negative) and energy (high or low), including mismatches between words and tone.
Match the overall mood and energy when appropriate, or acknowledge it aloud.
Name what you observe tentatively and ask about it (for example, 'What happened?').
Use shared laughter as a signal of connection, not a performance.
situations: Job interview rapport
Colleague agrees but sounds reluctant
Family gathering with unspoken tension
Sales call with a quiet client

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, Chapter 4 (How Do You Hear Emotions No One Says Aloud?): The Big Bang Theory writers and NASA psychiatrist Terrance McGuire; mood and energy chart; Duhigg's Next Big Idea Club summary (idea 3).
source.underlying_research: Mood and energy correspond to valence and arousal in circumplex models of emotion (Russell), which the book uses. Laughter as social signal: Robert Provine's observational research (most laughter follows non-humorous remarks), the likely source of the 80 percent figure; Bryant et al. (2016, PNAS) on detecting affiliation from co-laughter across cultures. Neither is confirmed as cited by Duhigg. The NASA laughter screening is narrative only and not documented in peer-reviewed form; accounts differ slightly on timing (1980s planning versus ISS selection).

insights.confidence_rationale: Now confirmed in the book. Attending to mood and energy is sound and grounded in standard emotion models, and laughter as a bonding signal has observational support, but the vivid NASA laughter test is a single secondhand anecdote and the idea that matched laughter reliably reveals emotional intelligence is not established science. Kept Low.

supporting_evidence.note: Nonverbal signals are informative for mood in general, but for judging honesty the body and face are among the weakest channels; audible content carries more.
Reading mood and energy is reasonable, but nonverbal research shows such reads are modestly accurate, so matching should be paired with checking rather than treated as sure.

insights.name: Social Identities Shape What People Hear
insights.takeaway: When a message threatens someone's identity, stop adding facts; find shared identities, ensure equal footing, and build common groups.
insights.explanation: People hear messages through the groups they belong to and the self-image they want to protect. When a message threatens someone's identity (as a good parent, an independent thinker, an expert), more facts often harden resistance. Duhigg's main example is pediatrician Jay Rosenbloom, whose evidence-heavy approach with vaccine-hesitant parents backfired until he challenged his own stereotypes of them and connected through shared identities (fellow parents with kids in the same schools). Remedies from the chapter: remember that everyone holds many identities, ensure equal footing, and build new shared groups, as in Salma Mousa's study where mixed Christian and Muslim soccer teams in post-ISIS Iraq built cooperation.
insights.when_to_use: Persuasion on value-laden topics, cross-team conflict, change management, conversations with people from different backgrounds or political views.
insights.worked_example: An IT lead rolling out a new tool meets resistance from senior nurses. Instead of presenting more features, she says, 'You are the people who catch the errors everyone else misses; I need your help making sure this doesn't create new ones.' Framed as protecting patient safety, a value the nurses identify with, the pilot gains volunteers.
common_mistakes: Responding to identity-based resistance with more data.
Reducing people to a single identity (for example, only their politics).
Invoking group identities in a way that stereotypes or divides.
steps: Ask what this issue means to the person and who they are in relation to it.
Listen for group language ('people like us', 'as a parent', 'in my field').
Check your own stereotypes about their group.
Acknowledge the identity and its legitimate values.
Surface identities you share (fellow parent, same team, same goal), and treat the other person as an equal.
Only then discuss facts, framed in terms consistent with their identity.
situations: Persuading a skeptical relative on a health decision
Rolling out change to a proud professional group
Cross-department turf conflict
Talking politics at a family dinner

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part IV, Chapter 6 (Our Social Identities Shape Our Worlds): Dr. Jay Rosenbloom, stereotype threat, identity maps, Salma Mousa's soccer study; physician Rima Chamie's COVID vaccine conversation; Duhigg's Next Big Idea Club summary (idea 5).
source.underlying_research: Mousa (2020), Building social cohesion between Christians and Muslims through soccer in post-ISIS Iraq, Science 369(6505), 866-870 (described in the book; a randomized field experiment on intergroup contact). Stereotype threat research (Steele and Aronson tradition) and a study in which women who mapped their multiple identities before a math test performed on par with men (described in the book; likely Gresky and colleagues, 2005, not confirmed). Social identity theory (Tajfel and Turner) and identity-protective cognition (Kahan) are consistent background, not confirmed as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: Social identity effects on persuasion are well supported, and the chapter's remedy draws on a randomized field experiment (Mousa) and stereotype threat research, not only physician stories. The doctor cases remain anecdotes, and the shared-identity remedy as applied to one-on-one persuasion is not directly tested.

supporting_evidence.note: Unity adds that shared identity between requester and listener, not only the listener's own identity, shapes how a request is received; mostly supported by social identity research and the author's reasoning.

Moral reframing works partly because the message matches the listener's identity-linked convictions and signals an ingroup source; messages framed in the other side's moral language can harden opposition.

insights.name: Make Conflict Conversations Safer
insights.takeaway: In heated disagreements, aim to understand rather than convert: loop back, acknowledge, find specific agreement, and speak from experience.
insights.explanation: In heated disagreements, Duhigg (drawing on a 2018 dialogue between gun-rights and gun-control advocates, including Melanie Jeffcoat and Jon Godfrey) suggests the goal is mutual understanding, not conversion. Understand why the conflict exists and the emotions beneath it, prove you are listening (looping), acknowledge what you have understood, find specific points of agreement, and temper sweeping claims in favor of personal experience. He also relays research that happy and unhappy couples argue about equally often, but happy couples focus on controlling their own reactions rather than each other. Success is measured by whether people feel heard and can keep talking.
insights.when_to_use: Polarized team debates, family conflicts over values, community or board meetings on contentious topics.
insights.worked_example: Two department heads are fighting over remote-work policy. The facilitator asks each to describe a personal experience that shaped their view. One talks about a junior hire who struggled alone; the other about caring for a parent. Each loops the other's story. They still disagree on the default, but agree on mentoring guarantees both can support.
common_mistakes: Measuring success by whether you won or changed their mind.
Skipping ground rules, so the first sharp comment derails everything.
Moving a sensitive conversation into a public online thread without shared norms (in Duhigg's case, the follow-on Facebook group turned hostile).
steps: Agree on ground rules (speak for yourself, listen to understand, no personal attacks).
Ask what experiences and feelings sit behind each view.
Loop what you heard until each person confirms they feel understood.
Name specific points of agreement ('I think you are right that...').
