Temper claims: avoid 'everyone knows' and 'your side always', and speak from your own experience.
Focus on controlling your own reactions, not the other person.
situations: Facilitating a polarized team debate
Holiday dinner political argument
Board or HOA meeting on a contentious issue
Siblings disagreeing about a parent's care

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, Chapter 5 (Connecting Amid Conflict) and 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part III' (how this changes in a conflict).
source.underlying_research: Essential Partners' Reflective Structured Dialogue in a 2018 project with Advance Local, with input from negotiation scholar Sheila Heen. The couples finding echoes Gottman-style marital conflict research (not confirmed as cited). Practitioner evidence, not controlled trials.

insights.confidence_rationale: Structured dialogue methods have long practitioner track records, and the advice converges with mediation practice. Duhigg's own case showed modest outcomes and a breakdown once the conversation moved online without the training.

supporting_evidence.note: Gottman's finding that all couples fight and that conflict is managed rather than resolved underlies Duhigg's point that happy and unhappy couples argue similarly often.

Adds rigorous evidence that non-judgmental listening and story exchange, not argument, is what moves people in heated disagreements, with the caveat that per-conversation effects are small (d about 0.04 to 0.08).

insights.name: Online, Default to Extra Warmth and Explicitness
insights.takeaway: Online, be extra polite and grateful, skip sarcasm, and never criticize people publicly, since tone is easily lost.
insights.explanation: Digital channels strip out tone, faces and timing, so emotional cues get lost and misreadings multiply. Duhigg's advice for online conversation is to overdo politeness (please, thank you), steer clear of sarcasm, which is easily misread, express more gratitude, greetings and apologies than feels necessary, and avoid criticizing people in public. He illustrates the stakes with the gun dialogue, which deteriorated when it moved to a Facebook group without the shared training, and improved when participants were reminded of the skills.
insights.when_to_use: Email, Slack or Teams, comment threads, texting with family, any asynchronous communication about something sensitive.
insights.worked_example: A teammate replies 'fine, whatever works' on Slack to your plan. Instead of taking it as approval, you DM: 'Thanks for looking. Reading your note, I wonder if the timeline feels rushed; is that right?' She explains a dependency you missed, and you avoid a public blowup in the channel.
common_mistakes: Using sarcasm or dry humor that reads as hostility.
Giving critical feedback in a public channel.
Assuming silence or short replies mean agreement.
Over-correcting into vague politeness that hides the actual request.
steps: Before sending, reread for tone as a stressed reader would.
Add explicit politeness, greetings and appreciation.
Remove sarcasm and ambiguous jokes.
Move criticism to a private message or a call.
When stakes are high, summarize your understanding and ask if it is right (an extension of looping; not stated by Duhigg specifically for text).
situations: Ambiguous Slack reply from a colleague
Giving feedback over email
Family group chat tension
Remote team disagreement

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part III, end of Chapter 5 (how this changes when we go online) and 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part III'.
source.underlying_research: Kruger, Epley, Parker and Ng (2005), Egocentrism over e-mail: Can we communicate as well as we think?, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 89(6), 925-936 (senders overestimate how well tone, including sarcasm, comes across); not confirmed as cited by Duhigg. The specific prescriptions are Duhigg's.

insights.confidence_rationale: The core problem (tone misreading in text, overconfidence in conveying sarcasm) is well documented. The SSIR review criticizes the online advice as overly simplistic, since politeness does not address harassment, mob dynamics or anonymous bad-faith actors.

supporting_evidence.note: Adds a specific case of making the implicit explicit in digital channels: receivers infer more urgency than senders intend, and an explicit note about timing corrects it (Giurge and Bohns 2021, Study 6).

Primary evidence for avoiding sarcasm online: email sarcasm was decoded at about chance in Study 2 while senders were as confident as when speaking. Qualifies one fix: in a follow-up, allowing emoticons did not reduce senders' overconfidence.

For practical requests, extra warmth can cost responses: the longer email that lost the 7,002-person test differed by added sentences, which the authors describe as expressing gratitude for the recipients' work. Warmth still matters for relationship messages, but in task requests keep pleasantries brief.

insights.name: Connection as Synchrony
insights.takeaway: Build connection together by attending closely to each other, rather than trying to win with a great argument or dominating.
insights.explanation: When a conversation goes well, people tend to fall into sync: their breathing, gestures, and even patterns of brain activity become more similar, which researchers call neural entrainment. Duhigg uses this as the underlying picture of what 'clicking' is. The useful takeaway for everyday life is modest: connection is something two people build together by attending to each other, not something one person delivers with a great argument, and dominating a conversation tends to reduce shared understanding.
insights.when_to_use: As a lens for reflecting on why some conversations click and others do not, and as a reminder to slow down and attend rather than perform.
insights.worked_example: After a frustrating meeting where he presented a strong case and nobody engaged, a product manager rethinks his approach. In the next one he presents half as much, asks the group what they see, and builds on their answers. The decision takes longer but the team actually commits to it.
common_mistakes: Treating brain-synchrony findings as proof that any specific technique works.
Trying to engineer synchrony through mimicry rather than genuine attention.
Equating feeling in sync with agreement.
situations: Reflecting on a meeting that fell flat
Leading a group toward consensus
Understanding why some friendships click instantly

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part I, Chapter 1 (The Matching Principle: neural entrainment, Uri Hasson, the Dartmouth group study); Behavioral Scientist excerpt.
source.underlying_research: Wheatley, Kang, Parkinson and Looser (2012), From mind perception to mental connection: Synchrony as a mechanism for social understanding, Social and Personality Psychology Compass 6(8), 589-606 (listed with the excerpt); Sievers et al. (2024), Nature Communications 15, 3936 (increased neural alignment after consensus conversation, lower alignment with dominant speakers); Hasson's speaker-listener coupling work (Stephens, Silbert and Hasson, 2010, PNAS). Parkinson, Kleinbaum and Wheatley (2018, Nature Communications) on similar neural responses among friends is related but not confirmed as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: Neural and behavioral synchrony during communication is a replicated finding, but it is correlational and measured in small fMRI samples. Popular retellings, including the book's framing of being 'hardwired' for entrainment, risk pop-neuroscience overreach; the practical advice does not depend on the brain data.

supporting_evidence.note: Group collaboration process predicted collective performance more strongly than individual members' skill, consistent with the view that good outcomes are built jointly rather than delivered by one strong contributor.

insights.name: Prepare and Set Norms for the Hardest Conversations
insights.takeaway: For identity-laden topics, prepare, plan how the talk will happen, name the awkwardness, and speak from your own experience.
insights.explanation: Conversations about race, politics, money or other identity-laden topics trigger identity threat: people feel their sense of self is under attack, become defensive and physically stressed, and stop listening. Duhigg's case is Netflix, whose no-rules debating culture collided with a 2018 incident involving a racial slur, after which inclusion lead Verna Myers introduced norms and training for discussing bias. The lessons he draws: prepare beforehand, do not avoid a conversation just because it worries you, think about how it will happen as much as what will be said, acknowledge the awkwardness at the start, speak from your own experience rather than in generalizations, and acknowledge others' experiences. The goal is understanding and inclusion, not a perfect conversation.
insights.when_to_use: Discussions of bias, politics, religion or money at work or at home; giving feedback that touches someone's self-image; team conversations after an incident that hurt people.
insights.worked_example: After a heated all-hands where a remark about older workers upset several people, a manager schedules a follow-up. Beforehand she writes down what she hopes to learn and what might go wrong. She opens by saying the talk may feel uncomfortable but matters, proposes two norms (speak from your own experience, no blaming individuals), and shares her own story of feeling sidelined early in her career. People describe their experiences, and the team agrees on concrete changes to how meetings are run.
common_mistakes: Avoiding the conversation entirely because it feels risky.
Starting without norms, so the first sharp remark derails it.
Speaking in sweeping generalizations about groups instead of personal experience.
Expecting one conversation or training to fix structural problems.
Treating discomfort as a sign the conversation is failing.
steps: Before: decide what you hope to accomplish, how the conversation will start, what obstacles may arise and how you will handle emotions.
At the start: set clear norms, share your goals and invite others' goals, and acknowledge that it may feel awkward.
During: invite people to share their backgrounds and multiple identities, and share yours.
Keep everyone on equal footing so all voices are heard.
Acknowledge experiences and look for genuine (not forced) similarities.
Choose a suitable setting and time when people can give full attention.
situations: Team discussion after a hurtful incident
Talking about race or politics with family
Workplace inclusion or bias training session
Giving feedback that touches someone's identity

source.citation: Duhigg, Supercommunicators, Part IV, Chapter 7 (How Do We Make the Hardest Conversations Safer?): Netflix and Verna Myers; 'A Guide to Using These Ideas, Part IV'.
source.underlying_research: Identity threat research (Steele and colleagues; specific studies cited by Duhigg not confirmed). The book itself notes that many corporate anti-bias programs show weak effects. The Netflix case is a single organizational narrative; Duhigg reports that Netflix later led large tech and Hollywood firms in hiring from underrepresented groups.

insights.confidence_rationale: The preparation and norm-setting advice converges with mediation and dialogue practice, and identity threat is an established concept, but the evidence presented is mainly one company's story, and diversity-training research is mixed.

insights.name: The TALK maxims
insights.takeaway: When a conversation stalls, check your topics, your questions, your levity, and whether you are prioritizing your partner's needs.
insights.explanation: Brooks organizes conversational skill into four maxims: Topics (choose good topics and manage them well), Asking (ask more, and better, questions), Levity (use humor and warmth to keep the exchange lively), and Kindness (try to prioritize your partner's conversational needs). She frames conversation as a coordination game that is harder than it looks, and the maxims as short reminders of where it usually goes wrong, so you can diagnose a stalled exchange and pick the right fix. They are a checklist, not a script.
insights.when_to_use: Before an important conversation to plan, and afterwards to debrief what worked and what stalled.
insights.worked_example: After a flat one-on-one with a new direct report, a manager runs the four letters: Topics, we only covered ticket status; Asking, I asked two questions, both yes or no; Levity, nobody laughed once; Kindness, I talked 70 percent of the time. Next week she brings two non-status topics, plans one open follow-up, and deliberately lets the report lead the first ten minutes.
common_mistakes: Treating TALK as a script to recite rather than a diagnostic lens
Working on only one letter (usually Asking) and ignoring the rest
Forcing humor or depth when the partner's needs call for something else
steps: Before: list a few topics you could raise and one or two open questions
During: notice which letter is failing (stale topic, no questions, no lightness, one-sided)
Adjust: switch topic, ask a follow-up, add a light remark, or hand the floor back
After: rate each letter briefly and pick one to improve next time
situations: Debriefing a conversation that felt awkward
Preparing for a first meeting with a new manager
Improving weekly one-on-ones
Reconnecting with a friend you have drifted from

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), overall structure: opening framing of conversation as a coordination game, then one part per TALK maxim, followed by material on difficult moments, groups, and apologies (per the author's TALK workbook); exact chapter titles not verified
source.underlying_research: Synthesis of Brooks's conversation research program at Harvard Business School (speed dates, sales calls, parole hearings, structured lab chats) plus wider literature

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the publisher description and the author's workbook. The acronym is an organizing device by a credible conversation researcher; the components draw on peer-reviewed work of varying strength, but the framework as a whole has not been tested as a unit.

insights.name: Prepare topics in advance
insights.takeaway: Spend thirty seconds jotting several topics before a conversation, as insurance against lulls and a nudge toward richer subjects.
insights.explanation: Most people walk into conversations expecting topics to arrive on their own, and feel that preparing them would be awkward or calculating. Brooks reports that only a small minority (about 18 percent) prepare topics, and about half think doing so would make the conversation less enjoyable. Yet in her research even about thirty seconds of planning made conversations flow better, with fewer awkward pauses and filler words, and left people less anxious and more confident; her MBA students, who resist the exercise, reliably enjoy prepared-topic conversations more. You do not have to raise every item: the list is insurance for a lull and a nudge toward richer subjects than whatever comes to mind first. People are also poor at predicting which topics will turn out well, so several options beat betting on one.
insights.when_to_use: Networking events, first dates, dinners with in-laws, client lunches, skip-level meetings, any situation where you fear dead air.
insights.worked_example: Heading to a client dinner, an account lead writes four possible topics in her phone: the client's recent office move, a book she knows the client posted about, a light question about weekend plans, and one industry trend she is curious about. When the conversation stalls after the menu, she pulls the office move topic, which turns into a twenty-minute exchange about remote work.
common_mistakes: Rigidly working through the list instead of following the partner's energy
Preparing only safe, generic topics (weather, traffic)
Preparing monologues rather than topics that invite the other person in
Assuming you can tell in advance which topic will land
steps: Take about thirty seconds before the conversation to write down around five possible topics
Mix light and more substantive options, and include something about the other person
Keep the list handy (phone or calendar note) but out of sight
Use it when a lull hits; drop it when the conversation has its own momentum
situations: Attending a networking event alone
First date
Client lunch or dinner
Holiday gathering with relatives you rarely see
Coffee chat with a senior leader

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), T (Topics) maxim; workbook exercise 'Prep topics'
source.underlying_research: Brooks and colleagues' topic-preparation studies (about 18 percent prepare; brief planning reduced pauses and anxiety) and Yeomans and Brooks topic-prediction study (about 1,000 people rated 50 topics, then discussed them; enjoyment was poorly predicted), as reported from the book by Greater Good; no peer-reviewed article located. Plus Brooks's classroom observations.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and the author's workbook. Rests on Brooks's own studies with Yeomans, which I could not find as peer-reviewed publications, plus teaching experience. Plausible and low-cost; Medium retained.

insights.name: The topic pyramid: climb from small talk, and switch before it goes stale
insights.takeaway: Use small talk to find better topics, and when pauses grow, climb deeper with a follow-up or switch topics.
insights.explanation: Brooks pictures topics as a pyramid with three tiers: small talk at the base (topics any group could discuss), tailored talk in the middle (topics personalized to the people present), and deep talk at the top (topics only this particular group could have). Small talk is not the problem; it is an unavoidable ritual and a treasure hunt for something better. The common mistake is staying on base-level topics, or any spent topic, too long. Signs a topic is running dry include uncomfortable laughter, longer mutual pauses, and repeated statements. When you notice them, either climb (usually with a follow-up question on something that sparked interest) or switch assertively to a new topic; you can call back to earlier topics later. In her studies, pairs asked to cover more topics enjoyed the conversation more without losing depth, and more people felt they had covered too few topics than too many. Not every conversation needs to reach the top.
insights.when_to_use: Whenever a conversation is polite but flat, or when you notice the same points being repeated.
insights.worked_example: At a school pickup, two parents have covered the weather and the bake sale twice. One says, 'That bake sale saga has had a good run. Can I ask, how are you finding the new job you mentioned last month?' The switch acknowledges the old topic and moves to something more personal, and the chat comes alive.
common_mistakes: Abandoning a topic abruptly without acknowledging it
Jumping straight to intense personal questions with someone you just met
Staying on a dying topic out of politeness
Assuming every conversation should end up deep
steps: Notice signals that a topic is spent: uncomfortable laughter, longer mutual pauses, repetition
When something sparks interest, climb with a follow-up question toward tailored talk
Otherwise switch assertively to a fresh topic, briefly affirming the old one if it helps
Call back to earlier topics that deserved more airtime, and match depth to the relationship
situations: Small talk that keeps circling
Team lunch with colleagues you barely know
Catching up with an old friend
Long car ride with a partner

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), T (Topics) maxim; workbook exercises 'Be a topic leader' and 'Stick with small talk'; LIFTOFF podcast episode 4 interview
source.underlying_research: Brooks and colleagues' topic-switching studies as reported from the book: strangers asked to cover 12 topics in 10 minutes rated enjoyment higher (about 5 to 6 on a 7-point scale) than those talking normally; in 30-minute online chats, 20 percent felt they covered too few topics versus 11 percent too many. Yeomans seminar abstract reports people are poor at detecting whether a partner wants to stay on or switch. No peer-reviewed article located.

insights.confidence_rationale: Pyramid and switching advice confirmed in the author's workbook, podcast interview, and Greater Good summary of the book. The pyramid is a teaching metaphor and the switching evidence comes from Brooks lab studies not located in peer-reviewed form, so specific switching claims are provisional.

supporting_evidence.note: Among students, a diet of small talk went with friends drifting apart while catching up, playful and serious talk went with growing closeness, consistent with climbing beyond small talk.

insights.name: Ask more questions, especially follow-ups
insights.takeaway: Ask more questions than feels natural, especially follow-ups on what the other person just said; it makes you more liked.
insights.explanation: People ask fewer questions than would serve them, overestimate how many they ask, and do not expect questions to make them more liked. In live online chats, people instructed to ask more questions were liked more, an effect the authors attribute largely to follow-up questions, the ones that build on what the other person just said, because they signal listening and care (responsiveness). Brooks also reports that in speed dates, people who asked more follow-ups got more second dates and nobody reached a point of asking too many.
insights.when_to_use: First meetings, interviews (on either side), one-on-ones, dates, and catching up with family; any time you want the other person to feel heard.
insights.worked_example: A colleague mentions she spent the weekend helping her father move. Instead of saying 'Nice, I went hiking,' you ask, 'How did he feel about leaving the old place?' Her answer leads to a real conversation about aging parents, and later that week she seeks you out for advice on a project.
common_mistakes: Asking a rapid-fire list of unrelated questions that feels like an interrogation
Asking a question only as a lead-in to your own story
Stacking several questions at once so the person cannot answer any well
Asking follow-ups without actually listening to the answer
steps: Listen for a detail, feeling, or surprise in what the person just said
Ask one open question about that detail (how, what was it like, what happened next)
Let them answer fully before sharing your own related experience
Balance: share about yourself too, so it stays reciprocal
situations: First conversation with a new teammate
Job interview, as candidate or interviewer
Speed networking
Catching up with a teenager after school
First date

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim; Brooks and Leslie K. John, 'The Surprising Power of Questions,' Harvard Business Review 96(3), May-June 2018
source.underlying_research: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson and Gino (2017), 'It Doesn't Hurt to Ask: Question-Asking Increases Liking,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113(3), 430-452 (two chat experiments with modest effects, plus speed-dating field data). Critique: Kluger and Malloy (2019), 'Question Asking as a Dyadic Behavior,' JPSP 117(6), 1127-1138, found the speed-dating association vanished once actor and partner effects were controlled. Integrity note: Gino-coauthored; listed by the Many Co-Authors project, where coauthor responses attribute none of its studies to Gino as data handler.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and the workbook. The experimental effects are real but modest (d about 0.3), and Kluger and Malloy's reanalysis argues the speed-dating link to second dates does not survive proper controls and that follow-up and switch questions were hard to separate. Gino coauthorship noted per user decision; the audit project shows no Gino-handled studies. Medium and 'contested' retained.

supporting_evidence.note: Asking engaged follow-up questions about someone's good news is the core of the active-constructive response, which Gable et al. linked to greater intimacy and satisfaction.
In negotiation research, asking diagnostic questions about priorities is a main route to joint gains, extending the value of question asking from liking to economic outcomes.

Independent, non-Gino evidence: in deep-talk conversations between strangers, observer-coded follow-up questions and verbal validation predicted connection rated by observers and partners, and a brief connection prompt increased follow-up questions, which in turn predicted connection.

insights.name: Four kinds of questions
insights.takeaway: Use introductory, mirror, and switch questions in moderation, and lean on follow-up questions to build connection.
insights.explanation: Brooks and John sort conversational questions into four types: introductory (opening, such as 'How are you?'), mirror (returning the same question, such as 'Good, and you?'), full-switch (changing the subject entirely), and follow-up (asking more about what was just said). Each has a use, but follow-ups are the most underused and the most valuable for connection. Mirror and switch questions are fine in moderation; too many switches can feel like a checklist. Open-ended phrasing and attention to sequence and tone also matter.
insights.when_to_use: When you want to audit your own question habits, or plan questions for an interview, discovery call, or check-in.
insights.worked_example: Reviewing notes from a sales discovery call, a rep notices most of his questions were full-switch ('Next, what is your budget? And your timeline?'). On the next call he deliberately asks a follow-up after each answer ('You said the last vendor was slow to respond; what did that cost you?') and learns the real buying criterion.
common_mistakes: Using only introductory and mirror questions and never getting past pleasantries
Treating a question list as a sequence to march through
Asking closed yes or no questions when you want depth
steps: Open with an introductory question
After each answer, default to one follow-up before switching
Use full-switch questions deliberately when a topic is exhausted
Prefer open phrasing (what, how, tell me about) for depth
situations: Sales discovery call
Interviewing a job candidate
Stakeholder interview for a project
Check-in with a struggling teammate

source.citation: Brooks and John, 'The Surprising Power of Questions,' Harvard Business Review, May-June 2018 (taxonomy read on hbr.org); related material in Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim
source.underlying_research: Huang et al. (2017) JPSP 113(3), 430-452; taxonomy developed from human coding and machine learning of conversation transcripts

insights.confidence_rationale: Taxonomy confirmed in the author's HBR article; the workbook confirms the book's emphasis on balancing follow-up and topic-switching questions, though I could not see the full four-type list in the book itself. It is a descriptive tool rather than a tested intervention, and the claim that follow-ups matter most rests on the evidence (and critique) noted for insight 04.

insights.name: Do not boomerask
insights.takeaway: If you ask someone a question, follow up on their answer; if you want to share your own story, just share it.
insights.explanation: Boomerasking is asking someone a question, letting them answer, and then answering it yourself instead of following up on what they said: 'How was your weekend?' followed by a long account of yours. Brooks and Yeomans identify three variants: ask-bragging, ask-complaining, and ask-sharing. Boomeraskers believe they come across well, but partners see them as insincere, self-focused, and uninterested, and prefer people who simply disclose directly. If you want to share, share; if you ask, stay with their answer.
insights.when_to_use: Anytime you notice yourself asking a question you are itching to answer, especially at social events and in team check-ins.
insights.worked_example: On Monday standup a teammate asks, 'Did anyone catch the game?' and then talks for three minutes about his own reaction. A better version: he says, 'I watched the game last night and loved the finish. Did you see it?' and then listens to what others thought. Personally, the same applies when asking a partner about their day only to pivot to your own frustrations.
common_mistakes: Using a question as a launch pad for your own story
Asking and then half-listening while you wait to speak
Thinking that announcing your news via a question is more modest or polite
Ask-complaining: asking about their week so you can vent about yours
steps: Before asking, check: do I want their answer, or a cue to talk?
If you want to share, just share, then invite their view
If you asked, follow up on their answer at least once before bringing in your own
situations: Monday check-in with the team
Dinner party conversation
Asking a partner about their day
Reconnecting at a reunion

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim (reported in the Greater Good summary of the book)
source.underlying_research: Brooks and Yeomans (2025), 'Boomerasking: Answering Your Own Questions,' Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 154(3), 864-893 (eight studies)

insights.confidence_rationale: Abstract read: multi-study paper in a top journal, but from the author's own team and recent, so not yet independently replicated. The first-pass claim that boomerasking makes partners like the topic less was not found in the abstract and was removed.

insights.name: Sensitive questions cost less than you fear
insights.takeaway: Ask the sensitive question you are avoiding; it costs less than you fear, especially when asked privately with an easy out.
insights.explanation: People avoid personal or sensitive questions (about money, health, relationships, setbacks) because they expect the other person to feel uncomfortable and think less of them. Research Brooks cites finds askers overestimate these costs: being asked sensitive questions did not make conversations less enjoyable or create worse impressions of the asker than mundane questions did. How you ask still matters, so phrasing with care, giving an easy out, and asking in private help. Her workbook suggests rehearsing hard questions with a trusted partner.
insights.when_to_use: When you need information that feels awkward to request, or when a relationship would benefit from going past surface topics.
insights.worked_example: A team lead suspects a strong performer is quietly job hunting. Rather than guessing, she asks privately, 'I want to make sure you are getting what you need here. Are you thinking about other opportunities?' He is relieved to talk, and they agree on a stretch project. At home, the same principle helps a sibling finally ask a parent how their finances are holding up.
common_mistakes: Asking a sensitive question in front of others
Leading with judgment or assumptions inside the question
Never asking because the fear feels convincing
Pressing after the person signals they do not want to answer
steps: Notice when you are avoiding a question purely from fear of awkwardness
Choose a private moment
Frame the purpose (why you are asking) and keep wording neutral
Make it easy to decline, then listen without judgment
situations: Asking a report whether they are thinking of leaving
Discussing salary with a peer
Asking an aging parent about finances or health
Asking a friend how they are really coping after a loss

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim (reported in the Greater Good summary of the book); workbook exercise 'Asking and answering hard questions'
source.underlying_research: Hart, VanEpps and Schweitzer (2021), 'The (better than expected) consequences of asking sensitive questions,' Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 162, 136-154 (corrigendum in OBHDP 165, 250); five experiments

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed as cited in the book via the Greater Good summary (which links this paper). Five experiments in one paper, consistent with broader findings that people overestimate social awkwardness. Still one paper, mostly with strangers; workplace power differences may change the calculus. Removed the unverified 'preregistered' and sample-size details.

insights.name: Levity: lightness over jokes
insights.takeaway: Keep conversations lively with low-risk levity like warmth, laughing at others' humor, and callbacks rather than ambitious jokes.
insights.explanation: Brooks treats boredom as a quiet killer of conversation and levity as the fix. Levity is broader than telling jokes: humor, warmth, laughing at others' humor, playful asides, and callbacks (references to something said earlier in the conversation or the relationship) all keep a conversation lively. When her students recorded talks with their favorite conversation partner, nearly all of those partners used callbacks. People underestimate how often humor attempts go well; successful humor can raise perceived competence and status, while failed or inappropriate humor lowers it, so low-risk levity is usually the better bet than ambitious jokes.
insights.when_to_use: Long meetings, tense negotiations at a safe moment, first meetings, family gatherings that are dragging.
insights.worked_example: Forty minutes into a budget review, a director refers back to a colleague's earlier quip about the 'haunted spreadsheet' when the same file errors again. The room laughs, energy lifts, and the group finishes the remaining items faster. She avoids jokes at anyone's expense and lets others' humor take center stage.
common_mistakes: Believing you must be naturally funny to bring levity
Telling edgy or inappropriate jokes, which can lower status
Using humor to dodge a serious concern the other person raised
Joking at someone else's expense
steps: Notice when energy is dropping
Reach for low-risk levity: laugh at others' humor, a light callback, a playful aside, or thanks
Keep humor inclusive and on-topic
Read the room and drop it quickly if it does not land
situations: Long or tense team meeting
Opening a negotiation
Family dinner that has gone quiet
Onboarding a new hire

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), L (Levity) maxim; workbook exercises 'Escalate' and 'Levity reframe'; author interviews (Think Fast Talk Smart episode 223 with Naomi Bagdonas)
source.underlying_research: Bitterly, Brooks and Schweitzer (2017), 'Risky Business: When Humor Increases and Decreases Status,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 112(3), 431-455; Brooks's classroom recordings of students' favorite conversation partners (callbacks)

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and workbook. The humor and status finding comes from a multi-experiment JPSP paper by the author's team; the callback observation is classroom evidence, and the broader claim that levity combats boredom is credible expert synthesis.

insights.name: Kindness as receptiveness in disagreement
insights.takeaway: In disagreements, acknowledge their view, validate feelings, hedge claims, frame positively, and aim to learn rather than win.
insights.explanation: For Brooks, kindness in conversation means trying to prioritize your partner's conversational needs, which includes being visibly open to views you disagree with. Her receptiveness recipe: acknowledge the other view, affirm and validate their feelings, hedge your claims, avoid argumentative explanation words such as 'because' and 'therefore', frame things positively, and even voice your own internal disagreement. Two misperceptions make conflict worse: we tend to judge people who disagree with us as poor listeners even when they listened well, and if you assume the other person is out to persuade you rather than learn from you, you behave in ways that escalate. Shifting your aim from winning to learning tends, ironically, to make you more persuasive.
insights.when_to_use: Disagreements at work, political or values conversations with family, feedback discussions, contentious online threads.
insights.worked_example: In a design review, an engineer disagrees with a product manager's launch date. Instead of 'That date is impossible,' she says, 'I understand the market window matters, and I agree we need to ship this quarter. My worry is the testing time; it might be that a two-week slip saves us a rollback.' The PM engages with the risk rather than defending the date.
common_mistakes: Faking agreement or hedging so much the point disappears
Acknowledging the other view in a sarcastic tone
Assuming the other person is purely trying to persuade or win
Treating kindness as niceness rather than responsiveness
steps: Acknowledge: restate the other person's view in a sentence
Affirm and validate: name a point of agreement or the sense in how they feel
Hedge: soften absolutes (might, in my experience) and skip 'because' and 'therefore' lecturing
Reframe to the positive: state what you want, not only what you oppose
Assume they are trying to learn too, and aim to learn rather than win
situations: Pushing back on a deadline in a meeting
Talking politics with a relative
Replying to a heated email or Slack thread
Disagreeing with a partner about money

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), K (Kindness) maxim and material on difficult moments; workbook exercise 'De-escalate' (receptiveness recipe); Greater Good summary of the book
source.underlying_research: Yeomans, Minson, Collins, Chen and Gino (2020), 'Conversational receptiveness: Improving engagement with opposing views,' OBHDP 160, 131-148; Collins, Dorison, Gino and Minson (2022), 'Underestimating Counterparts' Learning Goals Impairs Conflictual Conversations,' Psychological Science 33(10), 1732-1752; Ren and Schaumberg (2024), 'Disagreement Gets Mistaken for Bad Listening,' Psychological Science 35(5), 455-470. The related HEAR acronym (Hedge, Emphasize agreement, Acknowledge, Reframe) comes from Minson and Yeomans's teaching and was not found in Brooks's materials. Integrity note: the 2020 and 2022 papers are Gino-coauthored; the Many Co-Authors project lists both, with coauthor responses attributing none of their studies to Gino as data handler.

insights.confidence_rationale: Book's version (receptiveness recipe) confirmed in the author's workbook; the disagreement-listening and learning-goals findings confirmed via the Greater Good summary. Multi-study peer-reviewed work including field data, consistent with negotiation research. Gino coauthorship noted per user decision. Medium retained.

supporting_evidence.note: Receptive, non-judgmental engagement in disagreement produced durable attitude change in the field, whereas argument-only versions of the same conversation did not.
Experiments summarized in the companion review show that being listened to makes speakers' attitudes less extreme and more complex, one route by which receptiveness eases disagreement.

Receptive, validating communication is most useful for minor or unchangeable issues and with defensive partners; for serious changeable problems in close relationships, too much softening can reduce change.

insights.name: Give the compliment and the thanks you are holding back
insights.takeaway: Give the sincere compliment or thanks you are holding back, praising choices and efforts rather than appearance.
insights.explanation: People underestimate how good a sincere compliment or expression of thanks will make the other person feel, and overestimate how awkward it will be, so they give fewer than they should. Brooks recommends complimenting things you genuinely admire, especially choices and efforts, and steering clear of remarks about physical appearance unless you know they are welcome. Do not worry about perfect wording; the warmth is what lands.
insights.when_to_use: After a colleague does good work, when a friend helps you, when a family member's effort goes unnoticed, in written notes or messages.
insights.worked_example: A project manager notices a junior analyst rebuilt a messy dashboard overnight. She sends a two-line message: 'The way you restructured the filters made the exec review so much smoother. Thank you for taking that on.' The analyst later says it was the most motivating note she had received that year. At home, the same manager thanks her partner specifically for handling the school forms she had been dreading.
common_mistakes: Waiting for the perfect phrasing and never sending it
Giving vague praise ('great job') instead of naming what was good
Complimenting appearance in professional or uncertain settings
Using compliments as a set-up for a request
steps: Notice a specific action, choice, or quality you admire
Say or write it plainly, naming the effect it had
Skip the over-explanation and accept that it may feel awkward to you, not them
situations: Recognizing a teammate's extra effort
Thank-you note to a mentor
Appreciating a partner's invisible work
Congratulating a friend on a milestone

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), K (Kindness) maxim (compliment guidance reported in the Greater Good summary); workbook exercises 'Give a compliment' and 'Battle of the nice guys'
source.underlying_research: Zhao and Epley (2021), 'Insufficiently complimentary?: Underestimating the positive impact of compliments creates a barrier to expressing them,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(2), 239-256 (confirmed as cited via Greater Good). Kumar and Epley (2018), 'Undervaluing Gratitude: Expressers Misunderstand the Consequences of Showing Appreciation,' Psychological Science 29(9), 1423-1435 (supports the thanks part; not confirmed as cited in the book).

insights.confidence_rationale: Compliment advice confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and workbook. The miscalibration appears across multiple experiments in two separate papers and fits a broader set of social-underestimation findings, so High retained; the gratitude paper is not confirmed as cited, and the advice about avoiding appearance comments is the author's guidance rather than a tested result.

supporting_evidence.note: Cialdini lists sincere compliments as one of three drivers of liking, consistent with the advice to give the compliments people hold back.

Franco's first friendship tip is explicit platonic affection (telling friends what they mean to you, saying you are glad to hear from them), the friendship form of giving the compliments people hold back.
Both point to underused positive expressions: just as people hold back compliments, they often under-respond to good news, and enthusiastic responses predict closer relationships.
Extends the miscalibration pattern behind holding back compliments to refusals: here people overestimate the social cost of saying no, as they overestimate the awkwardness of saying something kind.

Same pattern from an independent team: people underestimate how much a small, warm gesture (here a check-in note or small gift to someone they had lost touch with) is appreciated, which keeps them from doing it.

insights.name: End before the well runs dry
insights.takeaway: Watch for fading energy and close a conversation warmly rather than staying too long.
insights.explanation: Conversations rarely end when both people want them to: in a study of 932 conversations, very few ended when both wanted, or even when one wanted, and people were poor at guessing when their partner wanted to stop. Brooks treats the ending as the final coordination problem of a conversation and, in interviews, says most of us stay too long, just as we do on topics. She finds this freeing: getting the end exactly right is hard for everyone, and a good conversation ending is not the end of the relationship but one in a sequence of conversations. Practical implication: watch for fading energy and close warmly rather than dragging on.
insights.when_to_use: Networking chats, phone calls with relatives, meetings that have covered the agenda, dates.
insights.worked_example: At a conference reception, a consultant senses a conversation with a prospective client winding down after a good exchange about supply chains. She says, 'This has been the best conversation of my night. I will send you that article on nearshoring tomorrow,' and moves on. The prospect replies to the follow-up email the next morning.
common_mistakes: Staying because you assume the other person wants to continue
Leaving abruptly without a warm close
Over-apologizing for ending
Letting meetings run to the full slot when the work is done
steps: Notice fading energy: repetition, shorter turns, glances away
Signal the close with appreciation or a callback
Name a next step if there is one
Exit cleanly
situations: Leaving a conversation at a networking event
Ending a long call with a parent
Wrapping a meeting early
Ending a first date on a good note

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025) (discusses the Mastroianni et al. study, per the Greater Good summary); Brooks interview on LIFTOFF podcast episode 9 'When it's time to end'
source.underlying_research: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney and Wilson (2021), 'Do conversations end when people want them to?' PNAS 118(10), e2011809118 (932 conversations, intimate partners and strangers)

insights.confidence_rationale: The book cites the Mastroianni study, and Brooks's view that we tend to stay too long is confirmed in her own interview; specific closing tactics (callback, next step) are general guidance not confirmed in the book. The mismatch finding is one well-powered PNAS paper by another lab; the advice is a reasonable inference, not directly tested.

insights.name: The conversational compass: plot your goals and your partner's
insights.takeaway: Before a conversation, map your goals and your best guess at your partner's, so you choose more intentionally.
insights.explanation: Brooks maps what people want from a conversation on two axes: informational (is the goal about accurate information exchange or not) and relational (is it in service of the partner and relationship, or of yourself). The four quadrants are labeled Advance (high informational, low relational, such as persuading or deciding), Connect (high on both, such as brainstorming or being honest), Protect (low on both, such as concealing or assigning blame), and Savor (high relational, low informational, such as reminiscing or having fun). Unlike many two-by-two models, the aim is not to live in one quadrant; everyone always has at least one goal and usually several, often in different quadrants, and they can conflict. Plotting your goals and your best guess at your partner's makes your choices more intentional.
insights.when_to_use: Before negotiations, feedback conversations, and any talk where you feel torn between getting answers and keeping things pleasant.
insights.worked_example: Before a salary conversation, an employee writes: my information goal is to learn the band and what would justify the top; my relationship goal is to keep my manager as an ally. That leads her to ask open questions about criteria first, rather than opening with a demand that could make the manager defensive.
common_mistakes: Assuming your partner shares your main goal
Sacrificing the relationship for a single piece of information
Being so pleasant that the needed information never surfaces
steps: Before the conversation, list your goals and place each on the compass
Do the same for your best guess of your partner's goals
Note shared and conflicting goals and decide which matter most
Afterward, check which goals were met and whether they shifted
situations: Asking for a raise
Giving critical feedback to a friend who is also a colleague
Vendor negotiation
Hard conversation with a teenager

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025) (conversational compass); workbook exercises 'Plot your goals ahead of time' and 'Plot your goals after'
source.underlying_research: Yeomans, Schweitzer and Brooks (2022), 'The Conversational Circumplex: Identifying, prioritizing, and pursuing informational and relational motives in conversation,' Current Opinion in Psychology 44, 293-302

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the author's workbook, which presents the compass and quadrants from the book. It is a theoretical review framework from credible researchers, not a tested intervention.

insights.name: Apologize, even for what is not your fault
insights.takeaway: Apologize sincerely for mistakes, commit to change and follow through; even small apologies for things beyond your control build trust.
insights.explanation: Brooks treats apologies as a core conversational skill. A sincere apology for a real mistake means saying you are sorry, committing to change, and then following through; she notes that taking responsibility tends to help rather than hurt (for example, physicians who apologize to patients are reported to be sued less). A smaller, surprising finding from her own research: superfluous apologies, expressions of regret for something you clearly did not cause (the rain, the traffic), signal empathic concern and increase trust. In a field study, a stranger who opened with an apology for the rain before asking to borrow a phone got far more yeses than one who simply asked.
insights.when_to_use: After you have let someone down, before asking a stranger or busy colleague for a favor, when someone is dealing with bad luck or a frustrating circumstance.
insights.worked_example: A project lead missed a client deadline because she underestimated testing time. On the call she says, 'I am sorry we missed Friday. I underestimated testing, and that is on me. From now on I will add a buffer and flag risk a week out,' then does so on the next milestone. Separately, when a visiting client arrives soaked, she opens with 'I am so sorry about this weather' before getting started, a small signal that she cares about their experience.
common_mistakes: Apologizing without any commitment to change, or not following through
Hedged non-apologies ('sorry if you were offended')
Over-apologizing until it sounds like low confidence
Avoiding an apology out of fear it admits weakness
steps: Say clearly that you are sorry and name what happened
Take responsibility for your part without excuses
Commit to a specific change
Follow through, and later show that you did
For bad circumstances you did not cause, a brief expression of regret can still signal care
situations: Apologizing to a client for a missed deadline
Making amends with a friend you hurt
Asking a stranger for a favor
Greeting a visitor who had a rough trip

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), material on apologies (a section named in the author's workbook); workbook exercise 'Apologize'; Greater Good summary of the book
source.underlying_research: Brooks, Dai and Schweitzer (2014), 'I'm Sorry About the Rain! Superfluous Apologies Demonstrate Empathic Concern and Increase Trust,' Social Psychological and Personality Science 5(4), 467-474 (four studies, including a field study at a train station). The physician-apology claim is reported from the book without a verified source.

insights.confidence_rationale: Apology advice confirmed in the workbook and the superfluous apology study confirmed as cited via Greater Good (abstract read: four studies, trust mediated by empathic concern). One paper from the author's team with no independent replication located; the sincere-apology steps are expert guidance.

supporting_evidence.note: Supports taking responsibility as the core of a sincere apology. Qualifies the emphasis on committing to change: a declaration of repentance ranked in the middle tier, below an offer to repair the harm, so a concrete fix should come before or alongside the promise.

insights.name: Find the layer where you differ
insights.takeaway: When a conversation turns hard, ask whether you differ on content, emotions, beliefs, motives, or identity, and address that layer.
insights.explanation: Brooks describes conversation as a coordination game in which partners try to build shared understanding across several layers: content (what is said and how it sounds), emotions (how each person feels), beliefs (what each knows), motives (what each wants), and identity (who each person is). Difficult conversations usually involve a difference at one or more of these layers, and misunderstandings are more common than we think. When an exchange turns hard, asking which layer the gap is on helps you respond to the real issue instead of only the surface words.
insights.when_to_use: When a conversation suddenly turns tense or confusing, and when debriefing a difficult exchange afterward.
insights.worked_example: Two cofounders argue about whether to hire a salesperson. The surface is content (budget numbers), but one realizes the gap is at the motives layer (she wants growth, he wants runway) and partly identity (he sees himself as the careful one). Naming that shifts the talk from line items to how much risk each can accept.
common_mistakes: Arguing over content when the real difference is emotion, motive, or identity
Assuming shared understanding because no one objected
Treating an identity-level difference as a simple factual disagreement
steps: Notice the moment the conversation becomes hard
Ask which layer differs: content, emotions, beliefs, motives, or identity
Name or ask about that layer directly
Re-check shared understanding before moving on
situations: Debriefing an argument with a cofounder
Family disagreement that keeps recurring
A meeting where people seem to talk past each other

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), opening framing of conversation as a coordination game and material on difficult moments; workbook exercises 'Coordination problems' and 'Sources of difficulty'
source.underlying_research: Author's synthesis; no single study. Related coordination findings the book cites include Mastroianni et al. (2021) on endings.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the author's workbook as a framework from the book. It is a credible expert's diagnostic model rather than a tested intervention.

insights.name: The Six-Step Spontaneous Speaking Method (Calm, Unlock, Redefine, Listen, Structure, Focus)
insights.takeaway: When put on the spot, calm your nerves, drop perfectionism, see opportunity, listen, give a simple structure, and trim.
insights.explanation: Abrahams treats being put on the spot as a trainable skill rather than a talent. His method moves through six stages that build on each other: settle your nerves (Calm), loosen the grip of perfectionism (Unlock), treat the moment as a chance rather than a danger (Redefine), take in what is actually being asked (Listen), give your answer a simple shape (Structure), and trim it so it is relevant and easy to absorb (Focus). The first four steps clear the mental and emotional clutter; the last two shape the words themselves. The book's first part teaches the six steps and the second part applies them to common situations such as small talk, toasts, pitches, Q&A, feedback and apologies.
insights.when_to_use: As a mental checklist for any unplanned speaking moment, and as a practice roadmap when diagnosing why you freeze or ramble (is it nerves, perfectionism, poor listening, or lack of structure?).
insights.worked_example: A project manager gets asked by a director in a hallway, 'Where are we on the vendor switch?' She takes one slow breath (Calm), accepts that a good-enough answer beats a perfect one (Unlock), treats it as a chance to show command of the project (Redefine), notices the director sounds worried about cost rather than timing (Listen), answers in three parts: status, why it matters, next step (Structure), and keeps it to three sentences focused on cost (Focus).
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to structure while still flooded with anxiety, so the structure falls apart mid-sentence.
Treating the six steps as a rigid ritual instead of a quick, mostly internal sequence that takes seconds.
Skipping Listen and answering the question you expected rather than the one asked.
steps: Calm: take one slow breath with a longer exhale and ground yourself in the present.
Unlock: drop the goal of a perfect answer; aim for a clear, connected one.
Redefine: tell yourself this is an opportunity to help or connect, not a test.
Listen: identify what the person actually needs, including tone and emotion.
Structure: pick a simple shape such as What, So What, Now What.
Focus: cut to what is relevant, precise, accessible and concise for this listener.
situations: Being called on unexpectedly in a meeting
Hallway question from a senior leader
Asked to say a few words at a family event
Answering a surprise question in a job interview

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Part I: Introduction (p. 1), then six chapters beginning at pp. 15, 34, 56, 75, 93 and 113 per the Google Books contents listing (Calm: Tame the Anxiety Beast; Unlock: Maximize Mediocrity; Redefine: Mind Your Mindset; Listen: Don't Just Do Something, Stand There; Structure: Structure Your Spontaneity; Focus: The F-Word of Spontaneous Speaking). Part II applications begin around p. 149.
source.underlying_research: Synthesis of the research and practitioner sources used in individual chapters; the six-step sequence itself is the author's own framework and has not been tested as a whole.

insights.confidence_rationale: Credible expert framework from an experienced Stanford communication teacher, and individual components draw on research, but the six-step sequence as a package is untested. Chapter order and page starts confirmed from the Google Books contents listing; the author reads Chapter 1 as 'Chapter One. Calm' in a podcast excerpt.

insights.name: Calm the Body First: Breath, Present Focus, and the ABCs of Anxiety
insights.takeaway: Manage speaking anxiety with long exhales, slower gestures, a confidence mantra, and repeating your last point when you blank.
insights.explanation: Abrahams breaks speaking anxiety into ABCs: Affective symptoms (feeling stressed, vulnerable, overwhelmed), Behavioral or physiological ones (sweating, trembling, racing heart, fast speech, dry mouth, blushing) and Cognitive ones (blanking out, negative self-talk, fixating on being watched). The aim is to manage anxiety rather than eliminate it, since a moderate amount helps. For feelings, he recommends mindfulness: notice the nerves, accept them as normal, and hold them at a little psychological distance, then reframe them (see the excitement insight). For the body, his main tool is slow belly breathing with the exhale about twice as long as the inhale (he credits Andrew Huberman), plus slowing your gestures to slow your speech, holding something cold to counter flushing and sweating, and reactivating saliva beforehand with warm water, a lozenge or gum. For the mind, he suggests a confidence mantra (for example, that you have value to add), going back to go forward when you blank (repeat what you just said), keeping a generic question ready to buy time, and rationalizing the realistic odds and consequences, helped by knowing that people overestimate how much others notice their stumbles (the spotlight effect).
insights.when_to_use: In the minutes or seconds before you speak, and in the moment when you feel your voice speed up or your mind go blank.
insights.worked_example: Before a tense call with his landlord about a deposit dispute, a renter notices his heart pounding and his thoughts racing ahead to worst cases. He tells himself the nerves are normal, breathes in for three counts and out for six, three times, and repeats 'I have a fair case to make'. He jots one fallback question ('Can you walk me through how the deduction was calculated?') in case he loses his thread. He starts the call speaking noticeably slower, and when he does blank once, he asks the question and regroups.
common_mistakes: Trying to eliminate anxiety entirely rather than managing it to a workable level.
Using only one remedy (for example breathing) when the main problem is catastrophic thinking.
Rushing the breath so the exhale is short, which does little to slow the body down.
Pre-apologizing or relying on alcohol or distracting visualizations, which Abrahams says tend to do more harm than good.
steps: Notice which symptoms dominate: feelings, body, or thoughts.
Feelings: name the nerves as normal and observe them from a little distance rather than fighting them.
Body: breathe in for about three counts and out for about six, two or three times; slow your gestures; hold something cold if you flush or sweat.
Before likely speaking moments: sip warm water or use a lozenge to counter dry mouth.
Thoughts: repeat a short mantra; if you blank, restate your last point or ask the audience a generic question to regain your footing.
Beforehand, rationalize: estimate the real odds and real consequences of a stumble, remembering others notice far less than you think.
situations: Waiting to present to senior leadership
Before a difficult conversation with a partner or family member
Job interview nerves
Speaking up for the first time in a large meeting

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Chapter 1, Calm: Tame the Anxiety Beast (begins p. 15; portions read by the author in a Think Fast Talk Smart bonus episode, 2024)
source.underlying_research: Confirmed in the chapter text (via the author's audio excerpt): Andrew Huberman's guidance that the extended exhale drives the calming effect; an unnamed statement that studies show slow breathing calms the nervous system within seconds; rat research suggesting acute stress can promote new nerve cell growth (study not named in the excerpt, plausibly Kirby et al. 2013, eLife); Stanford professor S. Christian Wheeler on psychological distance from emotions; and the spotlight effect (the phenomenon described by Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky 2000, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology; the excerpt names the phenomenon, not the paper). Related but not confirmed as cited: mindful breathing reduced test anxiety in a randomized study of students (Cho, Ryu, Noh, Lee 2016, Iranian Journal of Public Health). The ABC split mirrors the standard affective, behavioral, cognitive model in psychology.

insights.confidence_rationale: Slow breathing, mindful acceptance and the spotlight effect have reasonable research support; specific tips such as the cold bottle, lozenges and generic questions rest on practitioner experience. Content now checked against the author's own reading of Chapter 1. The earlier tongue-twister and counting-backward tips were not in the excerpt and were removed. Rated Medium because the bundle mixes well-supported and anecdotal elements.

supporting_evidence.note: The research literature organizes speaking anxiety in the same three systems (feelings and thoughts, body, behavior) that Abrahams's ABCs use, and pairs each with a treatment family; Bodie adds skills training as an anxiety treatment in its own right.

The in-the-moment calming tools are useful, but the strongest evidence for lasting change comes from structured, repeated cognitive and behavioral programs over weeks, with gains that continue after the program ends.

Slow breathing and grounding remain useful, but this review argues the goal should be an energized challenge state rather than calm; trying to eliminate arousal is often less effective than reinterpreting it.
Gives experimental backing to holding nerves at a psychological distance: non-first-person self-talk before a speech improved rater-judged performance and reduced distress and post-speech rumination.

Abrahams mentions that people overestimate how much others notice their stumbles; this paper adds that explaining the illusion to speakers, rather than merely reassuring them, lowered their nervousness and improved observer-rated speech quality.

insights.name: Relabel Nerves as Excitement
insights.takeaway: Before speaking, tell yourself 'I am excited' instead of trying to calm down, keeping the energy but aiming it at opportunity.
insights.explanation: Anxiety and excitement produce similar body sensations: a fast heartbeat, alertness, energy. Abrahams draws on research showing it is easier to relabel that arousal as excitement than to force yourself to calm down. Telling yourself 'I am excited' rather than 'I am calm' keeps the energy but points it toward opportunity, which can make you speak with more confidence and persistence.
insights.when_to_use: When calming techniques are not working fast enough, or just before a high-stakes moment where some energy is useful (a pitch, a toast, a first date, an interview).
insights.worked_example: A nurse who has to give a short update at a hospital-wide town hall feels her hands shaking backstage. Instead of telling herself to relax, she says quietly, 'I am excited to share this', reminding herself the energy means she cares about the work. She walks on still energized but framing it as eagerness.
common_mistakes: Using the phrase while still privately believing the situation is a threat, so the reframe feels hollow.
Expecting relabeling to fix lack of preparation.
Applying it to severe or clinical anxiety, where it is not a substitute for professional help.
steps: Notice the physical arousal (racing heart, adrenaline).
Say, out loud or silently, 'I am excited' rather than 'I am calm' or 'Do not panic'.
Connect the excitement to something specific you want from the moment.
Channel the energy into voice and gesture rather than trying to suppress it.
situations: Right before a pitch or presentation
Giving a wedding or birthday toast
Before a job interview
Before a first date or meeting a partner's parents

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Chapter 1, Calm: Tame the Anxiety Beast (author's audio excerpt), where he credits his friend Alison Wood Brooks; also Chapter 3 (Redefine)
source.underlying_research: Alison Wood Brooks, Get Excited: Reappraising Pre-Performance Anxiety as Excitement, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(3), 2014. Participants who said 'I am excited' before singing, public speaking or math tasks felt more excited and performed better than those who said 'I am calm'; in the speech study they reported more excitement but not less anxiety, and judges rated their speeches more favorably. Confirmed as cited: the author's reading of Chapter 1 describes Brooks's experiments by name. A later replication reproduced the self-reported excitement effect but not observable public speaking improvements.

insights.confidence_rationale: Rests on a well-known peer-reviewed paper with multiple experiments, and reappraisal broadly has strong support. However, at least one later replication reproduced the subjective feeling effect more clearly than the performance effect, so the performance benefit should be treated as promising rather than settled. Popular write-ups sometimes overstate the effect size.

supporting_evidence.note: Gives the mechanism and stronger physiological evidence behind relabeling nerves: reinterpreting arousal as a functional resource shifts the body toward a challenge pattern. The active ingredient is the meaning given to bodily signals, not only the word excited.

insights.name: Maximize Mediocrity: Connection Over Perfection
insights.takeaway: Aim for connection, not perfection: quiet your inner critic, dare to be obvious, and treat errors as just another take.
insights.explanation: Perfectionism is one of the biggest blocks to spontaneous speaking. Abrahams tells his MBA students to strive for mediocrity so they can achieve greatness: constantly judging every word eats cognitive bandwidth, like a computer slowed by too many open apps, so turning down the inner critic frees capacity to connect and respond. He borrows the improv maxims 'dare to be dull' and 'be obvious' (from Patricia Ryan Madson and Keith Johnstone's tradition), and the image of being a useful brick rather than trying to build the whole cathedral in one moment. A phrase journalist Joan Lunden coined after reading the book sums it up: connection, not perfection. He pairs this with reframing errors as missed takes, as in film, where another take is just another try rather than proof you got it wrong.
insights.when_to_use: When you notice yourself stalling because you are searching for the perfect phrasing, or when a past stumble makes you reluctant to speak up again.
insights.worked_example: In a team brainstorm, a junior analyst has a half-formed idea but keeps waiting to refine it. Remembering 'good enough to connect', she says, 'This is rough, but what if we bundled the two offers?' The group builds on it. Later, when she mixes up two figures, she says 'let me redo that take' and corrects herself without apologizing at length.
common_mistakes: Hearing 'mediocrity' as permission not to prepare for planned communication; the idea applies to in-the-moment delivery.
Over-apologizing for small errors, which draws more attention to them than the error itself.
Rehearsing exact wording for unplanned moments, which makes you brittle when the moment goes differently.
steps: Notice the internal demand to be perfect or impressive.
Replace it with the goal of being clear and connected.
Say your first reasonable idea and build from there.
If you stumble, treat it as a missed take: correct briefly and keep going.
situations: Contributing in a brainstorm
Recovering after a stumble in a presentation
Joining a conversation with new acquaintances
Responding quickly in a work chat thread

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Chapter 2, Unlock: Maximize Mediocrity (begins p. 34); Grit and Growth interview (Stanford GSB, 2023); Think Fast Talk Smart episodes 116 and 229
source.underlying_research: Mainly improv practice (Patricia Ryan Madson, Improv Wisdom, 2005; Keith Johnstone's 'be obvious') and Abrahams's Stanford teaching. The cognitive-bandwidth rationale is offered as an analogy, not a cited study. Related research links perfectionism with higher performance anxiety, but no controlled test of the 'maximize mediocrity' instruction was found.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the author's own interviews about the book (mediocrity, dare to be dull, connection not perfection, missed takes). Credible expert and improv-practice evidence, consistent with research linking perfectionism to anxiety, but the specific claim that lowering standards improves spontaneous speaking has not been directly tested.

supporting_evidence.note: The liking gap was driven by harsh judgment of one's own conversational performance against an ideal the listener cannot see, which supports the advice to aim for connection rather than a perfect performance.

insights.name: Redefine the Moment: Opportunity, Not Threat
insights.takeaway: Treat being put on the spot as a chance to connect rather than a threat, and see tough questions as gifts.
insights.explanation: Many people experience being put on the spot as an adversarial test. In the chapter he calls Mind Your Mindset, Abrahams argues that this threat framing makes us defensive: tight posture, curt tone, clipped answers. Reframing the moment as an opportunity to connect, learn where the other person is coming from, and collaborate opens up posture and tone. He reminds speakers that audiences rarely want them to fail (citing a Google executive's observation that questioners mostly want a good moment of connection with the speaker), and calls challenging questions gifts. From improv he borrows the idea of treating whatever others say or do as an offer to build on ('yes, and') rather than resist.
insights.when_to_use: Before tough Q&A, interviews, challenging questions from a boss or client, and in personal conversations where you feel on trial.
insights.worked_example: A father is cornered by his teenager's pointed question at dinner about why he changed jobs. Instead of hearing it as criticism, he treats it as a chance to show how adults make hard choices: 'Good question, and here is what I was weighing.' The conversation becomes one of the more open ones they have had.
common_mistakes: Faking positivity while still bracing defensively; the listener notices.
Using 'yes, and' to agree with something you actually disagree with; it means building on the offer, not conceding the point.
Assuming a challenging question means hostility, when it often reflects curiosity or concern.
steps: Notice threat language in your head ('they are testing me', 'I will be exposed').
Ask: what can I share, learn or help with here?
Accept the question or comment as a starting point ('yes') and add something of value ('and').
After the moment, note what you learned rather than only what went wrong.
situations: Facing a tough question from a client
Defending a proposal in front of skeptics
Being challenged by a family member at dinner
Panel interview

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Chapter 3, Redefine: Mind Your Mindset (begins p. 56); Grit and Growth interview (Stanford GSB, 2023)
source.underlying_research: Improv principles (offers, yes and). No accessible source confirms the book cites Carol Dweck. Related but not confirmed as cited: challenge versus threat appraisal research (Blascovich; Jamieson) links seeing a stressor as a challenge with better physiological responses and performance.

insights.confidence_rationale: The opportunity-not-threat reframe is confirmed in Abrahams's own description of the chapter. Reframing stress as challenge has a solid general research base, but the book's own research citations for this chapter were not seen; rating relies on expert practice and the general literature. The earlier summary link to growth mindset is not confirmed.

supporting_evidence.note: Distanced self-talk led people to appraise upcoming stressors as challenges rather than threats, a concrete way to move from threat to opportunity framing.

insights.name: Listen Before You Leap: Pace, Space, Grace and the Bottom Line
insights.takeaway: Slow down, listen for the content, emotion, and core need beneath the words, and paraphrase it back before answering.
insights.explanation: Under pressure, people start composing their answer before the other person has finished. Abrahams's Listen step reverses this: slow down and take in both the content and the emotion before responding. He adapts a framework from Collins Dobbs, a Stanford GSB colleague and former basketball player: Pace (slow down enough to really focus), Space (find both physical and mental room to be present), and Grace (give yourself permission to listen beyond the literal words for what is really going on). He also advises listening for the bottom line, the core need beneath the words, and paraphrasing it back, which both confirms understanding and buys time to think.
insights.when_to_use: Any time you are asked a question you did not expect, when emotions are running high, or when a request seems ambiguous.
insights.worked_example: A friend calls and says, 'So I guess you were too busy for my birthday.' Instead of defending himself immediately, the listener pauses, notices the hurt underneath, and says, 'It sounds like you felt I did not show up for you, is that right?' The friend softens, and the conversation becomes about repair rather than excuses.
common_mistakes: Preparing your rebuttal while the other person is still talking.
Paraphrasing mechanically ('What I hear you saying is...') in a way that sounds scripted.
Answering the literal question while missing the emotional subtext or real concern.
steps: Pace: deliberately slow your own reaction; a pause of a second or two is fine.
Space: make physical and mental room to take in the full message, including tone and body language.
Grace: allow yourself to listen beyond the words for the underlying need or emotion.
Identify the bottom line: what does this person actually want from me?
Paraphrase it briefly to confirm, then respond to that need.
situations: Responding to an upset partner or friend
Handling an ambiguous request from a manager
Customer complaint call
Clarifying a vague question during Q&A

source.citation: Matt Abrahams, Think Faster, Talk Smarter (2023), Chapter 4, Listen: Don't Just Do Something, Stand There (begins p. 75); Think Fast Talk Smart episode 238
source.underlying_research: Pace, space, grace framework from Collins Dobbs (Stanford GSB), whom Abrahams says he interviewed for the book. In episode 238 Abrahams also credits Alison Wood Brooks's research for the claim that paraphrasing deepens connection (no paper named). Consistent with the active listening literature (Carl Rogers onward), though the chapter's own citations were not seen.

insights.confidence_rationale: Active listening and paraphrasing have broad expert consensus and some supportive research on feeling understood. The pace, space, grace framing is a practitioner heuristic adapted from Collins Dobbs; the description of grace was corrected to Abrahams's own wording (listening beyond the words), and one transcript orders the terms as space, pace, grace.

insights.name: What, So What, Now What
insights.takeaway: Answer on the spot by stating the fact, why it matters to this listener, and the next step.
insights.explanation: Abrahams calls this his all-purpose structure for spontaneous responses. Start with the What (the fact, idea or update), move to the So What (why it matters to this listener), and finish with the Now What (the next step, recommendation or question). Having a ready-made skeleton frees mental capacity during stressful moments and makes your answer easier for others to follow and remember, because they get the point, the relevance and the action in a predictable order. He applies it widely: to emails (the Now What can serve as the subject line), to in-the-moment feedback, and even to small talk. To build the habit, he suggests drilling it after any podcast, meeting or article: what was it about, why does it matter, how can I use it, and then trying to say it again in half the words.
insights.when_to_use: Status updates, answering 'how did it go?', impromptu remarks, quick emails and chat replies, giving context to a family member about a decision.
insights.worked_example: A team lead is asked in a weekly meeting about a delayed release. What: 'The release is slipping one week because a security test failed.' So What: 'That means the client demo on the 12th uses the current version.'
