insights.when_to_use: Any prepared talk, pitch, toast or meeting contribution where the wait before your turn is the worst part, and especially when you are scheduled late in an agenda.
insights.worked_example: A sales lead is fourth on the agenda at a client quarterly review. Instead of sitting through the first three items rehearsing worst cases, she reviews her one-page outline and silently runs her first three sentences, which she has practiced until they are automatic: a thank-you, the headline number, and the one question she wants answered today. When her turn comes, her heart is pounding, but she knows this is the peak, delivers the opening on autopilot, and by the second slide she is settling. At a family wedding, a best man memorizes only his first two lines and keeps the rest as bullet points, because that is where he expects the jitters to hit hardest.
common_mistakes: Spreading preparation evenly when the opening deserves the most rehearsal
Opening with something hard to say, such as a complex joke or dense statistic, at the moment of peak arousal
Spending the wait before your turn rehearsing disaster scenarios
Reading the spike at the start as proof the whole talk will go badly
steps: Write your first two or three sentences and rehearse them aloud until they are automatic
Make the opening easy to deliver: a greeting, a clear statement of purpose, or a simple question
Plan what you will do while you wait (review the outline, note one thing a previous speaker said that you can connect to)
When the spike comes at the start, remind yourself it is the expected peak and that it usually eases within the first minutes
After the talk, note one thing that went well before reviewing what to improve
situations: Waiting for your turn on a meeting agenda
Opening a client presentation
Giving a best man or maid of honor toast

source.citation: Graham D. Bodie (2010), Communication Education 59(1), review of the etiology of public speaking anxiety; Behnke's findings as reported in TCU Magazine (1999)
source.underlying_research: Behnke and Sawyer's milestone studies of public speaking anxiety (anticipation, confrontation, adaptation, release), reported in Communication Education and related journals in the late 1990s and 2000s.

insights.confidence_rationale: The milestone pattern comes from a program of physiological and self-report studies by Behnke and Sawyer, which is credible and consistent, but I accessed it only through a university magazine feature quoting Behnke and through search summaries, not the original articles or Bodie's full text. The specific advice to over-prepare the opening is an inference from the pattern rather than a tested intervention.

insights.name: You Cannot Spot a Liar by Watching
insights.takeaway: Do not trust fidgeting, gaze, or nervousness as signs of lying; acting on such hunches risks wrongly accusing honest people.
insights.explanation: Across more than two hundred studies, people sorting lies from truths in real time were right about 54 percent of the time, barely above a coin flip, and the figure barely moved from study to study. People also lean toward belief: they called about 61 percent of truths honest but caught only about 47 percent of lies. Professionals whose jobs involve judging credibility were not reliably better than laypeople; the authors conclude that experts are not good lie detectors. The companion meta-analysis of 158 possible tells found that many popular cues have no link or only a weak link to lying, and that liars mainly differ in telling less forthcoming, less compelling stories. Practically, a hunch that someone is lying based on fidgeting, gaze or nervousness is weak evidence, and acting on it risks wrongly accusing honest people, especially anxious ones who want to be believed.
insights.when_to_use: Any time you are tempted to judge honesty from demeanor: a candidate's interview answers, an employee's account of a missed deadline, a vendor's assurances, a teenager's story about where they were.
insights.worked_example: A store manager suspects a cashier of skimming because he looked away and stammered when asked about a cash shortfall. Remembering that nervousness is a poor lie signal, she does not confront him. She pulls the register logs, asks him open questions about the shift, and finds the shortfall came from a refund keyed in twice by a different employee. At home, a father who feels sure his daughter is lying about finishing homework because she will not look up from her phone asks to see the assignment instead of accusing her.
common_mistakes: Trusting your gut because you feel confident or experienced; confidence and expertise add little accuracy.
Treating nervousness, averted gaze or fidgeting as signs of guilt.
Going to the other extreme and assuming everyone lies; most people are honest most of the time and the truth bias usually serves you.
Making accusations before checking facts that can be verified.
situations: Hiring interviews
Investigating a workplace problem
Doubting a teenager's story
Evaluating a vendor's claims

source.citation: Bond, C. F., Jr., and DePaulo, B. M. (2006). Accuracy of Deception Judgments. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 214 to 234 (abstract; results on receiver expertise and truth bias).
source.underlying_research: DePaulo, Lindsay, Malone, Muhlenbruck, Charlton and Cooper (2003), Cues to Deception, Psychological Bulletin 129(1), 74 to 118: 1,338 estimates of 158 cues; liars somewhat less forthcoming, less compelling and more tense, but many behaviors showed no or only weak links to deceit.

insights.confidence_rationale: Large meta-analysis with remarkably consistent results across studies, supported by a companion meta-analysis on cues and later work. Limits: mostly low-stakes lab lies, and the expert comparison rests on about 20 studies (a small, nonsignificant expert advantage cannot be ruled out). It shows that demeanor is a poor guide, not that deception can never be uncovered by gathering evidence.

insights.name: Listen More Than You Look
insights.takeaway: To understand someone, focus on what they say and how they sound compared with usual, and ask follow-ups instead of scanning faces.
insights.explanation: Visible behavior is the least informative channel for judging people. In the deception meta-analysis, judges who could only see a silent video were right about 50.5 percent of the time, essentially chance, while those who could hear the person did better; judgments from audio alone and from transcripts were about as good as full audiovisual ones. The authors suggest the common picture of a liar is mostly visual, so watching invites stereotypes while hearing the content invites more thoughtful judgment. Brief prior exposure to how a person normally talks also helped slightly. Separate experiments by Michael Kraus found that people judged others' emotions more accurately from voice alone than from video or from voice plus face, apparently because attention went to the words and vocal tone. The practical lesson: when you want to understand someone, put your attention on what they say and how they say it, compare it with how they usually sound, and ask follow-up questions, rather than scanning their face and body for tells.
insights.when_to_use: Interviews, sensitive one-on-ones, calls where you need to understand how someone really feels, and video meetings where the face grid pulls your attention away from content.
insights.worked_example: A recruiter used to judge candidates' sincerity by watching their faces on video. She now turns off self-view, looks away from the screen at moments, and listens closely to the substance: whether examples are specific, whether answers fit together, and how the candidate's tone shifts when talking about a former manager. She then asks one follow-up that probes the shift. With a friend who says she is fine after a breakup, a phone call where he can focus on her voice tells him more than a quick glance across a crowded dinner table.
common_mistakes: Staring at faces and posture for clues and missing what is actually being said.
Judging someone you have never heard speak before against an imagined norm rather than their own baseline.
Assuming video always beats a phone call for understanding feelings.
Mistaking this for permission to cross-examine; the goal is understanding, then checking.
steps: Shift attention from the person's body to their words and vocal tone.
Note specifics: concrete details, consistency, and where the voice changes.
Compare with how this person usually talks, if you know it.
Ask an open follow-up about the moment that stood out.
Check anything important against facts or the person's own confirmation before acting.
situations: Interviewing candidates
Checking in on a friend by phone
One-on-one with a struggling report
Video meetings

source.citation: Bond, C. F., Jr., and DePaulo, B. M. (2006), Personality and Social Psychology Review 10(3): moderator analyses on deception medium and baseline exposure.
source.underlying_research: Kraus, M. W. (2017). Voice-only communication enhances empathic accuracy. American Psychologist, 72(7), 644 to 654 (5 experiments, N = 1,772; two published comments followed). Bond and DePaulo report mean accuracy of about 56 percent with baseline exposure, a small gain.

insights.confidence_rationale: The medium effect in the deception meta-analysis is robust across many studies, and Kraus's experiments point the same way for emotion reading, but Kraus is one research program with published commentary questioning its interpretation, and the gains are modest. Listening better improves accuracy somewhat; it does not make anyone a reliable mind reader.

supporting_evidence.note: King reports that relationships are maintained better through voice calls than video, which she says adds distraction, consistent with voice-only research on empathic accuracy.

insights.name: The Liking Gap: You Were Liked More Than You Think
insights.takeaway: Assume a new acquaintance liked you more than you think, and follow up rather than letting self-doubt stop you.
insights.explanation: After talking with someone new, people reliably underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed the conversation. Boothby and colleagues found this gap between strangers in the lab, in short and long conversations, among members of the public at a workshop, and among new college suitemates, where it lasted for several months before closing near the end of the year. Outside observers who watched the videos could see the partners' signs of liking, so the signals were there; people simply discounted them. The cause traced to self-focused, overly critical replaying of one's own performance: people's thoughts about how they came across were more negative than their thoughts about the other person. Shyer people showed a larger gap. The practical takeaway is to correct your gut read after a first conversation upward, and not let a sense that it went badly stop you from following up, suggesting a coffee, or talking to that person again. The limits: the research measures beliefs, not what happens when people act on them, and it does not test a method for closing the gap.
insights.when_to_use: After a networking event, interview, first meeting with a new colleague, first date or meeting another parent at school, when you catch yourself deciding it went badly and that you should not follow up.
insights.worked_example: A new hire has lunch with a teammate from another department and spends the afternoon replaying a rambling story she told and a joke that got only a small laugh. Her instinct is to keep her distance. Remembering the liking gap, she assumes the teammate probably enjoyed it more than she thinks, and the next week she sends a quick note inviting him to the team's Thursday coffee. He says yes and mentions he had been meaning to ask her about her old job. In a personal setting, a parent who chatted awkwardly with another parent at pickup can still suggest a weekend playdate.
common_mistakes: Treating your own replay of awkward moments as evidence of how the other person felt
Waiting for unmistakable proof of liking before following up
Assuming the other person noticed your nervousness as much as you felt it
Overcorrecting into assuming everyone loved you and ignoring clear signs of disinterest
situations: Following up after a networking event
Getting to know a new colleague
Making friends as an adult
After a first date

source.citation: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark (2018), The Liking Gap in Conversations, Psychological Science 29(11), 1742 to 1756, Studies 1 to 5 and Discussion
source.underlying_research: Study 1a (lab dyads, about five minutes); Study 1b (outside observers rated liking from videos and could predict actual liking); Study 2 (negative thoughts about one's own performance mediated the gap); Study 3 (conversations from 1 to 45 minutes); Study 4 (personal development workshops with members of the public); Study 5 (suitemates surveyed five times in a year; gap at the first four time points, not the last; an accuracy incentive did not change estimates). Shyness moderated the gap in Study 1a.

insights.confidence_rationale: Five studies across lab and field samples, an observer study that rules out the idea that no liking signals were sent, a longitudinal study, open data and later extensions by other teams. It concerns perceptions only; the advice to follow up is a direct inference rather than a tested intervention.

insights.name: Stories Nudge, They Do Not Convert
insights.takeaway: Use a story to make your point felt and remembered, but back it with evidence and a clear ask.
insights.explanation: Stories really do move people, but by a modest amount. Across 74 experiments comparing a story with a non-story message, hearing a narrative shifted beliefs, attitudes, intentions and, in the few studies that measured it, actual behavior in the story's direction, with small effects (correlations around .17 to .23). That makes a story a dependable tool for tilting a decision, not a guaranteed winner over data, and it argues against inflated claims such as stories being ten times more memorable or persuasive than statistics. The practical model: use a story to make the point felt and remembered, and back it with the evidence and a clear ask rather than relying on either alone (that pairing is an inference from the small, variable effects, not something the meta-analysis tested). Limits: effects varied with unexplained moderators, the fiction versus nonfiction results were mixed (nonfiction stories moved beliefs more reliably in this data), the behavior estimate rests on only five studies, and outcomes were measured right after exposure.
insights.when_to_use: When deciding how much weight to put on a story in a pitch, proposal, presentation or personal appeal, and when someone tells you a story alone will win the room.
insights.worked_example: A nurse manager wants hospital leadership to approve a new fall-prevention protocol. A colleague advises skipping the data and just telling the story of the patient who fell. She instead opens with that true patient story, two minutes long, then shows the unit's fall rate against peer hospitals and the protocol's cost, and closes with a specific request. When one executive pushes back on the numbers, the story has already made the problem feel real, and the data answers the skeptic. In a personal setting, someone persuading a sibling to update an aging parent's emergency contacts might share what happened to a neighbor, then walk through the specific steps rather than hoping the anecdote alone will prompt action.
common_mistakes: Expecting one good story to overturn strong opposing views
Dropping the evidence entirely because stories are said to beat statistics
Repeating inflated claims about how much more persuasive stories are
Assuming a made-up illustrative story will change factual beliefs as well as a true one
situations: Building a business case
Choosing between a story and data for a presentation
Persuading a family member to act

source.citation: Braddock and Dillard (2016), Meta-analytic evidence for the persuasive effect of narratives on beliefs, attitudes, intentions, and behaviors, Communication Monographs 83(4), 446 to 467
source.underlying_research: 74 studies comparing narrative and non-narrative messages: beliefs k = 37, N = 7,376, r = .17; attitudes k = 40, N = 7,132, r = .19; intentions k = 28, N = 5,211, r = .17; behaviors k = 5, N = 978, r about .23. Medium did not moderate effects.

insights.confidence_rationale: The core finding (narratives persuade, modestly, across all four outcome types) comes from a large meta-analysis in a leading journal and agrees with other narrative meta-analyses. The recommendation to pair stories with evidence is an inference, and the behavior and fiction-versus-nonfiction details rest on fewer studies and secondary reporting.

insights.name: Give First, Make It Personal and Unexpected
insights.takeaway: Give first, making your help personal, meaningful, and unexpected, and never attach a visible hook to it.
insights.explanation: People feel obliged to return what they have received, and they are more willing to say yes to someone they owe. Cialdini's advice is to be the first to give, and to make what you give meaningful, personalized to the recipient, and unexpected; how a favor is given can matter more than its size. In a restaurant field study (Strohmetz and colleagues, 2002), servers who gave candy with the check received larger tips, and the effect varied with how much candy was offered and how it was offered. The ethical line is that the gift should be genuine help, not bait: a favor that comes with a visible hook feels like a transaction and loses its pull.
insights.when_to_use: Building relationships with colleagues, clients or neighbors you will later need to work with; starting a partnership; any setting where goodwill matters more than a single trade.
insights.worked_example: A new account manager inherits a client who has been cool toward the agency. Before asking for a renewal meeting, she reads the client's recent conference talk and sends a short note with two benchmark figures from a study relevant to the client's own project, saying no reply is needed. Weeks later, when she asks for 30 minutes to review the contract, the client agrees and is noticeably warmer. A new neighbor shovels the shared walkway for the elderly couple next door the first snowy morning, without being asked.
common_mistakes: Giving generic, mass-produced favors that feel like marketing
Attaching the request to the gift so it reads as a bribe
Reminding people of what you gave them
Giving only right before you need something
steps: Identify something the other person would genuinely value
Tailor it to them specifically
Give it without an immediate request attached
Let time pass and keep the relationship going
When you make a request, make it independent of the favor
situations: Warming up a cool client relationship
Starting a cross-team partnership
Getting to know new neighbors

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Reciprocation; Influence at Work principles summary
source.underlying_research: Reciprocity norm (Gouldner 1960); Strohmetz, Rind, Fisher and Lynn (2002), Journal of Applied Social Psychology 32(2), candy and restaurant tipping. Percentages quoted in popular summaries of this study differ from each other and are not used here.

insights.confidence_rationale: The reciprocity norm is robust and widely replicated, but the personalized-and-unexpected refinement rests on a small number of field studies, chiefly the restaurant tipping experiments.

insights.name: Show What Similar Others Actually Do
insights.takeaway: Honestly tell people that most similar peers already do the desired thing, and never advertise that bad behavior is common.
insights.explanation: When people are unsure what to do, they look to what others like them are doing. An honest statement that most of their peers already do the desired thing can therefore nudge behavior more than an appeal to benefits. Two cautions matter. First, the reverse also works: announcing that a bad behavior is common (lots of people are missing the deadline, many visitors steal petrified wood) can normalize it; in Cialdini's Petrified Forest study, a sign describing past theft led to more theft than a sign that simply asked visitors not to take wood. Second, the famous hotel towel result, where a peer-norm card beat a standard environmental card, did not replicate that advantage in two German hotels, so expect modest and context-dependent gains rather than a reliable boost.
insights.when_to_use: Encouraging participation in a survey, training, benefit enrollment or policy, when the desired behavior is genuinely common among the audience's peers.
insights.worked_example: An HR manager wants more employees to finish compliance training by the deadline. Her first draft reminder says 'Too many people are leaving this to the last minute.' She rewrites it: '78 percent of your colleagues in operations have already completed the training. It takes about 20 minutes.' Completion rises over the next week. A parent tells a reluctant child that most kids in the class are going to the field trip, which is true, instead of saying no one else complains.
common_mistakes: Complaining publicly that many people are doing the wrong thing
Citing a norm that is not true, or inflating it
Using a reference group the audience does not identify with
Expecting a large effect from a single norm message
steps: Check whether the desired behavior is actually common in the audience's peer group
State the norm with a specific, honest number or description
Choose the closest reference group (same team, same role, same building)
Remove any language that implies the undesired behavior is widespread
Measure the effect rather than assuming it
situations: Writing a reminder for overdue training
Encouraging benefit enrollment
Persuading a child to join a group activity

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Social Proof
source.underlying_research: Goldstein, Cialdini and Griskevicius (2008) hotel towel study; Bohner and Schlueter (2014), PLOS ONE 9(8): e104086, two German hotels, norm messages not more effective than standard message; Cialdini (2003), Current Directions in Psychological Science 12(4), Petrified Forest descriptive versus injunctive signs.

insights.confidence_rationale: Descriptive norm effects are broadly supported, and the warning about normalizing bad behavior has experimental support, but flagship results such as the towel study have failed to replicate their specific advantage, and effects are modest and context-dependent.

insights.name: Establish Credibility Before the Ask
insights.takeaway: Have someone else introduce your expertise before your request, and acknowledge a real weakness, then answer why it matters less.
insights.explanation: People follow knowledgeable, trustworthy sources, but they need to know your credentials before your request, not after. Since praising yourself backfires, Cialdini suggests arranging for someone else to introduce your relevant experience; his firm reports a real estate office where receptionists mentioning agents' years of experience before transferring calls raised appointments and signed contracts (a single field case). For trustworthiness, he recommends mentioning a real weakness early and then showing why it matters less than your main strength. That fits a larger meta-analytic finding (O'Keefe 1999): two-sided messages that acknowledge and then answer the counterargument are more credible and persuasive than one-sided ones, while two-sided messages that raise a drawback and leave it unanswered tend to be less persuasive.
insights.when_to_use: Presenting to a new audience, being introduced at a meeting, pitching a proposal with an obvious weakness, joining a new team.
insights.worked_example: A consultant is joining a client's steering committee for the first time. She asks the sponsor to introduce her with one sentence about the three similar rollouts she led. When she presents her plan, she opens with its main drawback: 'This approach takes six weeks longer than the alternative.' Then she explains why: it avoids the data migration failures that sank the client's last attempt, and she shows the numbers. The committee approves. When recommending a contractor to friends, someone says the contractor is not the cheapest but has never missed a deadline in three jobs, and explains why that matters for a kitchen remodel.
common_mistakes: Listing your own credentials at length
Waiting until after the request to establish expertise
Raising a weakness and then not addressing it
Inventing a trivial weakness that sounds like a humblebrag
steps: Decide which specific credential is relevant to this audience and request
Ask a host or colleague to mention it when introducing you
Identify a real drawback of your proposal
State it early and plainly
Answer it with the strength or evidence that outweighs it
situations: Being introduced to a new committee
Pitching a plan with a known downside
Recommending a provider to friends

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Authority; Influence at Work principles summary
source.underlying_research: O'Keefe (1999), Communication Yearbook 22, meta-analysis of one-sided versus two-sided messages (refutational two-sided more credible and persuasive on non-advertising topics; nonrefutational two-sided less persuasive). Real estate introduction case reported by Influence at Work (single field case). Obedience research (Milgram; Burger 2009 partial replication) is background, not used here.

insights.confidence_rationale: The two-sided refutational advice is backed by meta-analysis; the third-party introduction advice rests on a single field case reported by the author's firm.

insights.name: Ask for Small, Active, Written Commitments
insights.takeaway: Ask for small, voluntary commitments people state or write themselves, like writing their own appointment details, rather than pushing escalation tactics.
insights.explanation: People like to act consistently with what they have already said or done, so a small commitment can make later follow-through more likely. Cialdini advises seeking commitments that are voluntary, active, and public, and ideally written by the person themselves. One NHS study he cites found that having patients write their own appointment details on the card, instead of the receptionist doing it, reduced missed appointments (about 18 percent in that trial). The classic version, the foot-in-the-door technique (a small first request followed by a larger related one), is real but small and inconsistent across studies, and can backfire if the first request feels coerced, so treat the larger escalation tactic with caution and rely mainly on getting genuine, self-stated commitments.
insights.when_to_use: Closing a meeting with action items, confirming a volunteer or a deadline, helping someone stick to a plan they chose.
insights.worked_example: At the end of a project kickoff, instead of the manager summarizing who does what, each person types their own commitment and date into the shared doc in their own words. Deadlines hold better than in past projects. A friend who says she wants to start running texts her training plan to a friend, who replies with encouragement; she is more likely to show up on Saturday.
common_mistakes: Writing commitments on people's behalf
Pressuring people into a commitment, which removes the sense of choice that makes it binding
Using a small yes as a lever to spring a much larger, unrelated ask
Never following up on the commitment
steps: Ask the person what they will do and by when
Have them state or write it in their own words
Make it visible to the relevant people where appropriate
Keep the first commitment small and clearly voluntary
Follow up at the agreed time
situations: Closing a meeting with action items
Reducing no-shows for appointments
Helping a friend stick to a goal

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Commitment and Consistency
source.underlying_research: Martin, Bassi and Dunbar-Rees (2012), Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 105(3), written commitment on appointment cards; Freedman and Fraser (1966) foot-in-the-door; Burger (1999), Personality and Social Psychology Review 3(4), review of foot-in-the-door finding mixed results and reversals.

insights.confidence_rationale: Commitment and consistency effects are supported, but foot-in-the-door is small and moderated, and the appointment card result comes from a single uncontrolled before-and-after study in two health centers.

insights.name: Find a Real Similarity Before Business
insights.takeaway: Spend a few minutes finding a genuine point in common before getting to business, especially over email.
insights.explanation: People say yes more readily to those they like, and liking grows from similarity, sincere compliments and working toward shared goals. Cialdini highlights a negotiation finding: pairs who spent a few minutes on personal conversation before an email negotiation (Morris and colleagues, 2002, Schmooze or Lose) planned for cooperation and reached better economic and social outcomes than pairs who went straight to business. The practical move is to spend a little time finding a genuine point in common before getting to the ask, especially in thin channels like email where rapport is otherwise hard to build.
insights.when_to_use: Before a negotiation, a sales or partnership call, or any email-only exchange with someone you have not met.
insights.worked_example: A procurement lead is about to negotiate a renewal by email with a vendor rep she has never spoken to. She books a 10-minute video call first, learns they both started in logistics and both have kids in the same youth soccer league, then moves to email for the terms. The exchange stays constructive even when they disagree on price. A new parent at a school meeting chats with another parent about a shared hometown before asking them to co-chair the bake sale.
common_mistakes: Faking similarities, which is often detected and backfires
Turning small talk into a lengthy detour that wastes the other person's time
Skipping rapport entirely in email because it feels inefficient
Flattering rather than giving specific, sincere compliments
steps: Before the business part, ask one or two personal questions
Listen for a genuine point in common and mention it
If the exchange will be by email, try for a brief call first
Then move to the substance
situations: Starting an email negotiation
First call with a new partner
Recruiting a fellow volunteer

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Liking
source.underlying_research: Morris, Nadler, Kurtzberg and Thompson (2002), Schmooze or Lose: Social Friction and Lubrication in E-mail Negotiations, Group Dynamics 6(1), 89-100. Similarity-attraction research (Byrne). The 55 versus 90 percent agreement figures on the Influence at Work page refer to a related study and were not verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Similarity and liking effects are well supported in the broader literature; the specific email-negotiation finding comes from a small number of studies with student negotiators.

insights.name: Name What Is Genuinely Unique and What Would Be Lost
insights.takeaway: Say what is genuinely unique about your proposal and what they would lose, but only cite real constraints, never invented deadlines.
insights.explanation: People value things more when they are rare or about to become unavailable, and they respond to what they stand to lose. Cialdini's advice is to go beyond listing benefits: say what is truly unique about your proposal and what the other person would miss by passing on it, including exclusive information. The evidence is weaker than the principle's fame suggests. A meta-analysis (Lynn 1991) found a modest average effect of scarcity on perceived value with large variation between studies, and invented deadlines or fake limited supply are easily seen through and damage trust. Use it only for real constraints: a genuinely limited budget window, a one-time opportunity, a capability no one else offers.
insights.when_to_use: When an opportunity really is limited in time or availability, or your offer has a feature no alternative matches.
insights.worked_example: A program manager is pitching a training partnership. The provider has two remaining cohort slots this fiscal year, and the company's training budget expires in September. She tells the director exactly that, and adds what no other provider offers: instructors who have worked in their regulated industry. She does not invent urgency beyond those facts. A family deciding on a summer program learns that the early-registration price genuinely ends Friday and decides that night.
common_mistakes: Inventing deadlines or limits
Overusing urgency so that every request seems like an emergency
Claiming uniqueness without evidence
Relying on scarcity when the offer itself is weak
steps: List what is truly unique about your offer
Identify any real time or supply constraint
State the constraint plainly with its source
Describe concretely what would be lost by waiting
Leave the decision with them
situations: Pitching a time-limited opportunity
Making the case for a distinctive vendor
Deciding on a program with a registration deadline

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), Chapter on Scarcity
source.underlying_research: Lynn (1991), Psychology and Marketing 8(1), meta-analysis of commodity theory: average effect about r = .12 with significant heterogeneity (figure as reported by later reviews). Influence at Work cites the 2003 Concorde retirement as an anecdote.

insights.confidence_rationale: Scarcity effects exist on average but are modest and highly variable, the supporting examples are largely anecdotes, and misuse is common; the principle is presented here with honest-constraint limits.

insights.name: Check Whether the Trigger Is Real
insights.takeaway: When you feel pulled by a favor, crowd, authority, or deadline, pause and check whether the signal is genuine.
insights.explanation: Each influence principle is a shortcut people use because it usually works: return favors, follow the crowd, trust experts, keep your word, act before something runs out. Cialdini's point is that the same shortcuts can be triggered by fake signals, such as a gift designed to create a debt, invented popularity, borrowed authority, a manufactured deadline, or an inflated first ask designed to be refused. The defense is not to distrust every request but to pause when you feel the pull of a principle and ask whether the underlying feature is genuine. If a favor was a setup, you can treat it as a sales tactic and owe nothing. The same test keeps your own persuasion honest: use the principles only to highlight things that are actually true.
insights.when_to_use: When you feel unusual pressure to say yes quickly, when receiving an unsolicited gift or concession from someone selling to you, and when designing your own persuasive message.
insights.worked_example: A purchasing manager is offered a free analytics audit by a software vendor, followed a week later by a request to sign a three-year contract before 'pricing changes at month end'. He notices two triggers at once, reciprocity and scarcity, and asks whether either is real. The audit was a standard sales offer, and when he asks for the pricing change in writing, the rep cannot provide it. He evaluates the contract on its merits and negotiates a one-year term. Reviewing his own proposal later, he removes a 'most teams already use this' claim he cannot support.
common_mistakes: Assuming you are immune to these pressures
Becoming cynical about all generosity or expertise
Feeling obligated to repay a favor that was clearly a sales tactic
Using fabricated triggers yourself and assuming no one will notice
steps: Notice when you feel an urge to comply quickly
Name the principle you feel pulled by
Ask whether the underlying fact (the favor, the popularity, the expertise, the deadline) is genuine
If it is fabricated, set it aside and decide on the merits
Apply the same test to your own messages before sending
situations: Evaluating a vendor's pressure tactics
Responding to a high-pressure sale
Reviewing your own persuasive message for honesty

source.citation: Robert B. Cialdini, Influence, New and Expanded (2021), defense sections at the end of each principle chapter
source.underlying_research: Synthesis across the compliance literature; the defense advice itself is the author's reasoning rather than a tested intervention.

insights.confidence_rationale: Credible expert guidance grounded in well-documented compliance research; the defensive procedure itself has not been experimentally tested, and the chapter-level structure was not confirmed in the book text this session.

insights.name: The Exchange Model: Influence Without a Title
insights.takeaway: Without authority, treat others as allies, learn their pressures and incentives, and trade what they value for what you need.
insights.explanation: When you need cooperation from people you do not manage (peers, other teams, your boss, clients), you cannot order it, but you can trade for it. Cohen and Bradford's model runs as a sequence. Start by assuming the other person is a potential ally, not an obstacle, and that their resistance has legitimate reasons. Get clear on your own goals and priorities, including what you could give up. Diagnose the other person's world: the pressures they face, how they are measured, what their boss wants. From that, identify which currencies they value and which you can offer. Attend to the state of the relationship, since trust determines how directly you can ask. Then influence through give and take, offering something they value in return for what you need. Most resistance, in this view, comes from the other person's incentives and constraints rather than their character, so understanding their world is usually the turning point.
insights.when_to_use: Getting help from another department, persuading a peer who controls resources, influencing your boss, or leading a cross-functional project where nobody reports to you.
insights.worked_example: A product manager needs the data engineering team to prioritize a pipeline fix, and their lead keeps deferring it. Instead of escalating, she asks him what his team is measured on this quarter; he says platform stability and reducing on-call pages. She realizes the bug she needs fixed also causes a recurring overnight alert. She frames the fix as a stability win, offers her analyst's time to write the test cases, and promises to credit his team in the launch update to leadership. He schedules it for the next sprint. In a neighborhood association, a resident who wants volunteers for a park cleanup first asks the gardening club what they need, learns they want a spot for a plant sale, and offers one at the event.
common_mistakes: Assuming the other person is difficult by nature rather than responding to their incentives
Asking before understanding what they value
Treating the model as cold transactional bargaining, which erodes the relationship
Being vague about what you actually need, so no trade can be designed
steps: Assume they are a potential ally with legitimate reasons for any resistance
Clarify your goal, priorities and what you could concede
Diagnose their world: goals, pressures, metrics, boss, constraints
Identify the currencies they value and those you can supply
Assess the relationship and adjust how directly you ask
Propose a give-and-take that meets both sides' needs, and keep the relationship intact even if this trade fails
situations: Getting another team to prioritize your request
Leading a cross-functional project without authority
Persuading your boss to back an idea
Recruiting help for a community event

source.citation: Cohen and Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (2017), Part II: The Influence Model (Chapters 2 to 7)
source.underlying_research: Social exchange theory and the norm of reciprocity; no controlled tests of the model itself identified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Long-standing, widely taught practitioner framework consistent with robust reciprocity research, but supported by cases rather than experiments. The step sequence is confirmed in the table of contents and a secondary summary, not read in the book text.

insights.name: Pay in Their Currency
insights.takeaway: Offer what the other person actually values, from meaning to recognition to help, and build goodwill before you need it.
insights.explanation: What you can offer in exchange is much wider than budget or favors. Cohen and Bradford group the currencies people value into five kinds: inspiration-related (a chance to do something meaningful or excellent), task-related (resources, help, information, support for their own work), position-related (recognition, visibility to senior people, reputation), relationship-related (being understood, personal support, belonging), and personal (gratitude, ownership, learning, feeling competent). People differ in which currencies matter to them, and paying in a currency they do not value earns little. The authors also stress building credit before you need it: helping, informing and recognizing others routinely, so that when you ask, there is goodwill in the account.
insights.when_to_use: Before any ask to someone you cannot direct, and as an ongoing habit with the colleagues you depend on most.
insights.worked_example: A marketing coordinator needs a busy designer's help with a last-minute campaign. She knows the designer has asked for more visible work and cares about craft (position and inspiration currencies), and that money is not hers to give. She offers to present the campaign with the designer to the VP and to give her creative lead on the hero visual. Over the following months she routinely forwards the designer's best work to leadership with a short note of credit, so later requests land easily. At home, a partner who wants help with a weekend project realizes the other values time together more than a returned favor and suggests doing it side by side with lunch out afterward.
common_mistakes: Offering what you would value rather than what they value
Only trading when you need something, so every offer looks like a setup
Overlooking low-cost currencies such as credit, information and public thanks
Keeping a visible tally, which turns goodwill into bookkeeping
steps: List the people whose cooperation you rely on
For each, note which of the five currency types they seem to care about, based on what they talk about and how they are measured
Inventory what you can offer in those currencies, including recognition, information and help
Give some of it now, before you need anything
When you ask, connect the request to the currency they value
situations: Asking a busy colleague for help
Building goodwill with a partner team
Thanking and crediting peers publicly
Sharing chores with a partner

source.citation: Cohen and Bradford, Influence Without Authority, 3rd ed. (2017), Chapter 3: Goods and Services: The Currencies of Exchange; Chapter 6 on building relationships
source.underlying_research: Reciprocity norm and social exchange theory; the currency categories are the authors' practitioner taxonomy.

insights.confidence_rationale: Credible, widely used practitioner taxonomy consistent with reciprocity research; the five categories are confirmed in secondary summaries and the chapter title in the table of contents, but the taxonomy is not empirically validated as a set.

insights.name: Train the Fear Out With a Structured Practice Plan
insights.takeaway: Reduce speaking fear with a deliberate, repeated practice plan combined with challenging your catastrophic predictions, not one-off tips.
insights.explanation: Fear of public speaking is the most commonly feared social situation, yet it responds well to structured psychological programs. Across 30 randomized trials, people who went through a program (most of them cognitive and behavioral: repeated speaking practice, desensitization, relaxation training, and challenging catastrophic predictions) ended up substantially less afraid than control groups, with a moderate to large average effect. The benefit held at follow-up and on average kept growing slightly after the program ended, consistent with people continuing to use what they practiced. Programs delivered through apps, the internet, or virtual reality did about as well as face-to-face ones, although only seven such arms were tested. The practical takeaway for an ordinary professional is that one-off tips are not the main lever: a deliberate, repeated plan of speaking practice combined with rethinking your fearful predictions is what the strongest evidence supports. Two limits matter. Felt fear dropped more than outward, observable signs of anxiety, so expect the inner shift before others see a change. And the meta-analysis compared programs, not ingredients, so it cannot say which single component does the work.
insights.when_to_use: When speaking anxiety is persistent rather than occasional: you avoid presenting, turn down visible roles, or dread routine meetings for days beforehand. Also when you are coaching a team member whose fear is holding back their career.
insights.worked_example: A product manager who avoids presenting at the monthly all-hands commits to an eight-week plan. She lists speaking situations from easiest to hardest: giving a two-minute update in her own team meeting, asking a question at a town hall, presenting a slide to a peer group, then a ten-minute slot at the all-hands. Each week she does the next step at least twice, writes down beforehand what she fears will happen ('I will blank and everyone will notice') and afterwards what actually happened. By week six her dread before the team update has faded, even though a colleague says she still looks a little tense at the start, which she now expects. She keeps one speaking rep per week after the plan ends. In personal life, the same plan works for someone dreading a wedding toast: rehearse aloud for one friend, then for a small family group, before the event.
common_mistakes: Collecting more tips instead of committing to repeated practice over weeks
Stopping practice as soon as the fear eases, which forfeits the gains that tend to continue afterwards
Judging progress by whether you still look a bit nervous, when felt fear usually improves first
Jumping straight to the most frightening situation rather than climbing a ladder of steps
Treating a severe, life-limiting fear as a self-help project when a clinician could help
steps: Rate how afraid you are of speaking today (0 to 10) so you can track change
List five to eight speaking situations from least to most frightening
Choose a structure: a course, a coached group, a clinician, or a reputable self-guided cognitive behavioral program
Practice the easiest step repeatedly until it feels manageable, then move up one step
Before each rep, write the specific outcome you fear; afterwards, write what actually happened
Keep at least one low-stakes speaking rep a week after the plan ends
Seek professional help if the fear blocks work or daily life, since fear of public speaking can broaden into wider social anxiety
situations: Overcoming a long-standing fear of presenting
Preparing for a first conference talk
Coaching an anxious team member
Getting ready to give a wedding toast

source.citation: Ebrahimi, Pallesen, Kenter and Nordgreen (2019), Psychological Interventions for the Fear of Public Speaking: A Meta-Analysis, Frontiers in Psychology 10:488 (Results and Discussion)
source.underlying_research: 30 randomized controlled trials, 1,355 participants; pooled g = 0.74 post-treatment, g = 1.11 at follow-up, post-to-follow-up change g = 0.20 (0.12 after trim and fill). Earlier meta-analysis: Allen, Hunter and Donohue (1989), Communication Education 38, self-report data only.

insights.confidence_rationale: Preregistered meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials with low to moderate heterogeneity and effects robust against active controls. Caveats: effects on observable behavior and physiology are smaller than self-report, many trials are old with unclear risk of bias and completers-only data, there are some signs of publication bias, and the analysis cannot isolate which component (exposure, cognitive work, relaxation) drives the benefit. The ladder steps are standard exposure practice rather than a protocol tested by this paper.

insights.name: A Retreat Wins a Yes, Not Always a Follow-Through
insights.takeaway: A yes won after retreating from a bigger ask rarely means action, so secure a concrete commitment and follow up.
insights.explanation: The door-in-the-face tactic means making a large request that is likely to be refused and then retreating to the smaller request you actually want. The retreat feels like a concession, and people tend to reciprocate by agreeing to the second ask. A meta-analysis of 35 years of studies found that this reliably but modestly raises verbal agreement (about r = .13 across 78 effects), while its effect on actually doing the thing (showing up, giving, completing the task) was small and not statistically significant (about r = .05 across 39 effects). The effect also shrank in tougher contexts where few people would comply anyway. The practical takeaway: a concession can open a door, but a spoken yes obtained this way is a weak predictor of action, so pair it with a concrete commitment and follow-up. Only open with a larger request you would genuinely welcome, since an inflated first ask that is later exposed damages trust.
insights.when_to_use: When you are about to scale back a request in a negotiation, a volunteer drive, or a resourcing conversation, and when you are judging how much to rely on someone's verbal agreement after you have conceded.
insights.worked_example: A team lead asks a peer manager to lend two engineers for a full quarter. The peer says no. The lead then asks for one engineer for three weeks to finish the integration, and the peer agrees in the meeting. Knowing that a verbal yes after a concession often fades, the lead immediately proposes a name and a start date, sends a two-line confirmation email that afternoon, and books a short check-in for the first day. At home, a parent who scales back from asking a teenager to clean the whole garage to just clearing the bikes area gets a quick yes and then agrees on a specific time (Saturday at 10) rather than leaving it open.
common_mistakes: Treating a yes won through a concession as a firm commitment
Opening with a deliberately absurd first request, which reads as manipulation once noticed
Expecting the tactic to work when compliance is already hard to get; the effect weakens in tough contexts
Using it repeatedly with the same person, who learns the pattern
steps: Make your larger request only if you would genuinely accept it
If it is declined, retreat openly to the smaller request and name it as a scaled-back version
When they agree, convert the yes into specifics on the spot: who, what, by when
Confirm in writing and set a near-term check-in
Judge the tactic by what gets done, not by what was agreed in the room
situations: Scaling back a staffing or budget request
Recruiting volunteers after an initial refusal
Negotiating chores with a teenager
Deciding how far to trust a verbal agreement

source.citation: Feeley, Anker and Aloe (2012), The Door-in-the-Face Persuasive Message Strategy: A Meta-Analysis of the First 35 Years, Communication Monographs 79(3), 316-343
source.underlying_research: Original technique from Cialdini et al. (1975). Meta-analytic estimates: verbal compliance k = 78, r = .126 (significant); behavioral compliance k = 39, r = .052 (not significant). Baseline toughness of donation contexts negatively predicted effect size for both outcomes.

insights.confidence_rationale: Large meta-analysis in a top communication journal; the core contrast (reliable small verbal effect, negligible behavioral effect) is the summary estimate itself. The recommendation to lock in a concrete commitment is my practical extrapolation, and the primary studies are mostly older prosocial requests rather than workplace asks.

supporting_evidence.note: Cialdini presents rejection-then-retreat (reciprocal concessions) as a core reciprocity tactic; the Feeley et al. meta-analysis supplies the correction that it raises verbal agreement (r about .13) far more than actual follow-through (r about .05, not significant).

insights.name: Argue From Their Values, Not Yours
insights.takeaway: Before persuading, learn what the other person values and honestly connect your proposal to those values rather than your own.
insights.explanation: People naturally make the case for a position using the values that persuaded them, which is why their arguments often fall flat, or even offend, with someone whose priorities differ. Moral reframing means presenting the same position in terms of values the listener already holds. In US experiments, conservatives became more supportive of environmental protection when it was framed around purity and patriotism rather than harm, and liberals became more supportive of military spending when it was framed around fairness and opportunity rather than loyalty and strength. The effect appears to work because the listener sees a match between the message and their own convictions, and may read the speaker as someone on their side. Two practical cautions from the review: people rarely do this on their own (fewer than 10 percent did so even when offered a cash prize for persuading the other side), and reframing fails if the link to the value is weak, buried among other arguments, or delivered by a messenger the audience distrusts. The workplace version is simple: before persuading, learn what the other person cares about (cost control, risk, fairness to the team, customers, craft) and connect your proposal to it honestly.
insights.when_to_use: When your proposal is opposed by someone whose priorities differ from yours: a finance leader weighing a culture initiative, an engineer weighing a sales request, a relative on the other side of a political issue.
insights.worked_example: A people-operations manager wants a skeptical CFO to fund a mentoring program. Her own reason is fairness and growth for junior staff, and her first pitch on that basis goes nowhere. Before the second meeting she asks the CFO what worries him most this year; he names turnover costs and key-person risk. She reframes the program as a way to protect institutional knowledge and cut the cost of replacing early-career hires, with a modest pilot and a retention metric. He approves the pilot. At home, someone who wants a fiscally conservative parent to back a local transit measure talks about saving taxpayer money on road repairs and keeping the town's young families close, rather than about emissions.
common_mistakes: Guessing the other person's values instead of finding out
Making a strained or insincere link to their value, which reads as manipulation
Diluting the reframed argument by stacking it with your usual arguments
Expecting it to work when you are seen as an opponent they distrust
steps: Write down why you support the position; notice which values those reasons rest on
Find out what the other person cares about, ideally by asking
Identify a genuine way your position serves that value
Lead with that frame and keep it uncluttered
Check for fit: ask how it lands for them and adjust
situations: Pitching a people initiative to a finance leader
Persuading across functions with different metrics
Talking politics with a family member

source.citation: Feinberg and Willer (2019), Moral reframing: A technique for effective and persuasive communication across political divides, Social and Personality Psychology Compass 13(12), e12501
source.underlying_research: Feinberg and Willer (2013, 2015); Feygina, Jost and Goldsmith (2010); Wolsko, Ariceaga and Seiden (2016); Voelkel and Willer (2019); Kalla, Levine and Broockman (2019, canvassers framing appeals around a value elicited from the resident). Moral foundations theory (Graham, Haidt and Nosek 2009).

insights.confidence_rationale: Multiple experiments across issues support the effect, but much of the base comes from the authors' own labs, effects are modest and inconsistent in some studies, untargeted audiences usually show no change, and the underlying moral foundations theory is debated. Application to workplace priorities (as opposed to political morals) is an extension of the principle.

insights.name: Negotiate Over Interests, Not Positions
insights.takeaway: In negotiation, ask why the other side wants what they ask for, and look for ways both sides' underlying interests fit.
insights.explanation: A position is what someone says they want (a number, a deadline, a yes or no). An interest is why they want it: the worries, needs and goals underneath. Fisher and Ury argue that bargaining over positions locks both sides in, wastes time and strains the relationship, while exploring interests often reveals that the two sides want different things that can fit together. Their best-known example is the Sinai talks, where one side's security interest and the other's sovereignty interest could both be met. To find interests, ask why and why not, treat each side as having several interests, and talk about your own interests openly while staying firm on them.
insights.when_to_use: Any negotiation that has stalled on competing demands: scope and deadline disputes, budget requests, salary and role discussions, family logistics.
insights.worked_example: A product lead insists on a June launch; the engineering manager says September is the earliest. Instead of haggling over a month in between, the engineering manager asks why June matters. The answer is a trade show demo for three key customers. The engineering manager's interest is avoiding a rushed release that pages his team at night. They agree on a polished demo build for June and a general release in August. At home, two parents arguing over whether a child does summer camp or stays home discover that one cares about cost and the other about the child making friends, and they find a cheaper local day program.
common_mistakes: Arguing over the number before understanding the reasons
Assuming the other side's interests are the opposite of yours
Hiding your own interests so the other side cannot help meet them
Asking why in a tone that sounds like a challenge
steps: Write down your own interests behind your position
Guess the other side's interests, then test the guesses with questions
Ask why they want this and why they have not accepted what is on the table
Restate their interests to show you understand them
Look for options that meet the key interests of both sides
situations: Negotiating a deadline with another team
Discussing salary or role scope
Resolving a family logistics dispute

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapter 'Focus on Interests, Not Positions'
source.underlying_research: Integrative bargaining research; De Dreu, Weingart and Kwon (2000, JPSP) meta-analysis finding that cooperative motives combined with high resistance to yielding produced more problem solving and higher joint outcomes.

insights.confidence_rationale: The interests-versus-positions idea is the field's consensus foundation and is consistent with experimental research on integrative negotiation, including information exchange about priorities. The book's own support is anecdotal, but the principle is well supported elsewhere.

supporting_evidence.note: Thompson and Hrebec's meta-analysis of 32 experiments documents the cost of assuming opposed interests, giving research backing to the interests-over-positions principle (sibling extraction from this batch).

insights.name: Separate the People From the Problem
insights.takeaway: Be soft on the people and hard on the problem: acknowledge emotions, let them save face, and speak about yourself.
insights.explanation: Negotiators are people with emotions, egos and differing perceptions, and the relationship easily gets tangled with the substance, so that a concession feels like losing face and a hard stance feels like a personal attack. The authors advise working on the two tracks separately: be soft on the people and hard on the problem. On perception, put yourself in their shoes, discuss each side's view openly, and give them a way to agree that fits their values (face-saving). On emotion, recognize feelings on both sides, let people vent without reacting, and use small symbolic gestures such as an apology. On communication, listen actively and acknowledge what is said, and speak about yourself rather than about them.
insights.when_to_use: Negotiations with people you will keep working or living with; tense talks where the relationship is coloring every point.
insights.worked_example: A procurement manager and a long-time supplier are fighting over a late shipment penalty, and the supplier's account rep is angry about being blamed. The manager starts by acknowledging the rep's frustration and the supplier's good record, lets him explain what went wrong at the port, then turns to the shared problem: how to prevent the next delay and what compensation is fair. The rep agrees to a partial credit and an earlier shipping window. A couple arguing about holiday plans with in-laws uses the same split: first acknowledging feelings, then solving the scheduling problem.
common_mistakes: Making concessions to keep the peace, which rewards pressure
Attacking the person to win the substantive point
Assuming your perception of the facts is the only accurate one
Reacting to an outburst instead of letting it pass
steps: Acknowledge the relationship and any emotions openly
Ask how they see the situation and summarize it back
Describe your own view and its impact on you, not their motives
Reframe the issue as a shared problem to solve side by side
Offer a face-saving path to agreement
situations: Negotiating with a long-term supplier
Resolving a dispute with a colleague
Working through a family disagreement

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapter 'Separate the People from the Problem'
source.underlying_research: Authors' practice; overlaps with research on perspective taking and active listening (not cited here).

insights.confidence_rationale: Widely taught expert guidance consistent with later research on emotion and perspective taking in negotiation, but critics (for example Menkel-Meadow, 1984) questioned whether people and problems can be separated in practice.

insights.name: Invent Options Before You Decide
insights.takeaway: Generate several possible agreements before judging any, trade things each side values differently, and make yes easy for them to defend.
insights.explanation: People often jump to the single answer they came in with, assume the pie is fixed, or treat solving the other side's problem as their problem alone. The authors recommend separating inventing from deciding: generate several possible agreements first, without judging or committing, and only then evaluate. Broaden the options by looking at the problem from different angles, making weaker or partial versions of an agreement, and dovetailing differences: things one side values more than the other can be traded. Finally, make it easy for the other side to say yes by proposing something they can defend to their own boss or family.
insights.when_to_use: When a negotiation looks like a single number or yes/no choice, or when both sides keep restating the same proposals.
insights.worked_example: Two department heads both want the one open analyst position. Rather than fight over it, they spend 15 minutes listing options without critiquing: split the role 60/40, hire a contractor for one team, share the analyst for six months and then review, or have one team fund training for an internal transfer. They then pick the shared arrangement with a review date, which one head can sell to her VP as a pilot. Roommates deciding on a shared car use the same exercise before arguing about who pays what.
common_mistakes: Evaluating each idea the moment it is suggested
Searching for the single right answer too early
Ignoring differences in what each side values, which are the raw material for trades
Proposing something the other side cannot justify to their constituents
steps: Agree to brainstorm without commitment
List as many options as possible, including partial and provisional ones
Identify differences in priorities, timing or risk that could be traded
Evaluate options against both sides' interests
Shape the chosen option so it is easy for them to accept and explain
situations: Splitting a shared resource between teams
Breaking a deadlock in a contract talk
Dividing costs with roommates

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapter 'Invent Options for Mutual Gain'
source.underlying_research: Integrative negotiation research on logrolling and the fixed-pie bias (see Thompson, The Mind and Heart of the Negotiator).

insights.confidence_rationale: Consistent with experimental findings that negotiators miss joint gains when they assume a fixed pie; the book's brainstorming techniques themselves are expert guidance.

insights.name: Anchor the Deal to Fair Standards, Not Pressure
insights.takeaway: Settle conflicting interests using fair outside standards like market value or precedent, yielding to good reasons but never to pressure.
insights.explanation: When interests genuinely conflict, the authors suggest settling on the basis of standards independent of either side's will, such as market value, precedent, expert opinion, cost, or what a court or third party would likely do. Treat each issue as a joint search for criteria, be open to the other side's proposed standards, and yield to good reasons but never to pressure, threats or stubbornness. Fair procedures (one cuts, the other chooses; taking turns; letting a neutral party decide) can serve when no outside standard exists. Their example is a car owner and insurance adjuster settling on a figure by comparing market data rather than haggling.
insights.when_to_use: Distributive issues such as price, salary, cost sharing or deadlines where you need a defensible basis for a number.
insights.worked_example: A designer asked to take a 10 percent pay cut on a contract renewal asks the client what basis they are using. She brings two industry rate surveys and her own record of on-time delivery, and suggests using the median rate for her experience level. The client's procurement team, which needs a justification for its file, agrees to keep her rate and adjust scope instead. In a family, siblings dividing their late parent's furniture use a turn-taking draft order rather than arguing item by item.
common_mistakes: Picking a standard only because it favors you
Treating the other side's criteria as illegitimate without discussion
Giving in to pressure dressed up as principle
Using standards so rigidly that you ignore legitimate interests
steps: Research relevant standards before the conversation
Propose a joint search for criteria
Ask what standard their position is based on
Discuss which standards are most relevant and fair
Yield to good reasons, not to pressure
Use a fair procedure if no outside standard fits
situations: Negotiating a rate or salary
Settling an insurance or refund claim
Dividing shared property

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapter 'Insist on Using Objective Criteria'
source.underlying_research: Authors' practice; critics such as Steinberg (1982) note mutually agreeable criteria can be hard to find.

insights.confidence_rationale: Practical and widely taught, with indirect support from research on fairness norms and justification; not tested as a package, and critics note it can be hard to agree on criteria when stakes and power are uneven.

insights.name: Know Your BATNA Before You Negotiate
insights.takeaway: Before negotiating, work out your best alternative if talks fail, strengthen it, and estimate the other side's alternative too.
insights.explanation: Your BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) is what you will do if this negotiation fails: another job offer, another supplier, doing the work in-house, or simply keeping the status quo. Fisher and Ury argue it is the real measure of negotiating power and the right test for any proposal, better than a rigid bottom line that can make you reject good deals or accept bad ones. Develop it before you negotiate: list what you could do without agreement, turn the most promising ideas into real options, and choose the best. Then improve it if you can, decide whether and how to reveal it, and estimate the other side's BATNA too, since a weak alternative on their side is your leverage.
insights.when_to_use: Before any negotiation where walking away is possible: job offers, vendor contracts, internal resource requests, major purchases.
insights.worked_example: A software engineer with an offer from a startup is negotiating with her current employer for a raise. Before the meeting she clarifies her BATNA (accept the startup offer at its stated salary and equity), estimates the employer's BATNA (backfilling her role would take months during a key launch), and decides the startup offer is genuinely acceptable. Because she is not afraid of no, she calmly asks for a market-rate raise and a project lead role, and gets both. A car buyer who has a written quote from another dealer uses the same logic.
common_mistakes: Negotiating without any alternative in mind
Overestimating a vague alternative you have not actually tested
Treating a fixed bottom line as more useful than a real alternative
Bluffing about alternatives you do not have
Ignoring the other side's alternatives
steps: List the actions you could take if no agreement is reached
Develop the most promising into concrete options
Pick the best one: that is your BATNA
Improve it before or during the negotiation if you can
Estimate the other side's BATNA
Use your BATNA to judge every offer, and walk away when the offer is worse
situations: Negotiating a job offer or raise
Choosing between vendors
Buying a car or house

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapter 'What If They Are More Powerful?'
source.underlying_research: BATNA is a central construct in negotiation research; Galinsky and Mussweiler (2001) found that focusing on alternatives and targets weakens the pull of the other side's first offer.

insights.confidence_rationale: BATNA is the most widely adopted concept from the book and is central in experimental negotiation research; alternatives are consistently linked to bargaining power and outcomes.

supporting_evidence.note: Galinsky and Mussweiler (2001) found that focusing on alternatives and targets weakens the pull of the other side's first offer, supporting the advice to prepare and keep your BATNA in mind (sibling extraction from this batch).

Ury applies the BATNA idea to refusals under the name Plan B: knowing what you will do if the other person does not accept your no lets you say it calmly. Before refusing, he suggests checking three things: whether you have a real interest at stake, the power to back the no, and the right to refuse. Keep Plan B in reserve rather than leading with it, and if the other side pushes, state the consequence you will act on as a respectful warning (information about what you will do), not a threat meant to punish. Not separately tested for refusals.

insights.name: Negotiation Jujitsu: Redirect Attacks Onto the Problem
insights.takeaway: When attacked in negotiation, do not push back; ask questions, invite criticism, recast attacks onto the problem, and name tricks calmly.
insights.explanation: When the other side insists on hard positional bargaining or attacks you, the instinct is to push back, which escalates. The authors advise sidestepping instead: do not attack their position, look behind it for the interests; do not defend your ideas, invite criticism and advice; and recast personal attacks as attacks on the problem. Ask questions rather than make statements, and use silence after an unreasonable proposal. When the other side uses deliberate tricks such as false deadlines or good cop and bad cop, recognize the tactic, name it calmly, and negotiate about how you will negotiate. If direct talks stay stuck, a third party can draft a single text that both sides keep improving (the approach the book credits for the Camp David talks).
insights.when_to_use: When a counterpart is aggressive, stonewalling, or using pressure tactics, in business negotiations or tense family discussions.
insights.worked_example: During a contract renewal, a vendor's sales director says the client team is unreasonable and the price increase is final. The client manager does not argue; she asks, 'Help me understand what is driving the increase.' He cites rising hosting costs. She asks what he would do in her position with a flat budget, then waits. He suggests a longer term with a smaller increase. When he later adds a sudden end-of-day deadline, she says calmly that the deadline seems designed to rush her and proposes they agree on a realistic timeline first.
common_mistakes: Counterattacking, which escalates
Defending your proposal point by point instead of inviting critique
Filling every silence after an extreme demand
Ignoring a manipulative tactic rather than naming it
steps: Pause rather than react
Ask about the interests behind their position
Invite criticism of your own proposal and ask what they would do
Rephrase a personal attack as a problem to solve
Name obvious tactics calmly and propose ground rules
Consider a third party to draft a single shared text if stuck
situations: Facing an aggressive counterpart
Handling a pressure deadline
Breaking a stalemate in talks

source.citation: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes (3rd edition, 2011), chapters 'What If They Won't Play?' and 'What If They Use Dirty Tricks?'
source.underlying_research: Authors' practice and case examples (Camp David one-text procedure).

insights.confidence_rationale: Practitioner guidance from experienced negotiators supported by case examples, not controlled studies. The one-text procedure and negotiating the rules are confirmed in the summary read; the specific jujitsu moves are drawn from general familiarity with the book and were not checked against the text in this pass.

insights.name: Don't Wait for Friendship: Repeated Contact and Shooting Your Shot
insights.takeaway: Seek repeated contact with the same people, assume they like you, and take the initiative to follow up.
insights.explanation: Franco's starting point is that adults who assume friendship will happen on its own tend to become lonelier over time; adult life no longer provides the daily, repeated contact of school. Her prescription has three parts. First, put yourself in situations with repeated contact with the same people (a weekly class, team or volunteer shift) rather than one-off events like networking mixers, because familiarity builds liking. Second, go in assuming people will like you: research on the liking gap shows people underestimate how much new acquaintances like them, and expecting rejection makes people act colder, which then invites rejection. Third, take initiative explicitly: say you enjoyed talking, suggest exchanging contact details, and follow up yourself rather than waiting to be invited.
insights.when_to_use: After relocating, changing jobs, or when your friendship circle has thinned; when you feel awkward reaching out first.
insights.worked_example: A recently divorced father joins a Tuesday-night pickup basketball group instead of going to occasional parent mixers. By the fourth week he recognizes the same faces. After a game he tells one player, 'This has been the best part of my week. Want to grab a beer after next Tuesday?' He sends the follow-up text himself the next day instead of waiting.
common_mistakes: Relying on one-off events where you never see the same people twice
Reading normal first-time awkwardness as a sign you are not welcome
Waiting for the other person to initiate
Giving up after one unreturned message
steps: Join something that meets regularly with the same people
Keep going past the awkward first few sessions
Assume the other person likes you more than you think
Say explicitly that you would like to connect again and exchange details
Initiate the next plan yourself
situations: New in a city
After a divorce or breakup
Friend group scattered after kids or a move

source.citation: Marisa G. Franco, Platonic: How the Science of Attachment Can Help You Make and Keep Friends (G.P. Putnam's Sons, 2022); NPR Life Kit interview (2022); Terp magazine (Fall 2022)
source.underlying_research: Liking-gap research (Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom and Clark, 2018) and mere-exposure research are cited in her advice; the specific study linking belief in organic friendship to later loneliness was not identified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Franco's advice is confirmed in her own words in interviews and rests partly on solid research (the liking gap, repeated exposure). The claim that believing friendship happens organically predicts loneliness was not traced to a primary study.

insights.name: Dynamic Safety: Raise Issues With Friends by Leading With Value
insights.takeaway: Raise issues with friends by first saying you value the friendship, then share feelings, ask their view, and own your part.
insights.explanation: Many people avoid raising problems with friends to keep the peace, but Franco, borrowing from psychoanalyst Virginia Goldner, contrasts two kinds of safety. Flaccid safety means a friendship feels calm because nobody ever brings anything up; it creates the illusion everything is fine while resentment builds and people quietly drift away. Dynamic safety means the friendship feels secure because you have had ruptures and repaired them, so you trust it can survive problems. To raise an issue, start by saying how much you value the friendship, so the friend hears investment rather than attack; describe how you felt using 'I' statements; ask for their experience of what happened; say what you would like going forward; and own your part.
insights.when_to_use: When a friend has repeatedly canceled, said something hurtful, or let you down, and you are tempted to just see them less.
insights.worked_example: A man's oldest friend has canceled on him three times in two months, most recently the morning of a planned hike. Rather than quietly stopping invitations, he calls: 'You're one of my closest friends and I don't want this to turn into distance between us. I felt pretty brushed off when Saturday got canceled. What's been going on for you?' The friend admits he has been overwhelmed with a new baby and embarrassed to say so.
